For some reason, MAGA personalities decided that this very suggestion constitutes a dire threat to their political project. In truth, they’re not wrong about that last part. But this doesn’t make the point they think it does.

items.title: Trump Officials Gave Terrifying Order About Voting Machines
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump has made supposed voting integrity a fundamental component of his brand since the 2020 presidential election. So why did his administration try to hack a voting machine?

Insiders that spoke to ProPublica shared that political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security had asked the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, to covertly obtain a voting machine, break into it, and report back to the White House.

The directive reportedly shocked CISA employees, who felt the request was antithetical to their mission of thwarting potential hackers. Furthermore, staff were concerned by another DHS request that would have restricted CISA from notifying the voting machine companies of their findings.

“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any results they don’t like,” one former official told ProPublica. “This goes against everything CISA represents.”

The request was ultimately not fulfilled, in no small part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation were terminated by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. Eventually the political appointees stopped pressing the issue, according to ProPublica.

Over the course of Trump’s second administration, more than 1,000 employees have been pushed out of CISA—about a third of the agency. But CISA could be on the brink of more devastating cuts: The president’s 2027 budget proposal would shrink funding for the agency by $700 million, a number that could result in another 900 employees getting axed.

Against all democratic principles, Trump has repeatedly attacked the concept of voting and stoked election conspiracies for his own personal gain. He has continually made unfounded claims about voter fraud, pressured state election officials, strong-armed state legislatures to reshape their districts for the benefit of his agenda, and attempted to dismantle mail-in voting—all to remain in power and disregard or overthrow electoral results that he has perceived as less than favorable.

items.title: Alarmed U.S. Officials Secretly Try to Block Trump Election Meddling
items.content_text:
While the Trump administration is gearing up to interfere in November’s midterm elections, federal officials are secretly speaking with state governments and members of Congress on what to do.

The Washington Post reports that about 10 former and current employees with experience in the Department of Defense have been advising states on how to counter President Trump’s efforts under the radar. Some of the people have experience with opposing authoritarian governments overseas.

Two members of the group anonymously spoke with the Post, telling the newspaper that they were not motivated by political affiliation or bias but rather the fear that Trump is trying to damage democracy in the U.S. by undermining election integrity to protect himself and his Republican allies. The group, which also shared documents with the publication, has reportedly consulted with election officials, governors, and members of Congress comprising both Democrats and Republicans across 10 states.

The group is focusing on states and localities where races are expected to be close and could determine which party controls Congress after the midterms. The group is in constant contact with congressional staffers, and at least one state is holding ongoing meetings, according to the Post. In addition to raising awareness, the group is also trying to help states make their election protocols harder for the federal government to exploit.

“All of them have said ‘We’re concerned but we don’t know what to do,’” one member of the group told the Post. “The outcome that we hope for is that states would be prepared for any contingencies should they arise.”

In a statement, the White House attacked the group and claimed Trump is only pushing for stricter election laws.

The Trump administration “is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis.

Trump has continued to fuel election conspiracies and insist that the 2020 election was rigged against him. Administration officials have seized voting machines and ballots, demanded voter rolls from state governments, and taken legal action against Democratic states based on faulty or even fabricated evidence.

The White House has also sought to purge the federal bureaucracy of civil servants it deems disloyal to Trump, especially in federal law enforcement agencies like the FBI. Congress and state officials are right to be concerned about the election: Trump could interfere with the results, skirt or break laws, or outright disavow any losses without fear of legal action.

items.title: Legal U.S. Resident Dies in ICE Detention
items.content_text:
A 56-year-old father of three who died in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention over the weekend was a lawful permanent resident, The Texas Tribune reported Monday.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unconscious in his bed Saturday morning at the Rio Grande Processing Center. ICE had detained Andrade-Covarrubias on June 26, as he was returning to Texas from Mexico through the port of entry in Laredo. The agency claimed that he’d failed to disclose a prior arrest when applying for his green card in 2004.

Andrade-Covarrubias’s daughter, Estefani Andrade, told the Tribune that her father had disclosed his criminal record during his application process and was still approved. Andrade-Covarrubias was scheduled to appear at an immigration court hearing on November 2.

As of Monday, his cause of death was still unknown.

Andrade told the Tribune that her father had a heart condition, diabetes, high blood pressure, and experienced a lasting toll from being hospitalized with Covid-19 in 2021. She claimed that staff at the processing center had refused to give him his medication, and that when her father began reporting symptoms, such as a persistent cough, difficulty breathing, and tightness across the chest, medical personnel “would just ignore him.”

In a statement, ICE claimed that Andrade-Covarrubias received proper medical care.

A Bloomberg Law investigation concluded that 37 people died in ICE custody between October 2025 and September 2026, marking the fiscal year 2026 as the deadliest in the agency’s recorded history.

Under the Trump administration, ICE has subjected tens of thousands of people—including U.S. citizens, lawful immigrants, and immigrants with no criminal convictions—to overcrowded rooms, unsanitary conditions, and insufficient food and water. Immigrants have been denied adequate medical care and legal counsel, and were even locked in cages.

items.title: CNN Threatens New Legal Action Against Trump Over Media Ban
items.content_text:
CNN is threatening to file another lawsuit against the Trump administration for continuing to deny it access to the Air Force One press pool.

“These efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its news coverage are mistaken, counterproductive, and unlawful,” Ted Boutrous, the network’s outside counsel, wrote in a letter to the Justice Department on Tuesday. He added that CNN “will be forced to pursue additional judicial relief” if Trump does not stop.

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico all moved to sue Trump last month when he dramatically banned the trio of networks from the White House because he didn’t like the way they were covering him. While most access has been temporarily returned as the lawsuits continue in court, the administration has still decided to keep CNN off the presidential jet.

“Those spaces belong not to any particular president or administration but to all Americans, and CNN and other members of the press serve as surrogates for the public when covering the White House,” Boutrous continued. “If these actions persist … CNN will have no choice but to return to the court to defend its rights, and it is prepared to fight as long as is necessary to secure them.”

The White House maintains that its decision to shut out CNN is justified.

“No person and no journalist have a constitutional right to access to the President’s Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities,” it wrote in a statement. “When publications lie, fabricate, and ignore the truth, proximity matters less and they can write their fiction from outside of these secure facilities.”

items.title: Rubio Tells People to “Grow Up” About Trump Meeting Putin and Xi
items.content_text:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio doesn’t see anything wrong with how Donald Trump is interacting with America’s foreign adversaries.

The secretary defended Trump’s intended meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, telling reporters Tuesday morning that the U.S. president’s detractors need to “grow up.”  

“People need to grow up when it comes to foreign policy a little bit. I don’t think it’s unusual for the three most powerful, nuclear-armed nations on earth—for their leaders to communicate with one another,” Rubio said. “I think it makes all the sense in the world.”

Rubio argued that Trump “does not consider talking to someone to be a concession.”

“For example, how are you going to reach a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine if you don’t talk to Russia and Ukraine? You have to talk to them, right?” Rubio continued. “That’s the bottom line of diplomacy and negotiation.”

“Frankly, I think if there’s an opportunity … to have a conversation about things like arms control, that would be a very positive thing for the world,” he said. “I think the world is a safer place when the leaders of the world are at least communicating with each other.”

Trump mused Monday that he would be open to an unprecedented three-way meeting with Xi and Putin regarding nuclear weapons and disarmament. 

“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it. I’m sure we’d talk about other things like trade too.”

But the optics of Trump’s latest encounters with China and Russia have leaned more toward kowtowing than communicating. Last year, Trump had the U.S. military literally roll out a red carpet for Putin during his first visit to the U.S. in more than a decade. Trump did the same for Xi last month, when service members were filmed on their hands and knees picking and brushing imperfections out of the carpet fibers.

items.title: Did Trump, 80, Wave at and Salute No One on the White House Grounds?
items.content_text:
Editor’s note: This article has been updated to reflect new information about whom Trump might have been waving at.

Was President Donald Trump waving at empty space?

A video of the president departing for Kansas Monday afternoon appeared to show him wandering off across the White House’s newly renovated helicopter pad, waving, saluting, and bowing as if he were interacting with a crowd of onlookers. When the camera panned out, however, it seemed that there was no one in the vicinity.

From another angle, Trump can be seen dragging his right leg and patting it as he approaches Marine One. He suddenly stops walking and starts waving seemingly to no one. Meanwhile, his aides approach from an entirely different direction.

Photos indicate that Trump may have been waving at construction workers working on the ballroom. It is unclear if those workers realized the president was saluting him or acknowledged him in return. Trump said nothing at the time to clarify to whom he was waving.

Before the photos surfaced, users on X speculated that the president might’ve been hallucinating or waving at his reflection. Although that does not appear to be the case in this instance, there have been many examples of strange behavior by Trump that suggest cognitive decline. Since returning to office, the president has often appeared to lose track of his thoughts, his whereabouts, and even his grasp on the English language.

items.title: Texas’s Biggest County Shatters Early Voting Records
items.content_text:
Harris County, Texas—Texas’s most populous county, which Kamala Harris won in 2024 with 52 percent of the vote—broke its early voting record on Monday, eclipsing the previous mark by a whopping 41,000 votes.

More than 104,600 people in Harris County voted in person on Monday, the first day of early voting in Texas, according to the county’s elections department. That breaks the previous record set in 2018, when 63,188 votes were cast and Democrats went on to recapture the House.

While Monday’s turnout isn’t necessarily indicative of a Democratic advantage, the broken record indicates that Texans have been strongly compelled to participate electorally by any number of factors, which could include affordability, ICE raids, and President Trump’s war on Iran.

“The coffee that I buy two years ago was $12 for a big can, and now it’s $25 for the same thing, it’s ridiculous,” one voter told KPRC-TV’s Sandy Torres.

“[The] cost of living is way too high, war in Iran, our support to Ukraine,” said another.

“Thirty years of one party dominating the state; it’s time to get the other guy’s chance,” said one more.

This comes ahead of one of the most contested Senate races in the country between Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico—a contest that could turn the state blue for the first time in over three decades.

This positive development also comes less than a week after voting rights groups sued the Texas Department of Public Safety over a “glitch” that caused 600,000 Texans to have their voting registration delayed.

Early voting is open for 11 more days in Harris County.

items.title: Trump Warns America Will Burn if Republicans Lose This Election
items.content_text:
President Trump is claiming that the U.S. will burn like France if Democrats triumph in November’s midterm elections.

At a rally in Park City, Kansas, Tuesday, Trump referenced the student protests in France, using anti-immigrant bigotry and Islamophobia to try and scare Republicans into turning out over the next two weeks.

“Globalist left-wing have treasonously imported millions and millions of third world migrants who are totally incompatible with the West, and they are incompatible with Western values. They despise everything about France, and they’re destroying that country, and we’re not going to let that happen to this country,” Trump said during his speech. Despite interruptions by protesters, the crowd broke into applause at Trump’s words.

“When you see burning steeples and raging fires in ⁠France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America,” Trump added.

Trump is only in Kansas because the Republican Party is polling historically low, putting normally safe candidates in jeopardy thanks to his own bad economic policies and an ill-advised war he started. Republican Senator Roger Marshall was expected to coast to victory in the state, but is now polling neck and neck with Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton.

Trump’s fearmongering over the invented specter of riots is a desperate effort that isn’t likely to sway any voters on the fence, who can plainly see skyrocketing fuel prices and inflation with their own eyes. Besides, if Republicans lose big, which side of the American political divide, based on recent history, is more likely to violently protest?

items.title: JD Vance Forced to Acknowledge Trump Doesn’t Really Like Him
items.content_text:
Vice President JD Vance isn’t so sure that the president will have his back in the 2028 election.

The 42-year-old is theoretically supposed to be Donald Trump’s right-hand man and political successor. Yet nearly two years into Trump’s second administration, the two still aren’t on the same page. In a sit-down interview with conservative commentator Mark Halperin on Air Force Two Monday, the vice president didn’t seem so confident that he would definitely obtain Trump’s endorsement.

Halperin posed two questions to Vance: first, if he planned to run for president, and second, if he would “definitely” obtain Trump’s endorsement.

“I’ll tell you Mark that I’m focused on the midterm elections and I want to get as many good Republicans elected in early November as possible,” Vance said.

“Look, I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028, I really haven’t focused on it,” he continued. “You and I have talked about that. Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me.”

“Right away? Right at the beginning?” pressed Halperin. “In other words, the day you announce. He’d endorse you, right?”

“I don’t know, man, I haven’t talked to him about it,” Vance laughed.

“It would be kind of weird though if you said, ‘Mr. President, I’m going to run,’ and he said, ‘Let me think about it,’” Halperin said.

But Vance equivocated.

“No, it wouldn’t be weird,” Vance said. “I think I’d get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race. And because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what, we need to let this race play out and not preemptively prejudge the results.’”

“Sometimes media scrutiny, pressure, policy goals—” Vance continued before Halperin interjected that he “might be horrible at it.”

“I would be terrible at it,” Vance said. “So I don’t know, having never spoken to the president about this, I can’t speak to his psychology on it. But my attitude is, if I run, I think the president will endorse me. But I also haven’t talked to him about it.”

items.title: Dems and GOP Differ in One Big Way When It Comes to Cash
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

Dems and GOP differ in one big way when it comes to cash

With just two weeks to go until the midterm elections, competitive races are blowing through cash at unprecedented rates. “This is a whole new world, even in the post-Citizens United era,” said Jake Grumbach, a professor at UC Berkeley, about the amount of money raised and spent in the 2026 cycle. More than $15 billion has already been raised, and AdImpact predicts ad spending will hit a record-shattering $11.6 billion.

So far, Democratic candidates in the most competitive races have raised the most money. In some races, the difference is massive: In the Georgia Senate contest, Senator Jon Ossoff has outraised his competitor, Representative Mike Collins, by more than a factor of 10. But add super PACs and party spending into the mix, and suddenly Republicans have the advantage. “Republican megadonors and the super PACs they’re funding are more than making up that gap, and in our system, money matters,” said Eric Petry, counsel in the Brennan Center’s elections and government program. “It’s helping to keep Republicans in some of these key states, key races, competitive.”

Elon Musk is one such Republican megadonor. Musk, the richest person in the world, has poured more than a quarter of a billion dollars into super PACs and Republican groups. Over the summer, Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP’s PAC for Senate candidates. That single donation was more than the Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC raised from all its donors during that quarter.

The flood of money from wealthy donors like Musk has made this a uniquely expensive election. “In the past, it’s typically been not complete parity between Democratic and Republican candidates, but by and large, the two parties have kind of raised and spent relatively equal amounts,” Petry explained. “So far this election cycle, Republicans are on track to dramatically outspend Democrats in a way that we just really haven’t seen before.”

Super PACs like Fairshake, which is aligned with the cryptocurrency industry, and AI-focused Leading the Future, which is backed by tech giants like OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale, have also spent millions to support their preferred candidates and oppose those they see as hostile to their agendas. Experts worry that this unbridled industry spending will ultimately affect the legislation that Congress pursues, particularly now, when Americans want to see the AI industry regulated. “When you’ve got major tech titans spending just gobs of money to influence the political process, that sends a real message to members of Congress to think twice about how they’re approaching these issues,” said Michael Beckel, the director of money in politics reform at Issue One.

PAC money has been a lifeline to Republicans like Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, who has raised far less than his opponent, James Talarico. Between July and September, the GOP’s main Senate super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, raised a record $272.9 million, about $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart. In turn, the Senate Leadership Fund funneled $158 million into Texas PAC, which backs Paxton.

Republicans have also benefited from a June Supreme Court decision that struck down limits on the amounts that parties could spend in coordination with candidates. National parties, like the Republican National Committee (RNC) and the Democratic National Committee (DNC), can accept much larger donations than individual candidates can, and they can now coordinate their spending of that money with their preferred candidates. At the end of August, the RNC had more than seven times the amount that the DNC had in cash on hand, and the June decision made that advantage all the more powerful.

“Both parties feel like they’re in a political fundraising arms race that they don’t want to fight with one hand tied behind their back, and so they’re using every weapon available,” Beckel said. That’s led Democrats to engage in some strategies that others find unsavory, such as constant spam texts asking for donations and an embrace of their own megadonors like George Soros. (He and his family have  given $103 million to support Democrats this cycle.)

Whether Republican spending is enough to counter the mounting blue wave remains to be seen. But no matter the outcome, experts say, this election should change how we think about money in politics. “This election cycle is really kind of shining a spotlight on just how unequal our campaign finance system has become,” Petry said.

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

Josh Turek had a busy weekend in his campaign for Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat, knocking on doors with former Senator Tom Harkin. Talking to the Iowa Capital Dispatch’s Robin Opsahl, both politicians argued that they don’t see Iowa as an inherently red state: “I just think that a lot of Iowans felt—rightfully so—that people maybe in both parties were not really paying attention to their basic needs,” Harkin told Opsahl. “They then sort of said, ‘Well, we’ll try something new and maybe flashy, like Trump.’” Turek added: “I think that Iowans, more than almost any other state, they vote for the person, not just the party.” He contends that Trump “accurately identified the problem” that Iowans face, with lots of talk on the campaign trail about bringing prices down. But then he did “the opposite.”

Turek has been polling neck and neck with Republican Representative Ashley Hinson so far—some polls putting one a couple points ahead, some the other. Democrat Rob Sand, who is running for governor, by contrast has consistently polled between four and 12 percentage points ahead of Republican Zach Lahn. Newsweek’s Anna Skinner on Monday tackled the question of why Turek seems to be lagging behind Sand right now. One big factor that experts identified was name recognition—not just for Turek and Sand but for their opponents. Many people don’t know who Lahn is, which gives Sand an advantage. Turek’s opponent, Hinson, on the other hand, is much better known, since she currently holds one of the state’s four seats in Congress, while Turek as state legislator represents a “district on the far western part of the state,” University of Iowa professor Timothy Hagle told Skinner.

Elsewhere:

  • A new Washington Post/ABC News poll finds, alongside the usual dismal Trump approval rating, that 66 percent of likely voters think the president “is using the presidency to enrich himself, up from 56 percent last fall.” Also of note: For the first time since this poll began in 2014, more voters trust Democrats than Republicans to handle the economy—but that’s only 40 percent of people trusting Dems versus 33 percent trusting Republicans. A more useful way to think about this might be that voters think neither party is especially good at managing the economy!

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

On Wednesday at 10 a.m., the Brookings Institution hosts “AI on the ballot: Data centers and the 2026 midterms,” an in-person and online conversation with Elham Tabassi, Representative James A. Himes, Kyle Chan, Anthony F. Pipa, Mark Muro, Thomas Wright, Valerie Wirtschafter, and Sanjay Patnaik, probing “how decisions about where AI is built and how it is used have become part of the choices facing voters this fall.”

Government watchdog Public Citizen releases a report quantifying the strangeness of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s alliance with the Trump administration. In May 2025, Public Citizen notes, the Trump admin published a “MAHA report” on the dangers of various environmental contaminants. Yet “for 20 of 21 environmental chemical substances that the MAHA report focused on,” Public Citizen notes, “the administration has either moved toward loosening regulations that protect public health (nine chemicals), done nothing (ten chemicals), and endorsed one chemical’s use despite its links to cancer.”

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Political Trivia Question of the Day  

For a few days in October 2008, Ashley Todd seemed like she might loom large in that year’s election. But her story turned out to be false. What did she allege happened to her, and what was the bizarre tell that she was lying? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

* An earlier version of this piece misstated the tool used to create the charts.

items.title: Trump Goes Crazy Online After Judge Hammers Him on Golf Course
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump went on a late-night posting spree about debris and damage in his latest temper tantrum about East Potomac Park.  

“Here are pictures of Trash Island for the Judge to study. This is just a small area, and better than some!” Trump wrote on Truth Social overnight Monday, referring to a heavily overgrown area at the center of the course where the National Parks Service had already begun to fell dozens of trees. 

The president shared photographs of abandoned wooden pallets, construction equipment, large bins, and trucks for tree removal. It wasn’t immediately clear whether the debris was from the president’s stalled efforts to transform the public park into a high-end, exclusive golf course. 

He also shared images of damaged iron fences along the course and waterfront. “Collapsing Sea Wall—Very dangerous to one’s health!” Trump wrote, including a photograph of a fence that had been nearly swallowed by the Potomac.

Last week, District Judge Ana Reyes blocked the government from felling hundreds of trees at East Potomac Golf Links, and tore into the Trump administration lawyer for claiming that tree removal is not part of the president’s renovation plans. The Department of Justice demanded that she step down, claiming that her outburst proved she was biased against the government. The judge refused, sending Trump spiraling on social media.

Trump’s posting may have already landed him in trouble. At a hearing Monday, the preservation group mounting the legal challenge against Trump’s federal takeover of the course introduced the president’s own Truth Social post as evidence that the government plans to proceed with renovations “IMMEDIATELY!”

items.title: Trump’s FBI Killed Bribery Probe Into Lindsey Graham and James Clyburn
items.content_text:
The FBI was investigating South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham and Democratic Representative Jim Clyburn for a massive pay-to-play bribery scandal involving a Hawaiian naval defense firm. Then the FBI eliminated the team working on the case upon President Trump’s return to office.

New reporting from ProPublica details the dealings of the South Carolina politicians with Navatek executives, including CEO Martin Kao, who told the FBI that he was exchanging campaign donations and gifts for millions of dollars in naval contracts.

In March 2020, the late Senator Graham met with Navatek lobbyists at Charlie Palmer Steak in Washington, D.C, and made a deal to give a $10 million government contract to Navatek in exchange for $100,000 in campaign donations, on top of the $40,000 he charged just for the meeting, according to Kao.

“This is how much I want, and how much I am going to give you,” Graham allegedly told Kao.

Clyburn, one of the highest-ranking Democrats in the House, also met with Navatek leaders—and asked them to match Graham’s campaign gift of $100,000 in exchange for political favors. Fellow South Carolina Representative Joe Wilson, a Republican, also allegedly made cash-for-contract dealings with Navatek.

Kao was eventually arrested for campaign finance violations in September 2020 and confessed to federal agents that Navatek’s entire business model relied solely on bribing public officials in exchange for government contracts. The agents working on the case told their superiors their investigation could eventually include the lawmakers involved, but they were fired as the Department of Justice took revenge on the public corruption team, which previously investigated Trump.

This reporting from ProPublica is a continuation of its investigation into Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins, who also received hundreds of thousands of dollars from Navatek in exchange for tens of millions of dollars in federal defense contracts. Collins’s PAC received $150,000 from Kao right after their own D.C. restaurant meeting in 2019, and two months later, Kao informed Navatek that Collins committed to giving it $32 million in naval contracts.

This had the potential to be one of the biggest political corruption scandals of the modern era, a tangible exposé of just how much influence lobbyists actually have in Washington and how eager our self-interested politicians are to take money from them. And the FBI knew that. But as soon as Trump returned to office in 2025, the case was killed. This move inadvertently prevented a bipartisan whale of a corruption scandal from fully coming to light. And while Kao remains in jail, none of the powerful senators the FBI was investigating have faced any kind of repercussions—thanks to Trump. The team can’t even file a new case.

“You gotta hand it to Trump: he holds the consistent position that, Republican OR Democrat, bribery is not a crime,” journalist Matthew Chapman wrote on X. “He’ll cook up any number of bogus charges to take down his political enemies. But he’ll never go after bribery, even if it’s his enemies doing it.”

Kao has made political donations to dozens of politicians from both parties, including Joe Biden, Dick Durbin, Jeanne Shaheen, and Tulsi Gabbard. Clyburn, Graham, and Wilson’s offices all deny Kao’s quid pro quo allegations.

items.title: Trump Casually Tosses Out a Slur in Attempt to Defend MAGA Senator
items.content_text:
President Trump tried to defend Republican Senator Roger Marshall on Monday night at a rally in Park City, Kansas, but ended up using an antisemitic slur in the process.

“[Marshall] was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request strongly money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to by law go after these people, and they made it, like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” Trump said in a speech to the crowd.

The term refers to a Jewish character in Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice who is portrayed as a cunning moneylender, fueling stereotypes about the Jewish people. In a guide for educators, the Anti-Defamation League states “Shylock, and by extension, all Jews, are presented as money-hungry, conniving, and cruel.”

Trump used the term in a speech last year about a bill he was trying to pass, distinguishing between respectable bankers and exploitative ones.

“No going to the banks and borrowing from in some cases a fine banker, and in some cases Shylocks and bad people,” Trump said at the time. Following the event, when reporters questioned him about its antisemitic origins, Trump said he had “never heard that.”

Marshall, who was a doctor before entering politics, is under fire for suing hundreds of patients over unpaid medical bills, even pursuing criminal charges over debts as little as $101. His record has given Democrats an opening in the normally safe Kansas Senate seat, with Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, a pastor, seizing the opportunity and polling neck and neck with Marshall.

“There are 2,000 verses in the Bible that speak to caring for the poor,” Hamilton said at a debate with Marshall last month. “This is not happening under this man.”

items.title: Transcript: Trump Hits Brutal Poll Low—and MAGA Finger-Pointing Erupts
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the October 20 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

We’ve got tons of new developments in the battle for Congress. New polls show Donald Trump cratering and the Democratic lead growing. The GOP leaks of panic are growing more humiliating for the president. And Trumpworld is responding to all this in a way that some Republicans call shocking.

We think all signs are that Trump and his aides are already planning to blame a big loss on everyone but him, and we think that would be bad for the country in terms of what’s coming next. So we hope Democrats won’t let them get away with that.

We’re talking about all of it with Madison Andrus, a senior operative overseeing House races for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. She’s got some new polling to share, as well. Madison, thanks for coming on.

Madison Andrus: Thanks for having me Greg. It’s really great to be back on again.

Sargent: Well, the new Washington Post poll has Trump’s approval at a record low of 33 percent, with 66 percent disapproving. The Post has Democrats leading in the generic ballot matchup by eight points, 52–44. The new NBC poll finds Trump’s approval at 34 percent and Democrats leading in the generic matchup by 10 points, 55–45.

Madison, it’s clear that Trump’s approval is now dropping into the low 30s, and the Democratic lead in the generic ballot matchup is growing. Do you think Democrats are up by 10 points in the generic matchup right now?

Andrus: We are seeing in Trump plus 10 districts all across the country that Democrats are either leading or well within striking distance. You know, looking over to North Carolina with Jamie Ager, just an incredibly well-run campaign with a great candidate who’s a part of his community, and in a Trump plus 10 district. And we are feeling really good and confident about our odds there.

And so I think that there are a lot of districts all across the country, you know, that we’ve had on our map for months and months, if not years. And people thought we were crazy to kind of be going into these traditionally red areas and red districts. And now we are just a couple of weeks away from the election, and we see that it’s really paying off.

Sargent: I want to come back to that, but let’s talk about Jamie Ager in North Carolina’s 11th district for a second. It’s one of the ones I’m really watching closely. This is in western North Carolina, the western tip.

It’s in Appalachia. This is really heavy-duty Trump country. It does have Asheville, but it’s very rural in a lot of stretches. And like I say, Appalachia, Trump country. This is a place where you guys really think you’re going to win?

Andrus: Yeah, we feel very good about what is happening in western North Carolina. Just a couple of days ago, there was a huge, huge rally that Jamie Ager put on in North Carolina 11. Over 3,000 people came out to see and hear from Jamie Ager.

JD Vance is actually in that district today, and judging from the photos that I saw, he could barely pull together 30 people to come and see him.

Sargent: Well, that’s pretty striking that they’re sending JD Vance to North Carolina’s 11th district.

Let’s talk about some of these Republican leaks. They’re really off the charts now. Republicans leaked to Politico that there’s a new level of panic over their internal polling in the House races. A growing number of Republicans blame Trump directly for this situation.

And one House Republican blames GOP leaders for being too slow to deliver reinforcements to safer seats that are now at risk. This Republican says: “The leadership at the NRCC is living in a bubble. We’re getting killed out here.” The NRCC is, for folks who don’t know, the counterpart to the DCCC.

Madison, that strikes me as interesting. Has there been, like, a sudden deterioration in these safer seats? Can you give us a few examples of where you’re seeing that, if you are?

Andrus: I don’t think that this is a sudden deterioration. It feels like Republicans have just finally opened their eyes to what folks all across the country are feeling. They started out this cycle by gutting Medicaid, by nearly a trillion dollars, cutting Medicaid. They are cutting food assistance benefits, they’re backing this war in Iran.

Gas prices are up all over the country, diesel fuel hitting over $6 in many parts. You know, this is the reality that working families in America have been facing for over a year now. This is not a sudden shift. It just feels like finally, when they are actually staring down their election, they’re finally waking up, and it’s just too late.

Sargent: What are some of these districts that are really on the outer tiers looking like? I mean, these are places maybe where they haven’t really been on people’s radar at all, but now that Trump is just continually deteriorating the way he is, all of a sudden these outer-tier places are within play. Can you talk about a few places like that?

Andrus: Yeah, we talked about North Carolina 11, but we’re seeing it in so many other places. Kind of bringing us back down to Texas, in Texas 15 with Bobby Pulido against Monica De La Cruz—everybody’s been really talking about Bobby Pulido for a while, but folks were really questioning if a Democrat could win in this district that Trump won by a fairly large margin.

And what we’ve seen in the last two weeks is, absolutely he can. And even Monica knows this. When Mike Johnson was there just a couple of days ago, Monica was begging people not to believe the polls, because even their numbers are that bad for them.

We’re seeing over in Florida 25 with Jared Moskowitz against Scott Singer, Republicans are having to dump tens of millions of dollars into a district that was supposed to be an easy pickup for them. And so I think what we’ve clearly seen is that these gerrymandering attempts have backfired. And as we get closer and closer to Election Day, we are just seeing Republican chances in these districts absolutely crater.

Sargent: Well, there’s another development involving money. One Republican operative tells Politico this: “No one in the world expected that the Senate would need as much money as they did. All of this money that was expected to go to the House for the most part is now being wasted on the Senate because they fucked up so bad.”

So Madison, there you have it. House Republicans blaming Senate counterparts for overconfidence and sucking up the resources they want. But what I don’t get about this, and maybe you can shed light here, is, aren’t House Republicans currently outspending House Democrats right now, when you put together the candidates’ war chests with the national group spending? What’s the situation there?

Andrus: Look, there’s no doubt that there is a ton of money flying around everywhere. And that was what people had said about Republicans pretty much this entire cycle, is that they’ve got this huge war chest and they’ve got all this money.

And what we’ve seen in the last couple of weeks is that, you know, there’s a few things that money can’t fully buy. And we’re seeing that elections are one of them, when people are in just such a rough spot economically. Any money that they are pouring in is not actually changing the fact of the matter on the ground.

Sargent: Right. Although I will say, I pick up some angst from Democrats about the money. What I tend to hear from Democrats is that Republicans are spending so much now, like with Elon Musk’s millions, MAGA Inc.’s millions. They kind of say this is really uncharted territory, like no one feels confident about what the results will be of all the spending, because it’s just such a crazy amount. Is that an unreasonable fear?

Andrus: Yeah, I mean, we are not taking any of this for granted. Very recently we sent out a memo to donors saying that we wanted to make sure that we had the resources needed to fight, especially in kind of some of these outer districts, like in Florida 7 and in North Carolina 9.

And so we are still, you know, 15 days out from the election, we are still raising money to make sure that we are putting all of our candidates, all of our incumbents, in the best spot possible for November.

Sargent: So here’s something else that’s remarkable, as well. Trump’s super PAC officials are now telling Politico that they can’t really help embattled Republican incumbents and candidates all that much.

These officials are telling the Republican candidates that it’s on them to close on a positive message and tell voters what they will deliver to voters once they’re in office. This has left Republicans shocked, according to Politico.

So Madison, I mean, what’s surprising about this is how Trumpworld is just kind of washing its hands of the situation.

Andrus: They have not delivered in two years. As I mentioned, gas prices are up, the cost of health care is up, the Medicaid cuts endangered rural hospitals all over the country. They have no message on what they are going to deliver, because it has been a string of broken promises from day one with this Congress.

Sargent: Well, there’s more leaking coming from Republicans who are absolutely prepared to blame Trump. One GOP operative working on many races tells Politico: “He’s constantly been distracted and not focused on what the voters care about. It’s insane.”

That is really sort of a remarkable development that I don’t really know what might be a parallel in recent history—the degree to which Trump is just sort of out there, you know, talking about the ballroom, talking about his vanity projects, talking about what he’s doing next in the Capitol, a golf course now that he’s doing, and at the same time saying affordability’s a hoax and so forth.

But it sure looks to me like the situation that these Republicans are in, incumbents and candidates alike, is dictated wholly by the failures of Trump’s agenda, and that that’s just front and center in people’s minds. Right?

Like, so maybe they don’t pay close attention to Trump’s craziness day in and day out, but they are keenly aware that Trump is in charge, and that Trump is responsible for the situation in their daily lives. Is that something you see very clearly?

Andrus: That’s definitely something we’re seeing on the ground, is that voters are holding House Republicans responsible for co-signing this disastrous agenda that is just leading to higher costs across the board.

It’s higher prices at the grocery store, higher prices at the gas station, higher prices at the doctor’s office. And folks are really holding Republicans accountable for these failures of that agenda.

Sargent: So you have some new internal polling to share. This is in Texas’s 28th congressional district, where Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar is the incumbent. The new DCCC poll has Cuellar up by 54–34 over Republican challenger Tano Tijerina.

The poll has Trump’s approval at 34 percent to 57 percent disapproving. That’s 23 points underwater in a district that Trump carried in 2024 by over 10 points. Madison, is that what you found? And can you explain why you see it as significant?

Andrus: Yeah, these are just some really shocking and impressive numbers that we are seeing coming out of South Texas. And what’s interesting about this is that we’ve actually been hearing for months that Republican internal polling was showing some pretty equally horrendous numbers for them.

And putting all of this together and seeing these new numbers that we have, knowing that Republicans were seeing some pretty similar things, it really comes as no surprise why Republicans pulled out of this race and decided that they were no longer going to be funding Tano Tijerina’s campaign against Henry Cuellar, because they were just going to be flushing money down the toilet.

Sargent: Yeah, in fact, we should clarify that the Congressional Leadership Fund, which is, like, the leading Republican super PAC in the House races, recently pulled its funding, as Punchbowl News reported—pulled its funding out of this particular race.

This is a place that was a prize for Republicans, right? Like, they redrew Texas. They were aiming for Henry Cuellar’s district big-time, right? And so that’s a real sign of how much stuff has shifted. Can you talk about that?

Andrus: Yeah. At the beginning of all of this, they were calling Tano Tijerina their star recruit. He was the best of the best that they had, that they were propping up in South Texas. And to just go from, this is our prized recruit, to pulling millions of dollars away from him—I think it goes to show exactly how much Republicans have failed, but also just how strong of a candidate Henry Cuellar is, and how strong of a representative he is.

He has brought billions of dollars back to his district. He’s been a leader on how Democrats are talking about immigration. And he’s one of the most well-known people in all of South Texas.

And so I think we are just starting to see, one, the pipe dream that Republicans were ever really going to take him on fall apart, but also this Texas dummymander. Like you said, Republicans drew these districts, redrew these South Texas districts, to try to flip these seats. And this was one of their prime targets, and we are already seeing complete and utter failure there.

Sargent: Yeah, I mean, a collapse of this magnitude in a place like that is striking. What’s going on in Texas’s 35th district? That’s another one. It’s a Democratic-held seat that Republicans redrew in hopes of winning, right? Like, what’s going on in that place?

Andrus: Yeah. So Texas 35, San Antonio area, that is basically a completely new district now, thanks to the Republican redraw. And we are still seeing really, really great signs coming out of Texas 35. You have the Democratic candidate there, Johnny Garcia, is a longtime sheriff’s deputy. He’s a law enforcement guy who has been a part of this community for years.

I think actually last time we talked, we talked about how I had actually just been down in South Texas with Johnny Garcia, and we were just walking around a couple of neighborhoods. And we stop by a house, and it’s a guy cleaning out his boat to go fishing later that afternoon or that weekend.

And he said to Johnny, I remember you from the sheriff’s office. I’ve never voted for a Democrat before in my life, but I’m voting for you this time.

Sargent: Striking stuff. What races do you predict Democrats will win in South Texas? Which districts?

Andrus: I think we are sweeping the South Texas districts. So that includes holding on to Texas 28 with Congressman Henry Cuellar, as well as Texas 34 with Congressman Vicente Gonzalez. And I think we’re flipping Texas 15. You know, Bobby Pulido is this once-in-a-generation candidate, an incredibly strong candidate for this community.

You just saw, he did the last concert of his career, and just the incredible crowd that came out to celebrate Bobby Pulido 15 days out from the election. The momentum down in South Texas is just something that’s been so incredible to see. And I think we are also going to take home Texas 35. This entire Texas redistricting is shaping up to be probably one of the most embarrassing dummymanders we’ve seen in a long time.

Sargent: Well, that would essentially mean that Democrats are going to win Texas’s 15th, Texas’s 28th, Texas’s 34th, Texas’s 35th. That would be quite a sweep. And that’s what you’re predicting. You’re going to win all.

Andrus: Yep. We are winning all of those.

Sargent: OK. Brass tacks. How many House seats at the end of the day, at the end of Election Day, how many do you think you’re going to end up with?

Andrus: I am not in the business of making those predictions. I’m bad at it. But no, I will tell you, we’re fighting every single day from now until November 3 for every single vote and every single district that we can.

Sargent: Madison Andrus, if you guys sweep South Texas, it’s going to be a seismic event. So I really hope to see it. Thanks so much for coming on. Really great to talk to you.

Andrus: It’s shaping up to be a good night on November 3.

items.title: It Can Happen Here—and Everywhere: Democracy Is in Global Retreat
items.content_text:
According to many political theorists, Brazil did everything right after the corrupt and unpopular Jair Bolsonaro was voted out of office in October 2022. He attempted a January 6–like coup after his opponent was sworn in, which included plans to kill incoming President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, and Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. It failed, and Bolsonaro was convicted of multiple felonies and sentenced to 27 years in prison in 2025—effectively a life sentence for a 70-year-old man.

Then, last week, Brazil basically voted Lula out of office in favor of Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio promises to free his father, remove all the current Supreme Court justices and replace them with his own, and generally carry on the brutal and corrupt policies of his father.  There will be a runoff October 25, but Bolsonaro is widely expected to win it against his 80-year-old opponent.

In short, Brazilians, just like voters in the United States, went into an election knowing full well what they were getting and chose sadopopulism (i.e., an appeal to voters that a candidate will not so much help them as hurt the people they hate) over democracy.

To most external observers, the right-wing demagogue looks like a buffoon selling magical thinking. He claims that he alone can solve everything with austerity, mass incarceration, centering society around conservative religion, and eliminating transgender people from public life. Somehow, people lose sight of the fact that they’re also voting for a justice system that shields the president’s supporters from any legal accountability, no matter what they do, while weaponizing said system against his political opponents.

The supporters of the autocrat ignore these things for a variety of reasons. Some assume that, although Trump is an incompetent idiot, their Trumpist leader will do much better despite embracing the same sorts of policies. Others don’t believe the new leader will be corrupt. Worse yet, many accept the corruption because it will benefit “their” side, even if it doesn’t benefit them personally, or even if it hurts them.

The appeal of sadopopulism is a corollary to Adam Serwer’s observation that the cruelty is the point: For these voters, the main attraction is that the president hurts the people they hate as much as possible.

This phenomenon is not limited to the United States and Brazil. In Germany, the pro-Russian and neo-fascist Alternative for Germany Party, or AfD, is surging, while the center-right coalition led by Chancellor Friederich Merz is increasingly weak and unpopular. This situation resembles the Franz von Papen government that preceded Hitler in the Weimar Republic. Germany will hold its next federal election in January 2027, and the AfD is expected to win a plurality of the votes.

France’s Emmanuel Macron is a lame duck, and his coalition is collapsing too. Despite being convicted of felony embezzlement, Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally party was gifted the opportunity to run in the April 2027 federal elections by the court system, much the way Trump was. As a result, she is widely expected to win.

Both the AfD and National Rally are running on virtually identical platforms: pro-Russia, anti-Ukraine, mass deportations of immigrants, tax cuts for the wealthy, centering conservative religion in society, austerity for the poor, long mandatory sentencing, rejecting the EU and NATO, banning same-sex marriage, and forcing transgender people out of public life.

It’s not just France and Germany, though. Reform UK would be the second-most preferred party if elections were held today (they must be held by 2029). Italy, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Croatia are all in the middle of a democratic backslide toward right-wing autocracy.

There are many overlapping theories as to why democracy is faring so poorly in so many places. Many states suffer from a gap between formal rights and the rule of law, where public resources are coopted for personal wealth and political status. Another potential cause is massive wealth inequality leading to oligarchy and disillusionment among voters. Heightened ideological, ethnic, and religious polarization creates deep distrust in democratic institutions and mainstream political parties, pushing people toward demagogues promising miracles.

Consolidated authoritarian regimes like China and Russia have grown more brazen in domestic repression and more influential internationally through multipolar alliances and economic leverage (such as the 10-member BRICS formed in 2009). Simultaneously, traditional Western democracies have faced internal crises, political friction, and a reduced capacity or willingness to champion global democratic norms. Regardless of the cause or causes, the quantitative evidence shows that this is clearly happening worldwide.

According to the 2026 Report on Global Democracy created by the Varieties of Democracy, or V-Dem, project, which seeks to conceptualize, measure, and provide detailed data on democracy around the world, there are 92 autocracies and 87 democracies worldwide. Seventy-four percent of the global population (about six billion people) live under autocracy, while only 7 percent live in liberal democracies, the worst it has been since 1978. Currently, 44 nations (representing 41 percent of the global population) are becoming more autocratic, while only 18 countries are improving.

Six out of 10 of the new countries in the process of becoming autocratic are in North America and Europe. These include the United States, the U.K., Italy, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Croatia. V-Dem reports that the U.S. dropped from a liberal democracy to an electoral democracy, with its ranking falling from twentieth to fifty-first out of 179 nations amid rapid executive power concentration and attacks on judicial and media checks. Ironically, one of the very few “areas for hope” that the report listed was Brazil’s previous rejection of Jair Bolsonaro.

It is worth pointing out that all these new autocracies are right-wing, conservative movements. There are no Bolshevik or Marxist revolutions taking place; it’s all ethno-nationalism, selling sadopopulism to the portion of the public that feels it is no longer centered by society in an increasingly cosmopolitan world. As much as these people would like solutions, what they want even more is revenge. They want someone powerful to come in and brutalize the people they blame for their perceived loss of special status as “the right sort of person” now that immigrants, brown people, Muslims, and queers are no longer universally considered “the wrong sort.”

When did electing right-wing authoritarians ever work out well? They all seem to wallow in corruption, nepotism, grift, graft, and generally enriching themselves and their top-level cronies at the expense of the population. The law applies only to the everyday person and, of course, applies double to the regime’s political enemies. Let’s not forget the pointless wars that both the U.S. and Russia started and can’t back themselves out of, which threaten them with economic ruin.

Even if they do win these conflicts, the damage to their economies and prestige will linger for decades. Russia just surpassed 1.5 million casualties for the war in Ukraine, and the Pentagon is currently hemming and hawing about how many wounded and killed there have been in the war with Iran.

In the end analysis, it all feels so stupid. People have willingly traded away their say in government, a functioning economy, affordable cost of living and housing, and national prestige and maybe even sent their kids off to war in exchange for making some other people even more miserable than they already are. Incredibly, tragically, there will always be about a third of the population that looks at this trade, in retrospect, and says, “Yeah, it was totally worth it.”

It is hard to imagine, but in just a few years there will be up to a hundred million Americans who look back at Trump’s second term as a “golden age” and will go right back to voting for the next, even more far-right, aspiring autocrat. Sadly, people around the world will also look back at their own prior leaders, like Bolsonaro, Duda, Orbán, Duterte, and even Putin, and regard them as scions of a better, mythical past. This is how fascism keeps coming back repeatedly to haunt the next generation.

items.title: You Can See Everything Is Unexpectedly Heartbreaking
items.content_text:
In an unexpectedly wrenching scene in You Can See Everything, Elizabeth Holmes is posing under bright lights, a series of dots penned on her face. Her hair is scraped back and tucked under a bald cap, and a photographer instructs her to close her eyes and open her mouth, then open her eyes and close her mouth, and so on. The idea is to map each part of her face and body so that when she reports to federal prison the next month, she will leave behind a hologram of herself—an avatar to talk to her fiancé Billy Evans and their two very young children (a toddler and a newborn) while she is away. It’s a characteristically overoptimistic use of technology, and it becomes clear, as the camera flashes and a tear rolls down her cheek, that her apparent excitement about the magic of this process is barely masking a deep well of dread.

On paper, You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, does not exactly have the makings of a tearjerker. For many, Holmes is the opposite of a sympathetic subject: one of the few superstar CEOs of the 2010s to face actual consequences for engaging in a dangerous fraud. The fact that throughout her interviews with Fielder she admits no guilt for her deceptions at the blood-testing startup Theranos—insisting that the company had an invention that worked, and that she is now working on “Theranos 2.0”—does not help. When A24 dropped the trailer for the movie, her nodding, wide-eyed stare at Fielder inspired mockery and derision.

Nathan Fielder, meanwhile, is not best known for emotional range or psychological depth. His Comedy Central show Nathan for You was built around quick hits of shock value, as every episode he persuades small-business owners to run increasingly transparent scams in order to gain easy money or notoriety. It’s a premise he is able to execute so brazenly because the Nathan character in the show has such a flat affect; with a remarkable ability not to notice uncomfortable and often appalled reactions to his pitches, he exhibits a total lack of emotional intelligence. His 2022 show The Rehearsal is a self-consciously absurd attempt to avoid unruly feelings altogether, as he stages a simulation of a typical suburban life with actors playing his wife and child. When he starred alongside Emma Stone in The Curse in 2023, the New York Times’ critic called him a “stiff, limited actor.”

Fielder’s limitations, however, seem to make him less susceptible to manipulation than most people. There is never a moment when he is softer or more flattering than he should be for the sake of being polite. In an early scene, when Holmes shares with him her fear of being taken away from her family, he says woodenly, “That must be hard.” Later Fielder recalls that in his first meeting with Holmes he told her that, because of her reputation, he thought there was no chance anyone would ever believe anything she said.

The film he and Oppenheim have made is not interested in the science behind Theranos and does not indulge in any did-she-or-didn’t-she about the fraud. It is instead about living in the aftermath—about what happens to a person who has been blasted into little pieces by an overload of public attention, and whose efforts to hold onto an identity only seem to result in more fragmentation. The Elizabeth Holmes of this film appears as if in an eerie hall of mirrors: caught between the entrepreneur in the black turtleneck on the cover of Forbes magazine; the goofy, devious ingenue of the Hulu series The Dropout; the frazzled new mom sitting for interviews with Fielder; and the dozens of dots for a hologram created for her children. The effect is disorienting, sometimes trippy, and most often just very, very sad.


The first half of the movie is fairly straightforward: Fielder spends a month with Holmes and her family at the beachfront house they are renting in San Diego before she begins serving an 11-year sentence for fraud in a federal prison camp in Texas. (The sentence has since been reduced.) On Holmes’s side, the purpose appears to be to show that she has nothing to hide. On Fielder’s, it’s an opportunity to capture an atmosphere that is surreal even by his standards and ask some exceptionally blunt questions—a setup reminiscent of any number of Louis Theroux’s Weird Weekends. He approaches Holmes’s father with: “I read you worked at Enron. How was that?” He suggests to Billy that Holmes may have had an ulterior motive in coupling up with him: “Isn’t your family rich?” To the couple, he muses one evening that it’s funny he is known for a show about business scams and now he’s making a film about them.

Some of the tension here builds predictably on the distance between how much Holmes tells Fielder he can see and what he is really allowed to see, between what he can capture on camera and what is being staged for his benefit. The film’s title comes from a text Holmes sends him shortly after she agrees to let him stay in the house 24-7, promising “fyi you can totally see everything.” It’s a message that feels less direct than it might sound, since Holmes sends it moments after walking away from him. As she strolls on the beach not far away, he can see her both when he receives her message and when she checks her phone for his reply. There are times when Fielder seems to have way too much access—there is a shot of Billy taking a shower, for instance, that prominently features his penis—and times when his interviews get sharply cut off.

One thing that the Holmes camp appears eager to emphasize for the cameras is her weirdness. Billy often insists that she is not normal and that she just thinks differently. When Fielder grills her about false claims she made about Theranos’s technology (“the fact that we have a single device that can perform any test”), she insists, with the unblinking determination of someone who is living deep inside a delusion, that everything she said was true. (Could she be anything but deluded when contemplating holding weekly patent brainstorm sessions with Billy from prison, or, as she terms it, “inventing from a cage”?) In this sense the weirdness serves as a kind of alibi, creating the impression that at best Holmes was somehow unable to understand that she was doing anything wrong.

At other moments, the weirdness hints at darker dynamics: In one of the film’s first truly memorable and somewhat disturbing moments, Holmes is casually beating eggs in a bowl. When the camera zooms in on her hand, it looks as though she has never attempted this task in her life before. Without saying a word, Billy removes the bowl from her hand and finishes the job. There’s a strange shift in the balance of power in the room, as it begins to seem as if Holmes’s role is to be more or less helpless in everyday life and Billy’s is to be the capable one who will make most of the decisions.

Many of the more sobering moments happen in the background, as when Holmes slips away to take a call, presumably from her lawyer or another adviser, and we overhear her asking if you are allowed to choose when you shower in prison and what time you have to wake up. In another shot, she is heard asking what an invasive strip search is. Later, we see her laying out a crewneck sweater on the bed and muttering, “I could wear this when I surrender.” If there are times, elsewhere in the film, when she appears to be pushing an agenda or courting sympathy, these scenes feel like something different—glimpses of a woman making her best effort to deal with the situation in practical terms and suddenly realizing it will not be enough. Soon she will really be gone. You can appreciate how weirdness and delusion might feel more tolerable than the reality, when she is leaving the house for prison and tells Billy to remember there is pumped milk in the refrigerator for the baby.


The second half of the film is more complicated, and deals more creatively with Holmes’s fate, as a woman who is both everywhere—there are billboards of her face in L.A. and in Times Square—and nowhere, serving her time in Texas with extremely limited access to the outside world.

Notably, for Fielder, she has disappeared from his project, since he can’t really visit her without going through Billy, who doesn’t want him to record and is increasingly cagey about the whole endeavor. This is a problem because Fielder still has questions: Did Holmes know that Billy negotiated a deal with A24 that would give him a share of profits from the movie? And if she did, does she know how that would look? Does it undermine everything that we have spent the prior 90 minutes observing?

Fielder is left with a series of echoes and distortions to sift through. He meets the hologram Holmes was posing for: Billy has positioned a large screen at the family dining table, and watches the avatar reading out an email in a computer-generated approximation of Holmes’s voice. Billy has also created an AI deepfake of Holmes, which he shows Fielder on his phone, and he has taken over her X account, sometimes posting messages she has sent him, but also broadcasting his own thoughts and often angry replies under her name, sounding nothing at all like her. Those billboards in Times Square are paid for by a mysterious superfan, who also stages, at a strip club, a play about her in which he personally arrests the Holmes character at gunpoint.

Unable to track down the real Elizabeth Holmes, Fielder enlists the next best thing: Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy for playing Holmes in The Dropout. Together they recreate scenes between Fielder and Holmes that he was not able to film when they happened in real life, and Seyfried contributes her own interpretations of Holmes’s motives as they go. There’s something unseemly about her participation: There’s a difference between inhabiting a character in a scripted drama that is clearly marked as a fictionalization and dressing up like a real person and doing their voice in a documentary. There’s a danger of voyeurism, even gloating. The sense of intrusion is made literal when we see Seyfried and Fielder enter the now-empty San Diego beach house and begin their reenactments. We’re very close to parody—and cruelty.

Fielder has always been most comfortable playing with this boundary. From Nathan for You to The Rehearsal, he makes the audience wince. And of course, he’s adding to the hall of mirrors effect here, as he shows us Seyfried watching his footage of Holmes watching Seyfried play Holmes in The Dropout. Later scenes of Seyfried reenacting Holmes’s conversations with Fielder are cut with scenes of her running those same lines with Fielder and trying different styles of delivery. What started out as a straight documentary turns into an almost absurd, almost distasteful experiment, and an argument that the only real way to know something is not through hours of faithful recording but through an elaborate artifice.

Still, the most impressive thing about You Can See Everything is the way it recognizes the dangers of parody and makes room for Holmes’s humanity. It’s a portrait of a woman who broke the law and isn’t even close to sorry about it, but it’s also a film about a mother leaving her newborn baby while she is still breastfeeding and entering the largest prison system in the world. If there’s one part of the film in which a simple shot has a devasting effect, it is the final image of Holmes, shot through the bars of the prison camp. She is dressed in tan prison overalls, walking the prison yard with her daughter, now a toddler, who is wearing a gauzy polyester princess costume. There are no justifications or excuses for Holmes or Theranos here. That doesn’t make any of it less heartbreaking.

items.title: Pete Hegseth’s Pathetic Warrior Cult Has Undermined the Military
items.content_text:
Pete Hegseth and his “High-T Department of War” are having a rough go of it lately. Despite being hyper-focused on making sure U.S. troops “look like killers” and that none of them are “soft,” “fat,” or “mushy,” Hegseth’s Pentagon is burning through precision munitions stockpiles in its conflict with Iran, which despite his best efforts effectively controls traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. On top of that failure, DOD has lost Army Secretary Dan Driscoll over Hegseth’s disruption of the personnel pipeline and general mismanagement. And the cherry atop Hegseth’s failure sundae has come in the form of an impeachment effort from a Republican member of Congress over the conduct of the Iran war itself.

And yet Hegseth’s latest announcements suggest that he has learned remarkably little from his experiences. At a recent address at Quantico, he declared that the “warrior ethos has been revived” and “American deterrence is back,” even as he announced plans to eliminate 20 percent of general and admiral positions. He also briefly championed a plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, turning military violence into a public spectacle supposedly meant to demonstrate U.S. resolve, before a public backlash—strong enough to push Trump away from the planned display of public cruelty—put the kibosh on those plans. Still, the dissonance is jarring: The defense secretary is so thoroughly preoccupied with projecting toughness and glorifying lethality, all while presiding over a war that has exposed the limits of U.S. power potentially even more than its debacles in Vietnam and Iraq.

There is an older American story about what could happen when a nation selects military leaders based on their bravado and popularity among white supremacists. The Mexican-American War was one of the clearest early examples of the difference between U.S. military belligerence and effectiveness. The professional Regular Army, though small, was a highly military force whose officers understood logistics, discipline, command, and the unglamorous mechanics that allow a military to keep functioning when a war inevitably proves more difficult than the politicians who started it imagined.

However, alongside the regulars marched tens of thousands of volunteers, largely from the Southern states that would make up the Confederacy only 15 years later. Unlike the Regular Army, whose officers held federal commissions and whose junior ranks were increasingly dominated by West Point graduates selected for their demonstrated military effectiveness, volunteer officers were often elected by the men they commanded or appointed through state-level political patronage. These mechanisms rewarded political prominence, personal popularity, and the performance of masculine authority rather than professional military experience.

Compounding their lack of experience, the white supremacist attitudes of many of the volunteer officers convinced them without evidence that white Americans were naturally superior soldiers and that “yellow bellied Mexicans” were naturally inferior and would be easily defeated. Some Southern volunteers were so confident of an easy victory that they worried the war would be over before they even arrived on the battlefield. As one commander put the pervasive attitude of many volunteers, each U.S. victory demonstrated “the order of providence that the Anglo-Saxon race was not only to take possession of the whole North American continent, but to influence and modify the character of the world.”

Perhaps unsurprisingly, these soldiers’ confidence in their own whiteness alone did not equate to effectiveness on the battlefield, and selecting commanders based on their popularity and manly image proved disastrous in many cases. For example, Col. Archibald Yell of the Arkansas Mounted Rifles, a magnetic Jacksonian politician who had built his reputation through personal combativeness and political connections, easily obtained a command based on his experience as a former governor and congressman. He had served in earlier wars as a sergeant and later a lieutenant, but he had no significant command experience. This would prove to be his undoing.

When the Mexican-American War began, Yell enlisted as a private in a volunteer company and was elected colonel when the regiment organized. He was still trying to preserve his congressional seat and position himself for further political advancement even as he took command. Once the regiment reached Texas, the problems started almost immediately. Most of its companies rarely drilled, its camp was so disorderly that regular Army commander John Wool struggled to impose basic discipline and sanitation, and Wool eventually dubbed the regiment the “Arkansas Mounted Devils.” He complained that the troops were “wholly without instruction and Colonel Yell is determined to leave them in that condition.” Rather than address the poor training of the troops under his command, Yell instead cultivated rapport with them by positioning himself as their champion against their regular Army commander and providing lavish food and drink.

At the Battle of Buena Vista in February 1847, Yell’s regiment came under Mexican attack and fled in confusion despite Yell’s order to charge, exposing the rear of the rest of the U.S. column. Many of his men were captured or killed, and the regiment fell apart in the fighting and was distributed among different units. Yell charged alone and was killed. Yell embodied a recurring problem of volunteer command, where leaders’ ability to perform the role of a warrior and maintain esteem among their troops sometimes came at the expense of the less glamorous work of making them effective soldiers.

It is from this tattered cloth that Pete Hegseth is cut. While he spends plenty of time in front of the cameras, glad-handing troops and showing how many pull-ups he can do, he is fixated on projecting strength, whether real or imagined. This image that treats aggression, physical appearance, and ideological conformity as evidence of effectiveness, even going so far as to adopt absurd manosphere concepts as guides to military doctrine (see #lethalitymaxxing, language borrowed from incel subcultures obsessed with masculine appearance and status). Hegseth’s bizarre testosterone-screening proposal, later rescinded after questions about its medical basis, took the idea further by treating a biological marker of masculinity as a potential proxy for military readiness.

Donald Trump selected Hegseth for much the same reason that Arkansas volunteers elevated Yell. Hegseth had spent years on Fox News performing the role of the warrior who would liberate the military from timid professionals and ideological enemies. Trump wanted someone who looked and sounded like the defense secretary he imagined—a living cartoon warrior, as opposed to a military professional with a demonstrated record of managing a vast institution. Trump has said that Hegseth was straight from “central casting” and “obsessed with war.” Now Hegseth is using his authority to remake the military around the qualities that made him attractive to the president, pushing out senior commanders and disrupting promotion pathways while elevating a narrow vision of masculinity, race, religion, and ideological loyalty.

There is one crucial difference between Hegseth and the volunteer commanders of the Mexican-American War. Yell operated within a military structure led by professional officers who could challenge him, impose discipline, and help compensate for his shortcomings. Hegseth sits atop the entire military hierarchy, with the authority to remove the professionals who question his judgment and reshape the institution in his own image. The regulars once helped turn swaggering volunteers into an effective fighting force, but now the man with the volunteer’s mindset—the sort of person whom armed forces lifers refer to derisively as a “rear echelon motherfucker”—is deciding which of the professionals get to stay and who has to go.

This would all be dangerous enough if Trump were pursuing a cautious foreign policy, or the noninterventionist approach that he was somehow credited with by an ignorant pundit class, who were all too willing to be snowed by his dovish rhetoric. Instead, he is reviving the expansionist logic of the Monroe Doctrine, threatening other countries with military force and territorial demands while assuming American superiority will compel submission, even while the war with Iran has exposed the obvious weakness in that assumption. The United States can inflict enormous damage, but Trump’s and Hegseth’s belligerence has exposed a military far more confident in its capability to impose success than it is able to execute. Military effectiveness depends on professional judgment, institutional knowledge, technological adaptation, logistics, and an understanding of what force can and cannot accomplish, and these are all components of the job in which Hegseth has shown zero interest or competence.
