items.title: Sell The Bailout: Skydance Tumbles As Musk's $1 Billion Check Reminds Everyone Paramount Needs One
items.content_text:
Sell The Bailout: Skydance Tumbles As Musk's $1 Billion Check Reminds Everyone Paramount Needs One

It took about ten minutes.

Just after noon on Thursday, Semafor reported that Elon Musk has invested roughly $1 billion in Skydance (SKYD), the newly renamed Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery combo run by David Ellison. The stock did what stocks are supposed to do on a billionaire endorsement and spiked to $8.46, up 7.5% on the day. Then traders actually thought about it, and by 12:10pm the shares had been halted for volatility after tumbling, before printing a low of $7.53 once trading resumed, 11% below the post-headline spike.

*SKYDANCE HALTED FOR VOLATILITY AFTER SHARES TURN NEGATIVE (narrator: "not up")

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 22, 2026

Our own read of the headline was about as succinct as it gets:

Market: "wait, Paramount needs a bailout?"

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 22, 2026

Which, well, is probably the right question. Because while equity investors had been hoping for a white knight, credit investors have spent the past three weeks pricing Skydance like a company that would very soon need one.

The CDS Market Already Knew

Regular readers know we have been all over the Skydance capital structure since the deal financing hit the tape. On October 1, we documented how Paramount's record $52 billion bond offering sank before the ink was dry, with the 8-year second-lien notes trading around 95 within a day of pricing at par, and 5Y CDS jumping to 432bp, the highest since April 2009. Five days later, as the Warner deal closed, Fitch sent the old Paramount unsecured paper to the back of the line behind ~$57 billion of new secured debt, and the legacy 6.875% 2036s plunged to a record low of 77 cents.

It was all downhill from there: Paramount CDS soared to Global Financial Crisis levels on October 7, took out the Lehman highs on October 14 and, on Tuesday night, we put out this chart showing 5Y CDS at a new all-time record of 601bp, comfortably above anything on record.

Put differently, the credit market has been screaming for weeks that Skydance has too much debt and not enough equity. So when the solution to that problem turned out to be a $1 billion check, it maybe shouldn't come as a surprise that equity holders reached the same conclusion as the CDS desks: if the company is raising emergency-sized equity from friends of the family, there must be an emergency.

Malone Promised $10 Billion. Musk Sent One

The other problem is that the market had been primed for a much bigger number. Just one day earlier, billionaire media mogul John Malone told the Paley International Council Summit that a Musk investment was coming, and that it would be big:

"Who helped Elon finance Twitter when he bought it? Larry Ellison. How did Larry Ellison come up with some of the money to put into the creation of Skydance? Tesla stock. And I would not doubt for a minute that before very long you're gonna see an announcement."

Malone was right about the announcement, but he pegged the check at $8 billion to $10 billion. Musk delivered about one-tenth of that. Against Skydance's roughly $87 billion of total debt, the Musk money comes to a little over 1%, or about the same weight as a rounding error in the company's synergy targets.

Some napkin math: the fixed-rate notes sold in the deal financing alone carry about $3.3 billion a year in coupons, and the ~$9.5 billion of term loans at SOFR+275 add maybe another $650 million. Call it $4 billion a year in interest on the acquisition debt, which means Musk's $1 billion covers roughly one quarter's worth of interest. Generous, sure. Transformational, not quite.

Per Semafor, the Musk money came in around the same time as fresh equity from Skydance's other investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, though neither the size of those checks nor the price paid has been disclosed (and if the price had been flattering, we suspect someone would have mentioned it). Skydance declined to comment and Musk's camp didn't respond.

Who Needs The Money, Anyway?

None of this should be news to anyone who has followed the saga. When Semafor first reported back in September that Paramount was weighing tapping Musk for an equity check (Sep 24), the stated rationale was to "reduce Larry Ellison's financial burden" after the Oracle founder personally guaranteed more than $40 billion of the equity financing. Fitch, for its part, made it clear in its rating action timed to the close that hitting the company's 3x net leverage target by the end of 2029 would likely require issuing equity or selling assets on top of the promised $6 billion in cost cuts.

So here is the equity. A very small amount of it.

Meanwhile, the stock has been a one-way trip since the merger closed. Skydance ended October 6 at $9.53 and is now trading around $7.80, a drop of about 18% (some of that is the October 14 warrant distribution, which knocked 16% off the price as shares started trading ex-warrant, so the damage is less dramatic than it looks, but only a bit). That said, the real story is in credit, where the equity drawdown is a sideshow next to bonds at record lows and CDS above Lehman.

And there is one more wrinkle that we flagged when CDS first took out the 2008 highs: how much of this is effectively cross-collateralized with Larry Ellison and, by extension, Oracle (ORCL), whose own CDS was hitting record highs at the same time? With the Ellison family on the hook for a big chunk of Skydance's equity and Oracle's balance sheet already stretched by the AI capex binge, a little outside help is probably welcome. A little is what it got.

Friends With Benefits

Of course, there is more to the Musk check than finance. The world's richest man, who already owns X, now has a stake in the parent of CNN and CBS, and the Ellisons, via Oracle, are part owners of TikTok's US operations. Semafor's original September scoop was enough to cause panic at CNN; today's confirmation will probably do the same, even though David Ellison has insisted the newsrooms will stay editorially independent. Given how many times CNN has warned its viewers about Elon Musk, there is a certain poetry in Musk now being one of its shareholders.

Markets, however, trade the debt stack, and the debt stack says Skydance needs a lot more than $1 billion. If anything, today's tape suggests that each new "vote of confidence" will be read as a sign of how much more is needed, which is why we suspect this check is the first of several, and that the next one will have to be far closer to Malone's number than Musk's.

Until then, the CDS market will keep its own counsel. It hasn't been wrong yet.

Iran Deploys Artillery, Troops To Kurdish Border Areas Amid Renewed War Fears

Kurdish and Middle East regional news sources are saying Iran's military is building up artillery and personnel in the country's northwest Kurdish regions bordering Iraq amid an intensifying crackdown on Kurdish opposition groups, and as Israel and the US threaten new attacks.

In particular, the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) is being targeted, amid reports of recent clashes with security forces in the Shaho Mountains and other areas along the border with Iraqi Kurdistan.

The Kurdish population of Iran is a very sizeable minority of the country, commonly estimated at 10-15 million people primarily living in the northwestern and western areas of the country. Millions of Kurds also live on the Iraqi side of the border 

There's been an intensified target on Kurdish dissident groups given that in the opening months of Trump's Operation Epic Fury, US and Israeli officials openly talked about arming Kurdish groups along the Iran-Iraq border area.

Some reports said this external covert weaponization and funding campaign in order to put pressure on Tehran was already in full swing, but a slew of Kurdish political leaders in Iraq vehemently denied the reports.

Rudaw news reports from Irbil, "Iran has deployed artillery and heavy weaponry to Kurdish areas in the west of the country amid growing fears of a wider conflict with Israel and the United States, as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intensifies operations against armed opposition groups along the country's western and southeastern frontiers."

According to more from the Kurdish media report:

The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) reported late Wednesday that IRGC forces and military convoys carrying heavy and semi-heavy weapons had been deployed from other provinces to several cities in Iran's Kurdish region, including Sanandaj, Kamyaran, Sarvabad, Marivan and Baneh.

An informed source in Kamyaran told the rights network that "hundreds of IRGC special forces, believed to be members of the entity's Saberin Unit, have been dispatched over the past few weeks in military convoys to areas surrounding villages on the slopes of Mount Shaho in Kamyaran County."

There have been prior reports of sporadic drone activity and artillery fire in the areas of Shaho and Marivan.

These flare-ups have long predated the current US-Iran war, but the heightened state of alert and growing temperature of the region could bring an intensification to Tehran's anti-Kurdish opposition crackdown.

items.title: Virginia Governor Seeks 6-Year Rate-Freeze If Dominion-NextEra Merger Is Approved
items.content_text:
Virginia Governor Seeks 6-Year Rate-Freeze If Dominion-NextEra Merger Is Approved

By Charles Paullin of UtilityDive

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, D, has proposed a six-year rate freeze as part of a suite of conditions she says state regulators should impose if they approve a proposed merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy that could create the largest regulated electric utility in the world.

Spanberger’s stance comes amid review of the $67 billion merger that has prompted intense pushback from other state officials and local communities.

“Any proposed merger involving Virginia’s primary state-regulated utility must benefit families, small businesses, and Virginia’s workforce — not just the shareholders of these multi-billion-dollar corporations,” Spanberger said in a statement Monday.

“That’s why I am calling for a six-year freeze to Virginians’ base residential electricity rates, a tripling of monthly bill credits for ratepayers, and additional commitments to lower energy costs and meet our long-term clean and homegrown energy goals if the State Corporation Commission is to approve this merger,” she added. 

Expert witness testimony filed by Spanberger’s office with the State Corporation Commission outlined a plan to increase monthly bill credits to $29 a month for four years, as well as increasing the debt share of Dominion’s capital structure from 48% to 60% to lower its rate of return.

The witness, Richard McCann, an environmental consultant with M.Cubed, also called for requiring a “probability of dispatch” cost allocation method, improving disconnection policies and several other energy efficiency and clean energy commitments. 

“Mandatory, Comprehensive Enforceability provisions must be imposed to hold the Joint Petitioners fully accountable for any violation of commitments, including the labor and workforce commitments,” wrote McCann. “Unless these additional commitments are substantially addressed or alternative solutions are identified, the Commission should reject the joint petition.”

The filings coincide with filings from Virginia’s attorney general and SCC staff opposing the deal unless terms they propose are also agreed to. 

Dominion and NextEra proposed the merger in May, saying it would facilitate a more cost-effective buildout of Virginia’s electric grid to serve rising demand from large-load data centers. 

The utilities initially proposed customer bill credits amounting to $10 a month for two years. But as pushback mounted, including from Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, the utilities increased the proposed timeline to four years. The utilities also made assurances for more clean energy, in line with the state’s decarbonization law, the Virginia Clean Economy Act. 

“As expected in a proceeding of this size and significance, today’s testimony reflects a wide range of viewpoints and interests,” Dominion and NextEra said in a joint statement following the governor’s announcement. “We are reviewing the filings and will address the issues raised through the Commission’s established process.”

Spanberger plans to hold a call with the media Tuesday afternoon to discuss her proposal.

items.title: Trump Calls On Data Center Developers To Pay Communities A Dividend
items.content_text:
Trump Calls On Data Center Developers To Pay Communities A Dividend

Authored by Chris Summers via The Epoch Times,

President Donald Trump has suggested that companies building data centers in the United States should offer local communities a dividend to make them more popular.

“If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend,’” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Wednesday.

New data centers, which are required to fuel the growth of artificial intelligence (AI), have become politically controversial in some areas because of the amount of electricity and water they consume.

Local resistance blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects, worth $130 billion, in the first quarter of 2026, according to Data Center Watch.

The Trump administration has supported AI, and the president said last month that U.S. government documents would start referring to it as “super intelligence.”

On Oct. 4, Trump announced the creation of the Super Intelligence Force to coordinate federal efforts to maintain the United States’ lead over China in AI technology.

“As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion,” Trump wrote on Wednesday.

“New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data Centers are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is [an] electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease.”

‘Get Them Built’: Trump

“MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A,” Trump also wrote.

In February, during his State of the Union address, Trump said his administration had secured agreements with tech companies to pay a greater share of the costs electric utilities—and their residential customers—incur when data centers and other high-tech “large load” users boost demand and strain supply.

Trump introduced what he called “a rate payer protection pledge” in which tech companies, or “hyperscalers,” agree to pay more for the electricity they use to power data centers and vow to “pay their own way” so their high demand for electricity doesn’t affect utility customers’ bills.

The president said he supports “co-location” of new energy sources and data centers to accelerate AI infrastructure buildout through initiatives that fast-track permits, reduce regulatory hurdles, and make federal land available for these projects.

Meta has agreed to build a data center on the site of a planned 400-megawatt natural gas plant in New Albany, Ohio, and Google has partnered with Intersect Power to build co-located data centers in so-called energy parks alongside solar and storage generation in a nationwide $20 billion venture.

But how data center development affects residential consumer rates is hotly debated and will likely be an issue in the 2026 midterm elections, including in dozens of House races.

Evidence shows that the Chinese regime is seeking to use the issue of data centers to sow division.

Cleo Paskal, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, previously told The Epoch Times that while energy availability and water depletion were real issues, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) was trying to exploit them to block data centers.

“But it’s also a real issue that the Chinese Communist Party is perfectly happy to exacerbate to create even more division with the goal not of leading to any solution, but of paralyzing the United States,” she said.

OpenAI has accused CCP influence operators of jumping on the data center bandwagon.

“The targeting of OpenAI and US data center buildouts is significant not because the operation appears to have shifted public opinion, but because it shows [People’s Republic of China]-origin influence operators testing narratives against AI infrastructure—a foundation of US technological leadership, economic growth and the broader democratic AI ecosystem,” the company said in a report published in June.

items.title: "Gotten Too Old Not To Be Greedy": Virginia State Sen. Arrested, Accused Of Masterminding $4.5 Million Criminal Drug Enterprise
items.content_text:
"Gotten Too Old Not To Be Greedy": Virginia State Sen. Arrested, Accused Of Masterminding $4.5 Million Criminal Drug Enterprise

Virginia's Democratic Senate President Pro Tempore L. Louise Lucas, 82, has been indicted by a federal grand jury and taken into federal custody on charges of racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute marijuana, money laundering, honest-services fraud/bribery, and maintaining a drug-involved premises. Six co-defendants, including her daughters and grandson, were also charged. FBI Director Kash Patel put the alleged scheme at roughly $4.5 million.

The 45-page indictment unsealed Thursday in the Eastern District of Virginia alleges that Lucas led a multi-year "Lucas Enterprise" that, since at least 2019, acquired and distributed at least 100 kilograms of illegal marijuana, laundered the proceeds through various business entities, and used her official power to protect the operation while shaping cannabis legislation for personal gain. Lucas self-surrendered Thursday morning and faces an initial appearance before a federal magistrate judge. All defendants are reported to be in custody.

Who She Is and How the Probe Unfolded

Lucas has represented Portsmouth since 1991 and has served as Senate President Pro Tempore and Chair of the Finance and Appropriations Committee - the most powerful budget post in the chamber. She is a longtime, outspoken advocate for marijuana legalization who sponsored key bills and co-owns The Cannabis Outlet, a Portsmouth shop that sells hemp and cannabis products. She is a close ally of Governor Abigail Spanberger and played a central role in Democrats' 2026 redistricting effort that sought to add Democratic-leaning congressional seats before it was blocked by the Virginia Supreme Court.

The case became public on May 6, 2026, when the FBI executed court-authorized search warrants at Lucas's Portsmouth district office (which also houses her disabilities-services business, Lucas Lodge LLC) and at The Cannabis Outlet next door. Agents recovered marijuana and firearms from both locations. At the time, Lucas publicly described the raids as political intimidation. Federal sources told Fox News the searches were part of a major corruption probe. The underlying investigation itself predates the current administration and was opened under President Biden. Wiretaps were active for months; at least one Democratic congressman and a local reporter later received notices that their communications with Lucas had been intercepted.

Via Wavy.com:

The response was described as “court-authorized law enforcement activity,” according to FBI Public Affairs Specialist Cassandra Temple. She could not offer additional information.

A spokesperson for the FBI later elaborated in the following statement to WAVY: “The FBI is executing a court-authorized federal search warrant in Portsmouth, VA. There is no threat to public safety. This is an ongoing investigation, and no further information is publicly available at this time.”

The Allegations

Prosecutors say Lucas directed the purchase and sale of large quantities of illegal marijuana under the cover of her licensed medical-cannabis business and used her legislative position to "insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influenc[e] legislation to financially benefit themselves."

A central allegation involves an August 2022 payment of $750,000 by Lucas for a 100% stake in a shell holding company created so a co-conspirator could obtain a Virginia recreational marijuana license. She allegedly failed to disclose this interest on required Statements of Economic Interests. She is also accused of receiving a bribery payment from the co-conspirator and of meeting with him at her Capitol office to discuss partial repayment while lobbying other legislators on the license.

Intercepted calls are explicit. In February 2026 Lucas told an unindicted co-conspirator this was their "last chance at generational wealth" and added, "I've gotten too old to not be greedy." In another call she reportedly said she needed the recreational market to open because "when I did it, it was obviously illegal." She had earlier told a co-conspirator she wanted a recreational license specifically "to create generational wealth for her and her family" and that "this is my last chance."

The Cannabis Outlet itself received violation notices from the Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services in 2023 and 2024 for selling non-compliant products.

Co-defendants include daughters Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, grandson Ryan Eichelberger, former business partner Carlton Upton Jr., Prince Albert William Hudson III, and Tameka Johnson.

Statements and Timing

Attorney General Todd Blanche said the charges "reveal the behavior of a public servant who will put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve." Patel stated that Lucas "allegedly abused her position of public trust as a 30-year Virginia State Senator to put her own financial interests ahead of the people she represents - orchestrating a five-year scheme worth an estimated $4.5 million."

In a statement, Lucas said: "Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother. I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now."

Virginia recently cleared the path for regulated recreational retail sales beginning July 1, 2027. Lucas is not up for reelection until 2027. The charging decision comes roughly two weeks before midterm elections - an unusual window for overt action against a sitting political figure, though the investigation itself is not new.

* * *

items.title: US To Release Heating Oil Reserve In Northeast To Lower Prices
items.content_text:
US To Release Heating Oil Reserve In Northeast To Lower Prices

Authored by Jack Phillips via The Epoch Times,

The U.S. Department of Energy has announced it will offer a heating oil exchange in a bid to lower costs ahead of the winter as the war in Iran continues.

In a statement released on Wednesday, the department announced a proposal request for an exchange of up to 315,000 barrels of ultra-low sulfur distillate, a refined oil product used for home heating. Ultra-low sulfur distillate uses the same specification as most types of diesel, which has experienced high prices in recent days.

"This solicitation is structured to mitigate supply chain challenges disrupting fuel oil supply," the department said, adding the move is designed to keep the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve stocked ahead of the winter months.

"The Trump administration is committed to doing everything in our power to lower energy costs for the American people," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in a statement.

According to the Energy Department, the terms of the exchange mean that borrowing companies have to "return the same volume of fuel oil" and include a premium back to the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve.

After receiving letters from the two Maine U.S. senators, Wright said he then directed his agency to exchange barrels of fuel from the oil reserve to mitigate high heating oil costs.

"Of course, this is a temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption. I encourage the governors of New York and New England to work with the Trump Administration to build the Constitution Pipeline and replace home heating oil with low-cost natural gas," he said. "Doing so would save their residents billions of dollars in home heating and electricity costs."

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) wrote in a post on X that the move equals a roughly 13 percent supply increase for New England, essentially pushing down the northeastern United States' heating oil costs this winter.

The Energy Department's announcement added that it will loan the hundreds of thousands of barrels of heating oil from Connecticut, Maine, and Massachusetts. The deliveries will be completed by Nov. 13.

According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average retail price of diesel has remained over $6 per gallon for weeks. From Tuesday to Wednesday, the price for diesel remained virtually unchanged in the United States, standing at $6.31 per gallon.

Diesel hit a record high of $6.52 per gallon on Sept. 22, the AAA figures show. Those figures also show that regular gasoline dropped about 1 cent on Wednesday to $4.26 per gallon.

Oil prices have hovered around $100 per barrel for months now, with international Brent crude reaching $108 and U.S. West Texas International reaching $97, respectively, per barrel on Wednesday.

In an effort to control crude oil prices that have risen due to the war with Iran and amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Trump administration in March agreed to loan 172 million barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, located in Louisiana and Texas. Currently, the reserve has dropped to 282 million barrels, the lowest levels seen since the 1980s.

President Donald Trump also indicated that his administration may move to permanently allow E-15 gasoline, which is blended with 15 percent ethanol instead of the regular 10 percent, to be used all year long. Normally, some states bar its usage during the summer months.

During a rally in Kansas on Monday, Trump said he would initiate the move if Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) wins his reelection bid during the midterms next month.

items.title: Meta Says Zuckerberg To Stay In California After Considering Relocation
items.content_text:
Meta Says Zuckerberg To Stay In California After Considering Relocation

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

A possible new wealth tax in California prompted Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg to consider leaving the state, according to a new regulatory filing.

California voters will decide on Proposition 40 in November. It would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires.

If approved, Zuckerberg would have to pay a multibillion-dollar tax, Meta lawyers said in the Oct. 21 filing to the Securities and Exchange Commission that included frequent mentions of a special committee of independent directors.

"In light of this potential tax exposure, Mr. Zuckerberg informed the Special Committee that he was evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and that steps toward any such relocation, including any listing of his residential real estate in California on the market, would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by Company employees and, accordingly, raise questions for management of the Company going forward," the filing stated.

The committee said Zuckerberg "has been crucial to the Company's growth since its inception," that he is best-positioned at this time to ensure the company's continued success, and that it is important to keep him in a leadership position to drive the company's continued success.

Meta, Facebook and Instagram's parent company, faced challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, which it said stemmed from Zuckerberg's inability to be physically present with the company's management team, and the committee did not want similar challenges in the future.

The company said it is creating a new class of stock, beginning in January 2027, that will let it raise money for investment in artificial intelligence systems and incentivize Zuckerberg to remain a Meta executive.

An upcoming stock dividend will distribute class C shares to Zuckerberg and other shareholders.

"Again, the goal is to keep Mr. Zuckerberg continuing to lead the Company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs," the filing stated.

"In light of that importance, the Special Committee secured Mr. Zuckerberg's commitment to remain a resident of California, or any other jurisdiction in which the Company maintains its corporate headquarters, for eight years from the date of the Founder Alignment Agreement, for so long as Mr. Zuckerberg satisfies the Continued Leadership Condition, unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."

Meta on Wednesday reported a third-quarter profit of $9.89 billion, up from $2.79 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Earnings per share were $3.83, up from $1.05.

The jump stemmed in part from much lower taxes and higher revenue.

Meta's revenue was $64.6 billion in the third quarter, and it expects to make $73 billion to $76 billion in the fourth quarter.

"We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone - including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model," Zuckerberg said in a statement. "Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we're seeing velocity across the board."

items.title: AI Discovers Critical Security Flaw Affecting Technology Behind 70% Of All Websites
items.content_text:
AI Discovers Critical Security Flaw Affecting Technology Behind 70% Of All Websites

Artificial intelligence has uncovered a potentially catastrophic security flaw in one of the internet’s most widely used technologies, setting off a scramble among cybersecurity researchers, software developers, and website operators to prevent hackers from exploiting the discovery, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The vulnerability affects PHP, a programming technology that underpins as much as 70% of the world’s websites. Researchers discovered that weaknesses in the way PHP handles computer memory could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, potentially gaining control of websites, accessing sensitive information, and compromising visitors.

What makes the discovery particularly troubling is that the same AI technology used to identify the problem could also make it substantially easier for criminals to exploit it.

WSJ writes that the flaw, dubbed PHP2Shell, was uncovered in August by Ryan Austin of cybersecurity firm Calif, who used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol to examine PHP’s underlying code. Although the weaknesses had been present for years, researchers had previously considered them extraordinarily difficult to exploit. With AI assistance, however, Austin demonstrated that some servers could be compromised in seconds, while more complicated systems could be breached over several hours.

The findings prompted a coordinated effort involving PHP developers, independent security researchers, and teams from Google’s Wiz and OpenAI. The group spent weeks quietly developing fixes, ultimately modifying nearly 200 files and writing more than 10,000 lines of code.

The secrecy was intentional. Researchers feared that publicizing the vulnerability before a patch was ready would give attackers an opportunity to develop their own AI-assisted exploits.

That concern reflects a broader shift in cybersecurity. Historically, hackers needed considerable time and expertise to reverse-engineer software updates and determine which weaknesses developers were attempting to correct. Advanced AI systems can now automate much of that work, potentially allowing attackers to develop working exploits before website administrators have finished installing security updates.

Volker Dusch, a security engineer associated with the nonprofit foundation responsible for PHP, called the discovery the technology’s most serious security problem in more than a decade. He compared its significance to Heartbleed, the notorious 2014 vulnerability that forced organizations around the world to urgently secure their systems.

Wiz co-founder Ami Luttwak went further, describing PHP2Shell as an exceptionally serious AI-discovered vulnerability, suggesting that its complexity might have kept it hidden indefinitely without artificial intelligence.

The developers initially targeted October 22 for releasing the patches, but details of the upcoming security update leaked onto Hacker News on Tuesday. That prompted an accelerated rollout Wednesday, as some government and commercial website operators reportedly took systems offline as a precaution and reports of attempted attacks began circulating.

The larger concern is that artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the economics and speed of cyberattacks. The technology is allowing security researchers to uncover vulnerabilities that might otherwise remain buried for decades, while simultaneously giving malicious actors increasingly powerful tools to exploit those same weaknesses. For organizations responsible for securing the internet, the window between discovering a vulnerability and facing a potentially widespread attack may be shrinking dramatically.

items.title: The ants are definitely up to something
items.content_text:
Humans-B-Gone! is a labour of love animated series about a society of colossal sapient arthropods where humans are vermin. The series mostly follows a timorous tarantula, a mouthy mantis and the titular pest-control service. Don't worry - there's extensive translation (audio, pheremonal and visual) to make things legible to a human audience. You should thank Professor Gregorsa. Or possibly Rev Storm. With season 1 complete, episode 1 sets the scene, or jump right into the action with Episode 2.

Episodes have substantial unobtrusive footnotes explaining the real-world and in-universe science behind what you've just seen. There's even points to be scored! And don't worry pedants - the square-cube law is in full effect, it simply plays second fiddle to The Unknown Nature. Episodes also available on Newgrounds if you prefer.

items.title: The Adult Children Cleaning Up Their Parents' Feeds
items.content_text: Americans over 60 now spend more than half their leisure hours in front of screens. But unlike millennials and most Gen-Xers, who have spent years navigating engagement bait, stealth marketing, and AI slop — and have developed a working instinct for what to trust — older adults tend to have little idea of what they're looking at. This susceptibility is creating an entirely new type of responsibility for the adult children of these suddenly very online parents, who flock to Reddit to ask things like, How do I stop my dad from watching fake Bruce Lee AI slop? Is it possible to curate a feed for my anxious, elderly mother? and How can I stop my aging parents from believing fake news?

items.title: Kushner Phone Hack Reveals How Middle East Dictators Bought Him Off
items.content_text:
Jared Kushner oversaw foreign slush funds filled and managed by the leaders of the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Israel, Vanity Fair reported Thursday.

In the forthcoming book Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East, author Matthew Cole made a shocking revelation about Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s potentially illegal dealings with foreign dictators.

During the first Trump administration, the Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service discovered a way to hack into Kushner’s iPhone. Officials learned that he was secretly moving hundreds of thousands of dollars through a bank account at First Dubai Bank.

Crucially, Kushner did not own the account, but was merely a signatory for the account managed and owned by the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a government-funded charity run by Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi, a close friend of UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, referred to as MBZ.

Starting in 2017, the Saudis and Emiratis transferred roughly $750 million into the account to be used as a foreign policy slush fund. The charity was used to fund the UAE government’s covert intelligence operations overseas, as well as its secret weapons-purchasing programs, one confidential source told Cole.

First Dubai Bank is run by Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, MBZ’s brother. (Tahnoon also oversees a fund called Lunate, which is among the largest stakeholders in Kushner’s shady private equity firm Affinity Partners.) The money was sent by a bank in Azerbaijan, where banks have a well-established but unadvertised practice of exchanging Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams for an equal amount of American dollars.

Four senior Trump administration officials—including two national security advisers, a White House chief of staff, and a former CIA director—told Cole they were not aware that the president had authorized Kushner to access a foreign government bank account.

Kushner’s lawyer denied that his client had any knowledge of the charity or the bank account, and claimed that Trump’s son-in-law did not make any arrangements with foreign leaders that the president did not agree to.

But that wasn’t the only account Kushner managed. By the spring of 2018, MBZ had also put roughly $1 billion for Kushner into a second account at Israel’s Central Bank—at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s urging. Unlike the political slush fund, Kushner’s activity in this account indicated that it was for his personal use. The money was difficult to access, and so Kushner would channel requests to Netanyahu for the funds to be released through then-Ambassador David M. Friedman, and then move the money through an account in Cyprus. The former diplomat denied any involvement in the scheme, and claimed that “there are no accounts, and never were.”

Additionally, the UAE secretly put money into yet another account at Israel’s Central Bank as a “rainy-day defense fund” in case of an attack from Iran.

It should go without saying, but Kushner did not disclose his access to these accounts to the IRS—potentially violating federal law. At the time, Kushner was a government employee who worked in the White House, meaning he was required to submit both public and confidential financial forms and disclose any bank account on which he had access as a signatory or beneficiary. Kushner also failed to disclose himself as an agent of a foreign government, having been paid nearly $2 billion in total by foreign leaders. If he offered anything in return for the money, even just conversations with his father-in-law, then he would have violated U.S. bribery laws and the foreign agent statute.

This is far from the first time that Kushner has been accused of blatant self-dealing in his service to Trump. He used used peace negotiations with Russia to concoct a multibillion-dollar deal to benefit his business partners, invested in a firm that saw massive gains from Israel’s ongoing military campaign in Gaza, and used his gig as special envoy as an opportunity to try to raise funds from foreign governments and individuals in the Middle East.

items.title: Todd Blanche Floats Chilling Likelihood of Trump Election Interference
items.content_text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche is open to blocking states from certifying the November midterm elections.

Blanche made the comments during a Thursday press gaggle in Virginia.

“Is there any scenario in which DOJ would weigh in on that certification process or try to block states from certifying?” a reporter asked.

“Is there any scenario? Yes,” Blanche said. “Of course there’s scenarios that we could all come up with hypothetically, some doomsday scenario for example, right? I don’t think it’s proper to make any kind of conclusory statements about what’s gonna happen in the future.... It is not DOJ’s intention to—and it’s never our intention—to improperly interfere with our elections.”

“But to say that there’s no circumstances that we would ever do that, of course I’m not gonna say that,” he continued.

The federal government is not supposed to play a role in state certification of elections. The soundbite quickly raised alarm to Blanche’s left.

“THIS IS CODE RED !!” wrote California Governor Gavin Newsom’s press office. “Trump’s politicized DOJ is now saying out loud that they may interfere in the election in a desperate, unprecedented, and completely unAmerican and anti-democratic attempt to keep Trump and MAGA in power.”

“He answered the question of whether Donald Trump’s DOJ may interfere in the midterm elections with a ‘Yes,’” said Campaign for New York Health’s Melanie D’Arrigo.

It is incredibly abnormal for a sitting attorney general to float the possibility of interfering with an election, especially one who believes the Justice Department is not independent from the president (in this case, a president who has spent six years trying to manufacture a baseless voter fraud scandal). Yet Blanche, Trump’s formal personal attorney, did it with ease.

items.title: Rejected Ballots Skyrocketed in Five States Thanks to USPS
items.content_text:
Mail-in ballots are being rejected at a growing rate in rural areas thanks to U.S. Postal Service cuts. 

ProPublica reports that in the primaries this year in Oregon, North Carolina, Washington, California, and Ohio, a staggering amount of ballots arrived too late to be counted due to delays in mail delivery. Three days after primary elections in Stevens County, Washington, election workers checked the mail for late ballots. They found over 500 envelopes when they were only expecting a few dozen. 

The same thing happened in all of eastern Washington’s 11 rural counties. Over 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to just 600 late ballots in 2022’s midterm elections. The nonprofit news outlet traces the issues to a number of changes at the USPS. 

First, over the past three years, the postal service moved to process first-class mail at regional hubs instead of smaller plants closer to local post offices. Then, just after the presidential election two years ago, the USPS cut in half its pickups from post offices at least 50 miles away from those hubs.

That increased delivery time by at least one day. Postmarks, which are critical for legally verifying if a ballot can be counted, were also pushed back as those stamps aren’t added until mail reaches a regional processing center. In rural counties in the five states, late ballots have a grace period as long as they are postmarked by Election Day, but rejections still shot up compared to 2022 according to ProPublica’s findings. 

The postal service’s policy changes were pushed by Trump administration officials, and likely unintentionally hurt the Republican Party.  

“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, told ProPublica, noting that his state has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”

USPS officials claim that delays are much less likely for November’s general election because of “extraordinary measures.” The postal service sent a memo to every post office in the country earlier this fall instructing them to separate ballots from other mail for the 10 days preceding Election Day on November 3. The memo said that the post offices should deliver the ballots on the day they arrive. 

“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said the chair of the Postal Service board of governors Amber McReynolds in a press conference last week, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”

If they are wrong, though, many races could be affected. A few thousand or even hundred ballots could swing many contests in rural areas, leaving voters across the political spectrum disenfranchised. Trump’s attempts to undermine the entire process aren’t helping, either.

items.title: Van Hollen Demands Answers Over No Kings’ Blocked Accounts
items.content_text:
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen demanded answers Thursday from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg after the company suspended the No Kings Coalition’s official Instagram account during the group’s nationwide day of action.

In a letter shared exclusively with The New Republic, Van Hollen asked why the coalition’s Instagram was mysteriously shut down for more than an hour during a major day of early voting activations over the weekend. The administrators did not regain access for hours, restricting their ability to communicate with supporters.

Van Hollen asked the MAGA-friendly technocrat whether Meta had communicated internally about the No Kings Coalition, and to explain why it took so long to restore the administrators’ access to the account. So far, Democratic Senators Ron Wyden, Chris Murphy, Richard Blumenthal, and Jeff Merkley have joined Van Hollen’s probe.

Van Hollen also demanded an explanation for Meta’s vacillating excuses for the incident. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone initially claimed Sunday that the account was shut down due to high frequencies of posting, sharing, and commenting. The next day, however, he claimed it had to do with the account’s “reading” behavior.

“Not only are Meta’s shifting explanations alarming, the substance of the claims paint the picture that one of the largest social media companies in the world is somehow incapable of handling technical concerns about an account without shutting it down for hours,” Van Hollen’s letter stated.

The Maryland Democrat also questioned why the account was not included in Meta’s cross-check program, which allows the company to designate civic entities to ensure human review before a decision is made that could severely jeopardize participation in significant political events.

“This is not the first time that Meta has experienced shutdowns or lapses around political speech leading up to the 2026 elections,” the letter stated, referring to a so-called “glitch” that disrupted Ohio Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown’s campaign ads on Facebook and restrictions placed on Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s Instagram ahead of his country’s elections. On Tuesday, Meta’s Oversight Board called the incidents part of a series of “recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts,” and that it was unclear why the error was not caught by the company’s mistake-prevention systems.

“How will you guarantee that accounts sharing critical election and civic information are not incorrectly shutdown in the future? What steps will Meta take between now and election day to ensure that accounts sharing this information are not taken offline without notice?” the letter asked.

With the midterm elections fast-approaching, Van Hollen asked that Zuckerberg provide lawmakers with responses by October 29.

The incident raises serious concerns about Meta’s impartial handling of voting information and political speech—particularly in light of the company’s close financial relationship with the Trump administration. The company awarded nearly $25 million straight into Donald Trump’s pocket, $10 million to a Trump-aligned dark money group, $5 million to the president’s White House ballroom, and $1 million to his inaugural fund. In return, Meta stands to make billions in hefty government contracts and data center handouts.

items.title: Judge Orders Trump to End Election Probe Based on Error-Filled Data
items.content_text:
A judge has ordered the Department of Homeland Security to end its investigations into noncitizen voting in nine states. 

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín ruled Wednesday that DHS’s data  contains multiple inaccuracies and could be used to target U.S. citizens, The Washington Post reports. She barred the department from using the records in “elections-related field operations and field interviews” but delayed the order, allowing the Trump administration until 5 p.m. Friday to appeal. 

DHS agents have recently been spotted going door to door to look for noncitizen voters. Under the order, DHS would be barred from using the program to continue these operations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin. 

According to the Post, the department built target lists from commercial voter files, official state voter rolls, and other lists comprising 48.2 million voters that Martínez-Olguín, appointed by President Biden, said came from “questionable provenance.”

Because of pressure from administration officials, DHS employees were only given up to 12 minutes to clear someone from the list, Martínez-Olguín said. She ruled that this had a high likelihood of error because the government doesn’t keep a true master list of people living in the U.S. that includes their citizenship status. 

Groups including the California Nurses Association sued the government, claiming that the White House was violating the Voting Rights Act by intimidating people who try to increase voter turnout or help with voting. Martínez-Olguín ruled that these groups had valid claims. 

“The fear is objectively reasonable, and compounded by [DHS’s] use of data that is widely known to inadvertently include U.S. citizens, leaves citizens afraid that their name will be wrongly included in the hundreds of thousands identified for investigation,” Martínez-Olguín wrote. 

Earlier this week, the Department of Justice admitted that its list of noncitizens who illegally voted in California may not be accurate, and officials in the state as well as Los Angeles County attested the same in court. That hasn’t stopped the federal government from arresting people based on that faulty information, though.

items.title: AI Bots Are Accessing People’s Bank Accounts Unprompted
items.content_text:
Major American banks have reported unauthorized artificial intelligence bots inside consumer accounts, sources told Axios Thursday.

The infiltration is happening faster than the financial institutions can respond to it. Even more concerning, some of the agents appear to be acting independently, performing actions that users did not request or automate.

Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Wells Fargo are just some of the banks racing to contain the AI-related risk. Part of the containment strategy involves rapidly rewriting and redeploying terms of service to their clients in order to firmly restrict the use of AI from their platforms.

Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi are in the process of restricting third-party agents from accessing their platforms entirely, according to Axios.

Bank executives described the situation to Axios as “horrifying.” One official told the digital newsroom that the industry has “grave concerns” about whether the rampant threat could impact user finances.

Executives reportedly recognize that a growing demographic of banking clients are interested in using their own AI agents to perform financial tasks and transactions. However, the risk is currently too high to allow individual clients that kind of access, particularly at the rate at which the revolutionary technology is adapting and changing.

Another banking executive told Axios that it is difficult to distinguish between authorized AI agents and agents that have “gone rogue” and inappropriately accessed a customer account.

“Banks are investing in preventing worst-case scenarios, but they are also preparing in case they do happen, including with ‘day after’ scenario planning that would allow them to quickly secure or restore customer access,” Axios reported.

items.title: State Department Unveils Plan to Only Promote Trump Supporters
items.content_text:
The Department of State has asked civil servants up for promotions who they voted for in the 2016, 2020, and 2024 presidential elections.

Top State Department officials have indicated that the only candidates eligible for mid- to upper-level foreign service roles were people who had supported President Donald Trump, and that political donations to any Democrat would be disqualifying, The Washington Sun reported Thursday.

The publication spoke to six current and former State Department officials with knowledge of these conversations, including three sources who spoke directly to employees who were asked about their politics.

Federal law prohibits federal officials from making personnel decisions based on political affiliation, but it has seemingly become a regular practice during the second Trump administration. This latest move comes as the State Department has attempted to push out its most senior career officials, in order to ensure the top ranks are all politically loyal to the current president.

In a statement to the Sun, a spokesperson for the State Department declined to comment on the outlet’s reporting about voting history questions, but expounded on the importance of employees’ “fidelity.”

“Fidelity means upholding the Constitution and the law and executing policy with loyalty to the American people and their interests,” the spokesperson said. “It emphasizes the critical importance of service, integrity, and policy alignment across the Foreign Service. It is not about partisan behavior but rather about executing the president’s vision for foreign policy.”

In July 2025, the State Department added a “fidelity” section to the foreign service’s performance-evaluation process, requiring managers to assess whether their employees had succeeded at “completely aligning oneself and one’s team to the most current [U.S. government] goals.”

Apparently, the agency has taken that to mean high-ranking diplomats are required to have personally supported all of Trump’s bids for presidency over the last decade.

items.title: Three Male Escorts Say Lindsey Graham Paid Them—One Was a Minor
items.content_text:
Three male escorts have claimed that they had sex with the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham—with one engaging in relations with him when he was just 17.

The men are featured in a documentary from The Young Turks, which they worked on for a year. Graham, who was one of the most conservative, anti-LGBTQ senators during his long tenure, had also been plagued by rumors about his alleged homosexuality until the day he died.

“His last words to me were ‘I needed that,’” said Cory, who started as a sex worker after he was kicked out of his parents’ house for coming out in 2005. He detailed his first meeting with Graham at the Mayflower Hotel in Washington, D.C.

“He was very professional looking.… He looked like a different class than I’m used to.… But the thing that stood out to me was his accent. He had this big, grandiose Southern accent that I hadn’t heard in years,” Cory said. He then claimed that Graham liked being “degraded,” spanked, and called “faggot.” Cory said Graham paid him $1,500, and The Young Turks shared various travel logs that place both him and Graham in D.C. at the same time.

Two other men, Jesse and Kelvin, had similar stories with Graham.

“It’s not exactly a secret that he was a homosexual,” Jesse said.

Kelvin alleges he met Graham in Arizona in 2001 when he was 17 years old. “He contacted me, said that he had heard about me from someone, that I came recommended,” he said. “I asked Lindsey what was bringing him into town. He said that a buddy of his was having some major event that he was gonna be there for.” That buddy was Senator John McCain, whom Graham was visiting for a Fourth of July party.

“As he was adjusting his pants, he got a good look at me. And then that was when he was a bit startled, and almost terrified. He looked at me then with a very stern, angry scowl on his face, and he was like, ‘You’re under the age of 18, you’re 17 aren’t you?’” Graham panicked, but then gave in after Kelvin lied and told him he had just turned 18. He was paid $120.

“So after spending his whole life being homophobic, Lindsey was having sex with underage male prostitutes???” liberal commentator Harry Sisson wrote online.

This is one of the longest-running rumors in Washington. It matches what others said in the days after Graham’s death, and makes every one of Graham’s homophobic votes, policies, and comments—including voting against gay marriage multiple times—all the more despicable.

Watch the full documentary here.

items.title: Trump Ordered to Sit for Deposition as His BBC Lawsuit Blows Up
items.content_text:
A federal judge has ordered President Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 with attorneys for the British Broadcasting Corporation, which he is suing for $10 billion for defamation.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett ruled Thursday that Trump can’t delay answering questions from the BBC’s lawyers, the Associated Press reports. The president had canceled a planned October 16 deposition based on a “matter of national importance.” According to the BBC’s attorneys, Trump was in fact campaigning in Georgia for the midterms that day.

“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” BBC attorney Charles Tobin told the AP, adding that “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff” with only two months left in the discovery period of the case.

If Trump does not attend a deposition before the deadline, he could face sanctions including the dismissal of his case. The only reprieve he can get is if the lawsuit’s discovery period is extended beyond December 18.

Trump is accusing the BBC of defaming him in a 2024 documentary about the January 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection, claiming the media company used deceptive editing to make it appear that he was urging his supporters to use violence to overturn the 2020 presidential election results. The network denies Trump’s accusations.

But the president was almost certainly trying to shake down the network, which appears to have backfired. BBC attorneys are trying to get his nemesis, former special counsel Jack Smith, to testify, and Trump has also fought attempts to subpoena his children and dig into his finances. He should have known better than to go after the BBC, which, being backed by licensing fees from the U.K.’s TV-owning public, wasn’t likely to settle with him. Now, he either has to win his case on its nonexistent merits, or drop it altogether.

This story has been updated.

items.title: Here’s What’s Getting Lost in Headlines About the Amy Acton Attack Ad
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

In the past two days, near-universal condemnation of an attack ad featuring Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and her estranged mother has brought the governor’s race to national attention. But even before that, this race was full of personal attacks. Why voter issues seem to have taken a back seat in this race is a mystery, especially in a year when people seem extra eager for politicians to speak to their substantive policy concerns.

“This has definitely been a race that has been more about the character of the candidates than it has been about policy issues themselves,” said Dominic Wells, a professor of political science at Bowling Green State University. The candidates will not meet on the debate stage (Acton declined a debate invitation, while Republican Vivek Ramaswamy accepted). So much of the race has played out through campaign ads where the candidates portray each other as unfit for office. “Anti-Ramaswamy campaign ads have linked him to profiting off of [and] backing ineffective prescription drugs,” Wells said. “So they’re painting him as corrupt and dishonest.”

Ramaswamy’s campaign has tried to use Acton’s time as director of Ohio’s Department of Health to tap into conservative frustration over Covid-19 shutdowns and vaccination policies. “This isn’t a message that seems to be sticking with Ohioans as much. Ohioans generally don’t want to hear about Covid anymore,” Wells said. David Jackson, also a professor of political science at Bowling Green State University, agrees: “The people who are still mad about masks and still mad about vaccines were probably never going to vote for a Democrat anyway,” he said.

The ad circulated on Tuesday, which featured Acton’s estranged mother, however, represented a major escalation. In the ad, Acton’s mother calls her daughter “a liar” and tells voters: “Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself.” Acton has been estranged from her mother since she was 12 years old, after her mother stayed in a relationship with Acton’s stepfather, who sexually abused Acton between the ages of 9 and 12 (and then, when facing criminal charges for it, skipped town). Despite immediate blowback against the ad, the Ramaswamy campaign is planning to spend $4 million to air it on television.

Several Republicans have since denounced the ad. Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is running a tough race for Senate in Ohio, seems to be engaged in a difficult, and maybe physically impossible, balancing act on the topic. “Jon Husted is trying to present himself as a normal, mainline Republican, trying to get some independents to vote for him,” Jackson explained. In Ohio, where the governor’s race and Senate race have been somewhat linked in voters’ minds, the ad puts Husted in a challenging position.

“I would not have run that ad,” Husted said on Wednesday to The Associated Press. But also on Wednesday, he appeared at a rally with Vice President JD Vance and Ramaswamy. At the rally, Vance said he was “disgusted”—not by the ad itself, but by Republicans who criticized it.

When asked about the ad and the substantive debates that seem to be falling by the wayside in this race, Acton spokesperson Addie Bullock said: “Dr. Acton is going to every corner of Ohio to listen deeply to voters and share her plans to lower costs, fully fund public schools, end the corruption in our Statehouse, and ensure that every Ohioan has the opportunity to succeed. Her vision for Ohio stands in stark contrast with her opponent, billionaire scam artist Vivek Ramaswamy, who has spent his campaign spewing repulsive lies from the seat of the private jet he insists on taking everywhere.”

Contrary to the impression given by headlines from this race, there are plenty of policy issues that Ohioans care about this year. As in Ohio’s Senate race, data centers have become a standout issue forcing Republicans to play defense. Acton has called for a “conditional moratorium” under which data centers must use union labor, cover their own utility costs, and follow environmental standards. Ramaswamy, who used to speak positively about data centers, has backtracked somewhat and now says that they should only be built on abandoned industrial sites, must comply with environmental rules, and should provide free electricity for the closest 100,000 residential homes.

All evidence suggests that voters care even more about affordability. Acton’s campaign has put out a detailed affordability plan that includes proposals for working-class family tax cuts and lowering energy bills, among other things. Ramaswamy, meanwhile, has called for cutting property taxes and phasing out state income tax—moves that some experts say could decimate municipal services like police, firefighters, and libraries.

Education is another critical issue in the state. In 1997, the state’s Supreme Court ruled that Ohio’s method for funding public education was unconstitutional. Since then, politicians have tried and failed to reform the education system. The state spent more than $1 billion on voucher programs in the 2026 fiscal year. Acton opposes the voucher programs, and Ramaswamy would like to see them expanded.

The new attack ad against Acton, and the fallout from it, may not change the race, which has already been marked by negativity and personal attacks. Early voting has already started, and voters have been inundated with ads for months. But there’s always a chance that it could make a last-minute difference. “The common thought in Ohio politics is that the state tends to break towards Republicans in the final weeks of the campaign,” Jackson said. “Ramaswamy may have given up that built-in advantage in the last couple weeks here with this backlash.”

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

Protesters, community leaders, family members, and local news reporters in Senatobia, Mississippi, have been trying for months to get answers and keep the spotlight on the horrifying case of one-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was killed by police in June. Now, the story may finally be gaining national traction. On Monday, Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced her department’s finding that “use of force was justified” when police shot the one-year-old in his mother’s arms during a confrontation in a Walmart parking lot over a report of diaper shoplifting.

Outrage over the finding is growing now that body cam and surveillance footage published by Darkhorse Press, and subsequently verified by The New York Times, has shown police officers running and pulling their guns en masse at a car that, at the time, was traveling in reverse, away from them. You can read the Times’s analysis of the video, which then shows the sedan moving forward and at least one officer firing into it, here. In July, Mississippi Today reported that the officer involved had previously been accused of “exaggerating the risks that a vehicle posed to officers during another parking lot confrontation that escalated into violence in 2019.” (He has also been named in one other misconduct complaint and has been accused of racist speech toward a co-worker.)

Fitch, a Republican, is running for governor in 2027. The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus (MLBC) on Tuesday, prior to the new video emerging, condemned Fitch’s finding and called for the release of evidence and an independent review. “Kohen Wiley was a baby. He posed no threat,” MLBC Chairman and Mississippi Representative Kabir Karriem, a Democrat, said. On Tuesday, Mississippi’s Democratic Party leadership also issued a statement calling for a release of evidence, an independent review, “direct, respectful communication with Kohen’s family” (who reportedly first heard about Fitch’s finding via Facebook), and “strong safeguards governing the use of gunfire against moving vehicles.” The Intercept noted this week that Senatobia police in the past two years have “[jailed] a 10-year-old boy for public urination,” forcefully arrested two teenage sisters while the then-police chief told them to “get your Black ass out of the road,” and “on Mother’s Day 2025 — in the same Walmart parking lot where Kohen Wiley would be shot dead … forced a woman out of her car in front of her young children for sitting in a handicapped parking space.”

Elsewhere:

  • The Bush family increasingly seems to be backing James Talarico against Ken Paxton in Texas’s Senate race. Hot on the heels of last week’s news that Barbara Bush donated to Talarico’s super PAC, George W. Bush’s brother Neil Bush announced on Tuesday that he voted for Talarico, praising the candidate’s character. “I have been deeply troubled by Paxton’s conduct as Texas Attorney General,” he wrote, adding “I believe Donald Trump and those who have enabled him have done enormous damage to the Republican Party.” Last week, Trump called Texas GOP pillars John Cornyn and Karl Rove “WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks” for refusing to back Paxton, so… start your clocks.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

As the lawsuit against Cornell University and seven fraternity members over a gang rape continues to make headlines, Data for Progress releases a new survey that found that a majority of voters don’t trust “college administrations, elected officials, or fraternities and sororities to appropriately respond to sexual assault claims,” and they think fraternities and sororities are bad for campus life.

On Thursday at 4 p.m., University of Massachusetts Amherst’s Political Economy Research Institute, in conjunction with Third Act and the Better Futures Project, will host an online conversation between Bill McKibben, Michael Ash, James K. Boyce, and Joel Tickner on “Environmental Policies that Work for Working Americans.” It’s part of “an eight-week series this fall, highlighting policy proposals developed by more than 40 experts on the [university’s] Game Changers: Economic Policies for a Working America, team.”

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Here’s Why That’s B.S.

The Trump administration is escalating its “investigation” into Representative Ilhan Omar over whether the age that her now-deceased father put on her immigration application more than 25 years ago was accurate. Watch TNR’s Edie Olmsted make the case that this is really about the midterms.


Political Trivia Question of the Day  

With Rob Sand apparently poised to win Iowa’s gubernatorial race: When did the Hawkeye State last elect a Democratic governor?

(Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Trump Spends Entire Rally Speech Just Making Weird Noises
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump went post-verbal Wednesday at his rally in South Carolina.

After holding 20 campaign rallies in the span of just two months, the evidently exhausted 80-year-old president has started to insert wild sound effects into his already incoherent rants.

At one point, Trump appeared to short-circuit in the middle of a sentence. Instead of saying former North Carolina Governor Nikki Haley’s name, the president produced a gagging sound.

“I’d say 90 percent of the reason I took the governor—EUHH,” Trump said. “I took the governor, I put her over at the United Nations, because I wanted this guy to be, I wanted the guy to become governor.”

Trump has repeatedly misspelled or misstated Haley’s name. Recently, Trump has appeared to forget the names of candidates he’s shown up to support.

Later, Trump described the unlawful military strikes on alleged drug smuggling boats using one of his favorite sound effects. “We brought the flow of deadly drugs coming in by ocean and sea down by 97—pew, pew, pew. Ninety-seven,” he said. Trump has been repeating this number for months, but the Pentagon’s own statements don’t support this claim.

It then appeared that Trump has given up on pretending that the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz has been restored. He’s also given up on trying to say it.

“Oh, and when Iran ends. POW,” Trump said, miming a downward flow. “The oil,” he clarified.

Trump’s nearly eight-month “six-week war” against Iran has caused a sustained spike in energy prices, creating a quagmire for Republicans in the coming midterm elections. The president’s pathetic deal to lift sanctions on Russian oil hasn’t helped. Trump continues to promise that an end is near, but indirect negotiations are still ongoing.

It’s hard not to view this latest rally as one humiliating moment after another. Speaking in front of thousands of people, Trump ranted about wanting to change the name of the Atlantic Ocean to “Trump Ocean,” insisted that he should’ve won the Pulitzer Prize for writing (after confusing it for his much-coveted Nobel Peace Prize), cheered on a rallygoer who assaulted a heckler, and leered at Senator Tim Scott, of all people.

items.title: JD Vance Totally Humiliated as NFL Team Ignores Him
items.content_text:
JD Vance was ghosted by practically every player on the Cincinnati Bengals football team during what he apparently believed would be a spontaneous meet and greet Wednesday evening.

The vice president waited outside the locker room. Just about every team member looked at Vance and decided not to interact with him—save for tight end Drew Sample, who gave Vance’s son a fist bump. Sample then gave Vance a handshake.

The entire situation—and its terrible optics—echoed a similar locker room visit by FBI Director Kash Patel, who unexpectedly appeared in videos with the U.S. men’s hockey team after their Olympic gold medal win earlier this year.

At the time, Patel was caught on tape chugging beers inside the locker room in Milan, spurring nationwide backlash as the American public questioned if the conspiracy podcaster turned intelligence chief had utilized taxpayer funds for the excursion. But at least Patel made it inside.

Despite occupying the number two office in America, Vance quietly waited for attention in the Bengals’ hallway. When it became clear that a meet and greet wasn’t going to happen, Vance wandered off with his entourage.

It was not immediately clear why the team snubbed Vance, but either way, the vice president should have bigger things on his plate. Earlier Wednesday, Vance sparked statewide backlash across Ohio for defending a disturbing advertisement by Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that featured the estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s opponent, Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton.

The advert had Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, claim that “Amy has a serious problem.” Acton has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, ABC News reported. Arthur abandoned her two children to skip town with her husband, Acton’s stepfather, who was indicted for sexually abusing the Democratic candidate as a young girl.

“Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” Vance said on Wednesday.

items.title: “I Loved That”: Trump Celebrates as MAGA Fans Beat Protester
items.content_text:
President Trump celebrated violence at his rally in South Carolina Thursday night.

At least nine protesters interrupted his speech at Clemson University, according to a pool report. In one instance, a heckler was punched by a Trump supporter in the crowd, and the president loved it.

“Wow. Man, I love that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was, that was unbelievable. Is everybody OK? Who’s the guy that threw that punch?

“You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” Trump added, referring to the champion boxer in attendance.

“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally. He got whacked.”

In another instance, a MAGA fan followed a protester as security escorted him out, and hit him on the head.

Trump has a history of celebrating violence in his rallies going back to the start of his political career. In February 2016, Trump wished aloud at a rally in Las Vegas that he would have liked to punch a protester in the face. The next month, he told a rally crowd in Iowa, “So if you see somebody getting ready to throw a tomato, knock the crap out of ’em, would you? I promise you, I will pay for the legal fees. I promise. I promise.”

As the president’s dwindling popularity keeps setting records, more and more people are showing up to his pre-midterm election rallies to heckle and protest him. The economy continues to grow worse thanks to his failed economic policies and disastrous war in Iran, increasing dissatisfaction even in areas that voted for him by wide margins.

However, Trump still retains a core group of die-hard supporters, who are perfectly willing to engage in violence to demonstrate their loyalty, whether it’s storming the Capitol building or beating up protesters. To Trump, however, nothing can go too far.

items.title: Sheriffs Say Greg Abbott Is Lying About Their Endorsements
items.content_text:
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott publicized the endorsements of 11 Democratic sheriffs. Three of them denied ever endorsing him.

Zapata County Sheriff Ramon Montes, Val Verde County Sheriff Joe Frank Martinez, and Webb County Sheriff Marin Cuellar all publicly announced that they were not endorsing Abbot after he posted them on his endorsement list on Monday. While Cuellar has been removed from the list, Montes and Martinez are still on it.

“Please remove my name from this for the Governor Abbott. This is Sheriff Martin Cuellar. The governor endorsed Tano my brother’s opponent,” Cuellar wrote in a text screenshot he posted on Facebook. Cuellar is the brother of Democratic Representative Henry Cuellar, who is currently running for Texas’s 28th House district.

“I want to make it unequivocally clear that I have not issued a political endorsement of Governor Greg Abbott, and I did not authorize anyone to use my name as an endorsement,” Martinez wrote in his own official statement. “I made it clear to the Sheriff who submitted the endorsement that I could not endorse Governor Abbott. I also made it clear that no one from the Governor’s office ever contacted me regarding an endorsement, and that I do not need anyone speaking on my behalf.”

Sheriff Montes’s office told Border Report that he “is not endorsing anyone at this time.”

Recent polling has Abbott sitting just three points ahead of his Democratic challenger, former state Representative Gina Hinosoja.

items.title: Top Democratic Leader in Redistricting Fight Arrested
items.content_text:
Virginia Senate President Pro Tempore L. Louise Lucas, the Democratic leader behind the state’s redistricting effort, was arrested Thursday in connection with an alleged bribery and racketeering scheme.

In a 45-page indictment filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, Lucas and six co-defendants were charged with conspiring to distribute and possess marijuana, conspiring to launder money, laundering money, and committing bribery by distributing large quantities of illegal marijuana under the auspices of her legal medical cannabis business.

Lucas, an 82-year-old great-grandmother, has served in the Virginia Senate since 1992. She faces five of the eight charges included in the indictment. These charges arrive five months after the FBI raided Lucas’s office in Portsmouth, Virginia, and the neighboring cannabis dispensary she co-owns.

Speaking at a press conference, FBI Director Kash Patel claimed that Lucas had accumulated nearly $5 million in ill-gotten gains over the past five years.

Lucas has been a frequent critic of Republicans and President Donald Trump, and is an ally to Virginia’s Democratic Governor Abigail Spanberger. The state senator was a central figure in mounting her party’s redistricting efforts earlier this year, which were ultimately blocked by the Virginia Supreme Court.

Also listed in the indictment were Lucas’s daughters Theresa Lucas-Lamb and Lisa Lucas-Burke, who is currently running for Portsmouth City Council. The DOJ manual prohibits federal prosecutors from timing any action for the purpose of undermining a candidate in an upcoming election.

But speaking at the press conference, Attorney General Todd Blanche insisted that the government’s actions were proper and “consistent with past practices.” When asked whether the investigation was political payback, Blanche said: “We don’t do political paybacks,” and claimed the probe had begun years before Trump reentered office. The  attorney general couldn’t offer a good explanation, however, for why he and the FBI director had bothered to give an official press conference for charges related to a declassified drug.
