Vice President JD Vance called a brown man at his rally an “illegal immigrant” because he interrupted his rally to demand the release of the Epstein files.

“[The] corrupt, far-left cartel has subjected this country—” Vance was saying at his North Carolina rally, before the protester stood up directly behind him.

“God bless our children!” the man in the crowd yelled. “Release the Epstein files!”

Chants of “USA” began to drown him out as he was removed from the rally by security.

“Ladies and gentlemen, I’m gonna have to amend something I said earlier. I said that we have had zero illegal border crossings in the United States of America,” Vance said with a smile, implying that the protester was not a U.S. citizen. “But one isn’t bad, right?”

Vance’s response was lambasted by those to his left, as many saw his response to another call to release the Epstein files—something Trump himself campaigned on—as contradictory.

“They’re kicking people out of Republican rallies for shouting the same things they’ve been shouting at Republican rallies for years,” Puerto Rican journalist Benjamín Torres Gotay wrote on X.

“It’s insulting to suggest only ‘illegal immigrants’ care about justice for victims and accountability for perpetrators,” California Governor Gavin Newsom’s press office posted. “Most American citizens do too!”

The Trump administration promised its supporters a full release of the Epstein files that would expose the “deep state” and bring justice to survivors. Instead it has continued to obscure information and avoid transparency, with Attorney General Todd Blanche refusing to seriously meet with survivors, survivors getting kicked out of the GOP midterm convention, and now Vance’s assumption that a nonwhite individual calling for justice must be some kind of illegal alien.

items.title: Trump Says New Mexico Should Change Its Name to—Yep, You Guessed It
items.content_text:
President Trump now wants New Mexico to change its name to something that doesn’t offend him. 

Just like with the Gulf of Mexico, Trump wants the state to be called “New America” instead, he wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. 

“New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America! The name would add great value and prestige to the State! Home Values and Incomes would rise, and you would be even prouder while saluting our beautiful American Flag! Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” the president ranted. 

Trump’s attacks on New Mexico are almost certainly because the state has voted Democratic in eight of the last nine presidential elections and has always voted against him. Its entire congressional delegation is Democratic, as well as all of its statewide elected officials. Democrats also control both houses of its state legislature.  

But aside from Trump’s normal attacks on Democrats, he has fixated on unilaterally changing place names in his second term, possibly out of cognitive decline. He’s signed executive orders to change the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, and Lake Ontario to Lake America. His latest renaming is “artificial intelligence” to “super intelligence,” which isn’t sticking even in his own Cabinet. 

The people of New Mexico won’t take kindly to Trump’s suggestion, and the move will just invite mockery. Meanwhile, the midterms are approaching, and the president is supposed to be spending his time campaigning to save Republicans from getting shellacked in two weeks. It’s highly unlikely that changing a state’s name is going to win any votes.

items.title: Did Trump’s Kennedy Center Boss Rip Off Alina Habba’s Husband?
items.content_text:
And the scandals keep coming: President Donald Trump’s close ally Ric Grenell, who has recently served as both special envoy to Venezuela and acting director of the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, came under fire Monday for new evidence that he offered a pay-to-play scheme with wealthy Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon. Mildon recently married former Trump attorney Alina Habba.

The accusations came to light on October 9, after Habba stormed into the Oval Office to tell the president that Grenell had never deposited a nearly $6 million donation her husband made to the Kennedy Center in 2025. Grenell and Mildon were in touch in early 2025, before Mildon and Habba met, because Mildon had business contracts in Venezuela and had also expressed interest in the Kennedy Center. According to documents from Mildon’s lawyers, Grenell offered to support Mildon in Venezuela, including making him the “American face down in V.”

Mildon eventually transferred $17.6 million to an account supplied by Grenell, purportedly for a deal involving a private Texas defense company and the Democratic Republic of Congo, with the understanding that $5.6 million of that sum would end up at the Kennedy Center. But according to Habba, the $5.6 million never made it there.

White House counsel Will Scharf is now investigating the donation, including texts from Grenell supplied by Mildon’s lawyers.

“Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre, and you’ll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS,” a May 3, 2025, text from Grenell to Mildon allegedly said.

Grenell has vehemently denied the accusations. “I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I’ve never received any payment from him at all,” Grenell told Axios, referring to Mildon. “Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations.”

“There’s no way this is true. This is crazy,” Grenell allegedly told the president.

A source told Axios that Grenell claimed he would never use the British English spelling “centre,” rather than “center,” so the text could not be legitimate.

Kennedy Center staff went looking for Mildon’s donation last year but never found it. Instead, financial staffer Lisa Dale found that Mildon actually owed the center a pledged donation of $270,000. “There was nothing about $6 million,” Dale told Axios. “I would have heard about that.”

“POTUS doesn’t want to deal with this. Of course, he’s concerned, but if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem,” said another official with knowledge of the conflict.

“Nobody wants to get in the middle of Alina Habba and Ric Grenell going to war,” a different official said.

items.title: Black MAGA Influencer Says She Was Thrown Out of Ken Paxton Rally
items.content_text:
A Black MAGA influencer says she was booted from a Ken Paxton rally in Texas on Sunday.

Thelma Louise runs a large TikTok account in which she makes pro-Trump content, particularly from her perspective as a Black female conservative. On Sunday, she was excitedly documenting her experience at Paxton’s rally for his upcoming Senate race—before she was asked to leave without cause.

“And there’s no one that I can talk to about this?” Louise asks as she appears to be escorted out. “Wow. Oh my gosh. I cannot believe this.… Someone just came up to me and said that Ken Paxton’s campaign manager wanted me to leave. I am just—my mouth is wide open right now. I really can’t believe this.”

“I was just asked to leave this event, and I did nothing wrong,” she continued. “I was told that Paxton’s campaign manager didn’t want me here. I’m not making any of this up.… I have done nothing but support everyone on the Republican side, and this is how I get treated? I cannot believe the disrespect that I was just given. I left the Democratic Party two years ago, I have volunteered for President Trump’s campaign, and I have worked very hard promoting members of the Republican Party. I’m not quite sure what’s going on, but to be walked out of a room full of people and isolated as if I’d done something wrong—I cannot believe it.”

Louise noted that she drove two hours to get to the rally, and even showed her press credentials for Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas over the summer.

Some online mused that the color of Louise’s skin may have had something to do with her unexplained removal—and noted that it might not have happened at a James Talarico rally because there would likely be more Black people there.

“‘Being MAGA while Black’ chapter 293,” Democratic strategist Ameshia Cross wrote.

“Conservative whites excluding black people? I’ve never heard of such a thing,” said another.

“Was I mistaken for someone else? I don’t know what it was. And I don’t blame any of this on the Republican Party. Because they have loved me, and they have welcomed me with open arms. But Ken Paxton’s campaign manager, that person is 100 percent responsible for the disrespect that I received this evening.”

items.title: Trump’s Border Czar Hints at Sick Next Steps to Target Ilhan Omar
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump’s border czar, Todd Homan, seemed to suggest that the FBI was mounting its own investigation into Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar.

During an appearance on Fox News’s The Big Weekend Show Sunday, Homan was asked whether the Trump administration was investigating any other alleged misconduct by the congresswoman, in addition to immigration fraud allegations.

“I’m not gonna go there,” Homan said.

“Not even a little bit?” asked host Rich Edson.

“Not even a little bit. We’ll leave that up to—that’s a question for the FBI. I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI,” Homan said, smiling.

It was not immediately clear what the FBI would be investigating, or whether it was the same case being mounted by the Department of Homeland Security.

Homeland Security Investigations conducted a raid last week on Omar’s Washington, D.C., home as part of a racist campaign to get her denaturalized and deported. The probe ostensibly centers on whether Omar’s father put her age as 17 rather than 18 on her citizenship application to allow her to qualify immediately for citizenship alongside his own application. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that the government was building a RICO case against her and her family. It’s still unclear what, if any, evidence DHS has found to support its case.

In a letter to the Department of Justice Friday, Omar’s attorney asked for the return of her belongings seized in the raid, including a phone, and argued that there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status,” Fox News 9 reported.

The apparently multiplying probes into Omar represent a lawless campaign by the Trump administration against one of the president’s most outspoken critics. The DOJ manual prohibits federal prosecutors from timing any action, including investigative steps, criminal charges, or statements, for the purpose of undermining a candidate in an upcoming election. Early voting in Minnesota began last week.

items.title: Trump Tries to Ban Jack Smith Testimony as BBC Lawsuit Implodes
items.content_text:
President Trump doesn’t want former special counsel Jack Smith to testify in a deposition as part of Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation.

The BBC has subpoenaed Smith to defend itself from Trump’s accusations that the network defamed him with deceptive editing in a 2024 documentary about the January 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection. In a court filing Friday, Trump’s lawyers tried to fight the subpoena by claiming that “Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter.

“He was not present when President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech (the ‘Speech’) was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump’s state of mind at the time the Speech was given. Any evidence that Smith gathered during his investigation consists of secondhand knowledge based on materials that he and other third parties collected from various sources,” Trump’s lawyers wrote in their complaint.

In response, the BBC’s attorneys wrote, “None of [Trump]’s arguments for blocking the deposition of Mr. Smith can withstand scrutiny,” pointing out that Smith himself doesn’t object to testifying in the deposition and that Trump still has to prove that “he did not foment or incite the January 6 Capitol riot,” as he claims the BBC’s documentary falsely implied.

“No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim, including Plaintiff’s burden to prove falsity,” the BBC’s lawyers wrote.

This is only Trump’s latest attempt to dodge actually having to prove that the BBC defamed him. His attorneys are also fighting attempts to have Trump himself testify, to subpoena his children to testify, and to dive into his finances. Now he either has to give in to the BBC’s lawyers and drop the case or actually try to prove his point and deal with the consequences.

* This story has been updated to remove references about the BBC’s funding.

items.title: They Retired Here for a Country Idyll. But Meta Had Other Plans.
items.content_text:
Outside Mansfield, Georgia, just under an hour’s drive from Atlanta, Jeff and Beverly Morris live right where the road turns from pavement to gravel. They have horses, a dog, a small aboveground pool in the back of their Cape Cod house, and a sign in the kitchen that says, “I was raised on Country Sunshine.” And they have one other thing—a big problem.

Whatever rural idyll they imagined when they bought the home and moved there in 2016, it was shattered when, about a year later, Meta began building a data center less than 400 yards away. The hulking concrete building peeks out through the evergreens, visible from their mailbox.

Last Wednesday, Congressman Ro Khanna, a Democrat who represents part of Silicon Valley, came to visit. The Morrises showed Khanna the canning jars full of the well water they’d kept, in various stages of opacity from whatever brown material had infiltrated their well and clogged their filters. They showed him how the water came straight up from the earth that same solid gray-brown. They showed him a thoroughly corroded hot water heater in their shed, which they’d had to replace, along with just about every other appliance that has water running through it. They say that out of three usable bathrooms in their home, they are down to one. “I did hire a well guy to come out, and I said, ‘Is my property just full of sediment? What is happening here?’” Beverly Morris told Khanna. “And he looked at me, pointed across the road, and he goes, ‘There’s one answer to your question, and it’s not going to change.’”

They showed Khanna a map of their well-water catchment area: Their well is the only water source they have, though their lawyer said Meta has a municipal water hookup for the data center. Brown water sometimes floods their front ditch. Photos of their rural, pastoral nights show them now lit bright as day from light pollution by the data center. “This affects not only your everyday living and what you’ve got to do to adjust your life, but you can’t change, you’re trapped,” Beverly Morris said.

“We’ve got to develop the technology in a way that’s going to help all of us,” Khanna said. “Right now, it’s just helping a few of these tech billionaires, and they’re riding roughshod over communities.” He listed the other threats from Big Tech—the Hugging Face incident, the potential loss of jobs—but zoomed in on the kinds of hits the Morrises and so many Americans like them were taking in their own home, and questioned the costs and the benefits, which right now seem to only be enriching billionaires.

Khanna is pushing for a Data Center Bill of Rights to outline new rules around where and how data centers can be built, meant to protect the people and environments they might impact. He also sent a letter to Meta demanding answers for the Morrises and their co-plaintiffs: They filed a lawsuit against Meta, development companies, and authorities in August.

The fight highlights something even bigger, though. From the center-left, pro-building “abundists” have been putting pressure on Democrats to fund and build more and do it all faster—whether it’s housing or new transportation or research around the technologies that could change our futures—and ease up on the kinds of community-led concerns often dismissed as Nimbyism, which has become a dirty word. They’ve been arguing that this approach can increase unalloyed goods, like more green energy that will slow climate change.

But the data center explosion shows that sometimes bad things that may harm us and the environment can be built just as quickly if we let them, and that there are real questions about who bears the cost and who benefits when rules are waived. Some things might not belong in backyards, or front yards, at all.

The Morrises are just a tiny part of the data center rebellion unfolding across the country, the embattled front lines that illustrate the downside risks to letting the data centers go into residential neighborhoods. They want the harms they’ve listed to serve as a warning.

Meta named one of the roads leading to the data center “Move Fast Way,” borrowing from the early motto of Facebook, before it became the larger Meta, “Move fast and break things.” Breaking things is what the Morrises and their co-plaintiffs said the company did, and they want answers. They say the company has suggested that the problems they’ve encountered are their fault or due to lack of routine maintenance. The Morrises say they never had the problems they’re encountering now, especially with their water, before the data center moved in.

Beverly Morris told Khanna she felt like she was living in the early nineteenth century, having to boil water or cart it in from elsewhere for her animals to drink, which harkens back to the Flint, Michigan, water disaster, which began in 2014. Big blue tubs of clean water sit in the bed of a side-by-side off-road vehicle in their front yard. “That shouldn’t be happening in twenty-first-century America,” Khanna said.

Khanna asked about whether they could move, but the Morrises said they wouldn’t be able to sell their home for what it is worth. They are retired and wanted this to be their home. For them to move would mean cutting their losses.

Democrats have seen a political opportunity in the data center and artificial intelligence fights, both of which have united Americans across the political spectrum in opposition. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the congresswoman from New York, also visited the Morrises earlier this year, and took a jar of their water back to the House floor in May to give a speech. Other Democrats, like Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, have argued for public stakes in AI development so that people can benefit from the money it generates for Wall Street and cushion themselves against possible job losses as the technology changes workplaces.

Americans have grown sharply more negative about data centers, according to Pew Research Center, and states are considering moratoriums on building them, like the one New York passed, until more environmental and community impacts can be studied. There’s a rare bipartisan sense of unity around the issue. Yet the Morrises’ attorneys said none of their representatives, including their current congressman, Representative Mike Collins, who’s running for Senate against Democrat Jon Ossoff, have reached out to them or visited. The Republican Party dismisses data center opposition as driven by Chinese propaganda, and House Republicans have urged the Trump administration to investigate China’s influence on the matter.

Whether or not Khanna and Ocasio-Cortez have presidential ambitions, they both seem to be acting like it, appearing on morning shows and visiting parts of the country far from their districts. The most likely end result is that they will raise their profiles in their own big, influential states, California and New York, where they could have an outsize impact on these issues for the country as a whole because of their prominence.

But what should they influence Big Tech to do, and how? Khanna said the companies keep bringing up competition with China as the justification for building out new data centers so quickly. But he says it can come at irreparable cost. “We can compete without compromising our values,” he says in his letter to Meta. “As such, I also request a briefing from Meta on how, if at all, it will be revising its process of selecting sites for data centers and incorporating community inputs based on its clear failure to do so.”

It’s not the first time in history that rural areas have been asked to bear the brunt of rapid change for technology meant to benefit others. It wouldn’t be the first time in history that a rural or otherwise disregarded neighborhood had to disproportionately bear the brunt of any kind of development. And environments around the country show the scars left when boom and bust cycles destroy local ecosystems and communities only to leave ruin in their wake when they move on to the next big thing. If AI is a bubble and it crashes, it will leave an empty, hulking building in its wake, and studies from abandoned mining communities to urban brownfield sites show how declining infrastructure can damage individual health, further drive down property values, and leave communities empty and vulnerable to crime.

That history is why the hurdles that sometimes slow development, like environmental reviews and community meetings, existed in the first place. I asked Khanna about that tension: How do policymakers reconcile the need for more development around green energy and housing while showing caution around developments like data centers?

“We need to have strong safeguards and guardrails for clean water, for preserving the land, for keeping the air clean,” he said. “I am for building out clean energy, but I’m not for doing that at the expense of environmental standards, and that has to be a conversation about how we do that in the context of building out clean energy. But this is not building out clean energy. This is a data center that is making billions of dollars for these hyperscalers, and there’s no reason to give any waiver from our environmental protection for these data centers.”

That ability, to decide what’s beneficial and what is not, is exactly what so many voters don’t trust that their representatives have right now. Khanna may have been trying to build that trust when he went to visit the Morrises: People want to know someone will listen to their concerns. “Local communities should get to decide first of all whether they want them, and they shouldn’t be near residential communities or farmland,” Khanna said. “I think it’s a pretty commonsense view, and until we get that, there should be a moratorium, on a state-by-state local basis, because we can’t build in ways like this.”

items.title: Meta Weakly Defends Blocking No Kings Instagram in the Middle of Event
items.content_text:
Meta offered a weak excuse for shutting down the No Kings movement’s official Instagram account for several hours during the group’s nationwide action over the weekend to mobilize early voting.

During a major day of activations Saturday, Meta suspended the No Kings account without providing any explanation, the activist group said. Meta eventually restored the account’s visibility, but the administrators did not regain access for hours.

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone provided an updated explanation for the official account’s hourslong suspension: There was a high volume of activity on the page.

“Our engineering team discovered that the spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s ‘reading’ behavior. Specifically, our network security systems detected the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags, the rate of which sharply increased (~4x volume) in intense bursts on October 17,” Stone wrote on X Sunday.

“These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems. This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline.

“An automated re-review of the removal action an hour later recognized that shouldn’t have happened and restored the account. It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account,” he continued. “We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error.”

The No Kings coalition claimed that Meta’s explanation still didn’t make sense.

“In the 24 hours before our account was shut down, we posted only a handful of times and livestreamed to thousands. Meta’s ‘high frequency’ excuse doesn’t add up,” the group wrote on Bluesky Sunday.

“Beyond shutting down our Instagram, we’ve received reports that #NoKings and early voting content was inaccessible, restricted or seemed suppressed across Meta platforms,” the group wrote in a separate post.

Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy responded to Stone’s statement, calling on X for an investigation into the No Kings account’s sudden suspension. “Let’s assume this is true. It’s still a total indictment of Meta’s outsized influence on our culture and politics,” he wrote.

“An investigation is warranted, at the very least, to understand why Meta (which effectively functions these days as a private government) was unable to protect protest against Trump, while it spends so much time trying to get close to Trump,” he added.

By cozying up to the Trump administration, Meta stands to make billions in hefty government contracts and data center handouts. Now it appears that the company may be doubling down on its allegiances by outright silencing the president’s critics.

items.title: Supreme Court Gives Trump More Power Over Independent Agencies
items.content_text:
The Supreme Court just signed off on President Trump’s firing of a member of the National Labor Relations Board despite laws against at-will dismissals, further cementing his power over independent agencies.

On Monday, the high court decided not to review a ruling from the lower U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia allowing the firing of Gwynne Wilcox, who Trump decided to axe just after his inauguration last year. Wilcox was the first Black woman member of the NLRB, and had been appointed to a second five-year term on the board by President Biden in 2023.

The Supreme Court’s decision is in line with its earlier ruling in June allowing Trump to fire a member of the Federal Trade Commission, Rebecca Slaughter. The D.C. circuit decision in Wilcox’s case came before the Supreme Court’s decision in Slaughter’s case.

The NLRB and the FTC, along with other federal regulatory bodies, are supposed to be independent from the president’s control, with bipartisan boards. But in his second term as president, Trump has ignored rules protecting agency members from being fired without cause, pushing out members simply because they were appointed by Democrats.

While the Supreme Court has enabled Trump in the cases of Slaughter and now Wilcox, it has drawn the line with Lisa Cook, a governor on the Federal Reserve Board, and prevented the president from firing her. That hasn’t stopped Trump from attempting to smear Cook with a cooked-up investigation over alleged mortgage fraud. Cook has not been charged with any crimes, but Trump isn’t interested in sniffing out wrongdoing: He wants to assert total control over regulatory agencies.

items.title: Christiane Amanpour Announces Exit From CNN With Farewell Warning
items.content_text:
Longtime CNN chief international anchor Christiane Amanpour will be leaving the network next June.

“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement Monday. “[I look] forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”

Amanpour’s resignation announcement comes just two weeks after pro-Trump billionaire David Ellison bought the media outlet in Paramount’s massive acquisition of Warner Brothers Discovery. This includes ownership of HBO and HBO Max, Warner Bros. movie and TV studios, DC, CNN, TBS, TNT, HGTV and Discovery+. David Ellison is the son of Larry Ellison, a Trump supporter, staunch Zionist, and billionaire founder of Oracle. The father-son duo have been vocal about their desire to regulate media narratives via TikTok, CBS, and now, CNN.

Amanpour’s announcement did not mention Ellison.

“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” CNN head Mark Thompson wrote in a statement. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”

This story has been updated.

items.title: Disaster Survivors Still Waiting for Billions From Trump Admin
items.content_text:
Americans who survived tornados, floods, and wildfires are still waiting on $10 billion in aid from the Trump administration over a year later.

A Guardian analysis finds that FEMA has not doled out long-term recovery funds to survivors of the 2025 tornado in St Louis, the central Texas floods, or the wildfires in Los Angeles. These natural disasters crippled infrastructure, destroyed homes, and displaced thousands.

“To find out that your own country can’t even do what it has historically done for other survivors of disasters, that’s very disheartening, and it’s also what kind of galvanized me to get involved,” Los Angeles resident Sylvie Andrews, who lost her Altadena home in the wildfires, told The Guardian. “There are people in Congress who are resistant to the idea of pre-funding anything when they’re not sure there’s going to be a disaster, and the reality is there will be more disasters every year because of climate change.… I guarantee there will be communities that need it.”

“The insurance didn’t cover much of anything. And the Fema just kind of backed you up for a little while, but didn’t get you back on track,” said Demetrice Davis, who lost his home in a St. Louis tornado. “The government agencies are not really doing what they’re supposed to do. “It’s just a matter of asking, as a taxpaying citizen, what are we paying for? ... As a taxpaying citizen, we are putting in the pot. We are supposed to get some type of return. But it seems like that’s not happening. And there seems to be a lot of excuses and passing the buck because most of the lawmakers we talked to blamed it on other lawmakers.”

Both Davis and Andrews traveled to Washington, D.C., last month with Rebuild: the National Disaster Survivors Association to lobby lawmakers to reactivate the Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery program, or CDBG-DR, which is supposed to allocate funds to rebuilding homes and infrastructure after natural disasters.

“Let’s be clear: this is funding FEMA had already approved and that we have been demanding the agency release for weeks,” California Democratic Representative Judy Chu said last month. “And while today is progress, President Trump still has not delivered the long-term federal disaster recovery funding Los Angeles communities need to rebuild.”

This is not the first instance in which Americans caught in natural disasters have been hung out to dry by the Trump administration. Last year, President Trump denied disaster aid requests from multiple blue states while awarding it to red ones. He did it once again over the summer, putting millions of Americans at risk in the process.

items.title: Republican Official Warns Election Threats Are “Coming From Within”
items.content_text:
The Republican lieutenant governor of Utah, Deidre Henderson, is warning that the federal government is threatening the integrity of American elections.

“In the past two elections that I oversaw as lieutenant governor, the threats were all external: non-state actors, cyber security threats and other things,” Henderson told CBS News. “But now we also have threats coming from within our own government.”

Henderson pointed to the Justice Department’s demand for every state to hand over their full voter rolls, including information that is legally required to remain confidential.

“They wanted things that we typically are required by law to keep private: social security numbers, full dates of birth, driver’s license numbers,” Henderson, whose job includes overseeing Utah’s elections, said to CBS. Out of concerns for the federal government’s motive, she refused to provide the data alongside officials in 29 other states.

Last month, the DOJ notified Henderson in writing that she is under investigation.

“I have to tell myself it doesn’t matter what the consequences are, as long as I feel like I’m doing what’s right,” Henderson said. “I think this is an important thing for me to do, holding these guard rails, holding the line. Someone has to.”

Federal agents acting on orders from the Trump administration have seized ballots and voting machines this year, and President Trump himself has continuously pushed election conspiracies. Trump has signed executive orders requiring proof of citizenship to vote and restricting mail-in ballots, and last week, his Department of Justice sued California, claiming, without proof, that the state was sending ballots to 20,000 noncitizens.

California’s top elections official, Secretary of State Shirley Weber, said that the Trump administration didn’t say where the “20,000” number came from or how they verified those individuals’ citizenship status.

“The USDOJ’s relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said in a statement.

items.title: Trump’s Ex–Press Secretary Screwed Up One Last Time on Her Way Out
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump’s press secretary-for-a-day Katie Zacharia couldn’t even exit the White House without making one last mistake.

Zacharia posted two photographs with Trump in the Oval Office after her unceremonious firing that were digitally altered to conceal an image sitting on the president’s desk, The Washington Post reported Saturday.

The first post, on Friday, contained a photograph with just the two of them, where a document on the president’s desk was blurred but still identifiable to preservation advocates as a renovation plan for the East Potomac Golf Links, the public golf course the president has decided to transform into an exclusive, high-end one without any legal approval.

The second post, on Saturday, contained a photograph that included Zacharia’s family standing behind the desk, and this time the document appeared to have been removed altogether. The Post identified the book sitting beneath it as The White House Historical Association guidebook—noting that the digital alterations had removed an image on the book’s cover of the executive mansion.

The censored image could prove controversial considering that government lawyers have insisted that there is no final design for East Potomac Park, as the plan undergoes a legal challenge from a historic preservation group. Such a slipup is par for the course for Zacharia, who crashed and burned out of the White House after just five days as the president’s spokesperson.

Last week, District Judge Ana Reyes blocked the government from felling hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park. The judge tore into the Trump administration lawyer for claiming that tree removal is not part of the president’s renovation plans. The Department of Justice demanded that she step down, claiming that her outburst proved she was biased against the government. The judge refused, sending Trump spiraling on Monday.

So long, Zacharia, we barely knew ye. I would say don’t let the door hit you on the way out—but it appears you already have.

items.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle Went on Last-Ditch Desperation Tour to Save Her Job
items.content_text:
After Kimberly Guilfoyle was fired on live television last week, she reportedly begged MAGA allies to rescue her, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, conservative media magnate Rupert Murdoch, and U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack. None of them did.

The ex–ambassador to Greece was unceremoniously dumped from the Trump administration during then–White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s first and last press briefing on October 13, following a Wall Street Journal report that Guilfoyle had engaged in pay-to-play schemes, including offering a MAGA donor special access to Trump administration officials in exchange for covering her $100,000 credit card bill. The donor, Eric Deters, has since filed a defamation lawsuit against her.

After Zacharia announced to the world that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign, Guilfoyle went off the deep end. She considered rescinding her resignation, and begged Hegseth and Barrack to speak to President Donald Trump on her behalf. Barrack reportedly tried, but obviously made no impact on the president’s decision. Guilfoyle also allegedly asked 95-year-old Murdoch—whose media empire includes both Fox News and the Journal—to limit the Journal’s unfavorable coverage. He refused.

“Kimberly was spiraling, calling people and suggesting, ‘Maybe I don’t resign,’” an official familiar with the situation told PunchUp Wednesday. “I don’t think she was serious, but she was in her feelings last night. She was processing what had happened—but not very well.”

As fewer and fewer MAGA allies and conservative influencers agreed to take Guilfoyle’s calls, many scrubbed the internet of any evidence that they ever knew her. In Greece, where Guilfoyle remains ambassador until the end of the month, her authority has dissolved.

“The people in the embassy are no longer afraid of her. Nobody is listening to her or taking her orders anymore,” a source in Greece told the Daily Mail. “She is all alone in that house, screaming at her old staff that they are leakers, and waiting to get kicked out. It’s an insane situation.”

items.title: Trump’s Big Mouth Already Comes Back to Bite Him in Golf Course Case
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump on Monday attacked a federal judge who blocked his lawless construction on a public golf course in Washington, D.C.—and it immediately came back to haunt him.

At a hearing, the preservation group mounting the legal challenge against Trump’s federal takeover of the East Potomac Golf Links introduced the president’s own Truth Social post as evidence that the government plans to proceed with renovations “IMMEDIATELY!”

Ahead of the hearing Monday morning, Trump raged against District Judge Ana Reyes, who barred the National Parks Service from cutting down any more trees on the East Potomac Golf Links. The tree clearing is part of a plan to transform the public course into an exclusive, high-end one.

“The United States Department of Interior wants to take a terrible and very unsafe golf course, and make it into a great, safe, and prestigious golf course. They have an absolute right to do so. It’s as simple as that!” the president wrote on Truth Social.

Trump’s meltdown comes after Reyes refused the Department of Justice’s request that she recuse herself, over the fact that she yelled at a government attorney last week. A furious Reyes slammed the Trump administration for giving last-minute notice that it would resume cutting down trees during the previous holiday weekend. When Justice Department attorney Marissa Piropato argued the actions over the weekend were “not a renovation,” Reyes tore into her excuse as “preposterous,” “doublespeak,” and “completely beyond the pale.”

“The judge on the case is a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane?” Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday. “The tapes have been blocked from usage by the judge.”

The Trump administration’s determination to proceed with expensive demolition projects without receiving a whiff of congressional or legal approval would make anyone a little crazy.

This story has been updated.

items.title: Bari Weiss Exposed for Pushing CBS to Smear Democratic Candidates
items.content_text:
CBS News editor in chief and anti-woke crusader Bari Weiss urged her newsroom to cover right-wing conspiracy theories regarding Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed. 

Semafor reported that Weiss was particularly focused on El-Sayed’s (nonexistent) ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and 9/11, and Talarico’s (also nonexistent) trip to a mental health facility. El-Sayed, an Egyptian American Muslim, has denounced the Muslim Brotherhood numerous times amid Islamophobic attacks from both the right wing and the Democratic establishment. 

Weiss “personally advocated” for a deeper dive into El-Sayed’s personal history, and she even faced internal pushback for her insistence that the newsroom inaccurately tie El-Sayed to the 9/11 terror attacks, as she published an August headline reading “Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s deleted tweets on Sept. 11 attacks invite scrutiny of past remarks.”

“Anyone discussing this race needs to be very careful about putting the name of a man who would be America’s first Muslim senator next to ‘9/11’ on very thin grounds. It reads like a dog whistle,” Atlantic journalist Helen Lewis wrote at the time.  

As for Talarico, his whole “mental health” episode was thoroughly disproven as a smear campaign, even though Weiss thought it was worth spending time on. It’s notable that both Talarico and El-Sayed are progressive candidates who have been critical of Israel’s genocide of Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, something that Weiss, her pro-Israel The Free Press blog, and CBS have covered with extreme bias. 

This is not the first time Weiss has experienced internal pushback for inserting herself into stories. She initially pulled the plug on former 60 Minutes correspondent Cecilia Vega’s CECOT megaprison story in El Salvador, and was “very, very hands-on” with a story covering Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.

items.title: MAGA Operative Behind Muslim Brotherhood Question to Abdul El-Sayed
items.content_text:
A Republican political operative tried to trap the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, into a viral “gotcha” moment. He ended up becoming the story instead.

On Saturday, a man posing as a young Michigan voter named Tommy at a town hall in Caro, Michigan, asked El-Sayed if he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed, sensing the bigoted motive behind the question, immediately disavowed the question, and pressed Tommy on why he was asking him specifically that question.

Tommy was evasive, repeatedly saying that he had not heard El-Sayed disavow the organization, and El-Sayed pointed out that Tommy was assuming that El-Sayed had a “higher order allegiance” than the Constitution. El-Sayed asked Tommy if he would “disavow any attempt to read any religious doctrine into the laws of our country.” Tommy said he wouldn’t, and El-Sayed called him out for failing to understand the Constitution.

This is Tommy. Tommy had a question about my allegiances. Listen to the end to hear about his. https://t.co/p09eMtsh0x

— Dr. Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed) October 18, 2026

El-Sayed’s campaign quickly turned the exchange into a video clip, which subsequently went viral. As of Monday morning, the clip has 13 million views on X alone.

Not surprisingly, later reporting revealed that Tommy is actually Thomas Teepell, the operations director for Missouri Republican Senator Josh Hawley and the son of Timmy Teepell, who used to work for former Louisiana Republican Governor Bobby Jindal.

The whole Q&A appears to be part of a Republican influencer campaign to try to embarrass Abdul El-Sayed. Earlier this month, The Michigan Daily reported that the conservative PAC America Next offered College Republicans $200 to boo El-Sayed at a town hall in Flint and ask provocative questions.

The Teepells are involved in a similar campaign, with Thomas’s father’s organization, Breakthrough LLC, receiving $250,000 from Jindal’s dark money organization for influencer marketing against Abdul El-Sayed. The attempt has clearly backfired, as El-Sayed turned the exchange into a positive clip for his senatorial campaign.

items.title: Transcript: Trump Rages over Texas Senate Race—and Even Fox Is Rattled
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the October 19 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

In the last few days, Donald Trump has repeatedly erupted over the Texas Senate race. He’s unleashed wild rants about Democrat James Talarico, calling him juvenile names and raging at Republicans who, in Trump’s mind, are to blame for the strength of Talarico’s campaign. It sure looks like Trump is panicking about Texas, yet the polls are sending a mixed picture. Talarico is still up, but the race seems to be tightening. And a huge amount of Republican money is still set to pour into this race.

So we thought we’d check on the state of things with Nancy Zdunkewicz, a Democratic pollster who’s based in Texas and knows the state well. Nancy, thanks so much for coming on.

Nancy Zdunkewicz: Hi, Greg. Thanks for having me. It’s exciting to get to talk about my home state being competitive!

Sargent: It is competitive, and it’s been a long time. So let’s just quickly recap what the polls are saying right now. Marist has Talarico up two points on Republican Ken Paxton, 47 to 45. Siena Research Institute has Talarico up four, 48 to 44. A Republican pollster, Trafalgar, had Talarico up four as well. YouGov had it at plus three.

Nancy, bottom line, the polling averages have the race narrowing to a Talarico lead of 2.6 points. That’s basically a knife’s edge, isn’t it?

Zdunkewicz: Yes, and I am also seeing this same margin in my own polling. And yes, that is within the margin of error, technically. But what sets this apart for me is that this is the first time that a Democrat has ever led a Republican consistently throughout the entire general election campaign.

It’s Paxton who’s picking up an inch here, an inch there. This is basically the mirror image of what my polling looked like for Colin Allred at this point two years ago.

Sargent: Right. So basically what you’re saying is that what really sets this apart is that every other time we’ve had a Democrat who appeared to be mounting a strong challenge, that Democrat wasn’t leading in every single poll.

And here Talarico is leading. You see maybe Paxton pulling back a few Republicans here, a few Republicans there, but it’s just sort of staying more or less where it’s been. Is that your feeling?

Zdunkewicz: So as you go throughout the general election campaign, you are going to expect to see undecideds go to where their homes are. This comes along with general voter education and people starting to tune in, because, believe it or not, not everybody’s lives revolve around politics.

And so we expect that we see this. It actually makes me nervous when I see a large number of people who say they’re undecided, because I know that they’re actually ultimately going to vote for the Democrat or the Republican.

And so what we saw was that they had to spend a ton of money. Hundreds of millions of dollars just got spent in a month. And that allowed you to pick up a point, two points, to bring home some people who, let’s say, at the end of the day, were pretty much always going to vote for a Republican, or maybe already voting for Republicans for other offices, too.

Sargent: Right. It’s the huge influx of money that’s starting to pull a few people back.

So Trump exploded on Truth Social over this race. He accused Texas Senator John Cornyn and GOP strategist Karl Rove of sabotaging Paxton’s chances. Trump raged that James TalaFREAKO is a “radical left lunatic”, and said:

“If Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like Cornyn and Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career.”

Trump went on and on like that at really great length, like really losing it, calling Talarico “FREAKO” again and again. Nancy, what do you make of that?

Zdunkewicz: Gosh, you know, he really shot himself in the foot here, didn’t he? He didn’t need to endorse Paxton in this race. He helped secure his nomination in the first place. So maybe he’s feeling a little bit insecure about his poor decision-making.

Sargent: I’m glad you brought up Trump’s role in this. I think it’s worth reminding everyone, this is Trump’s fault. He ordered Texas Republican voters to support Paxton over Cornyn, and Cornyn would probably have had a much easier time here.

And there is a deep perversity about this that’s just Trump all over. Trump forced Paxton on everyone because he thinks Paxton is loyal to him. And now that Paxton could lose, he’s blaming it on everyone but himself.

Zdunkewicz: I’ve never seen so much money get so little. It has not produced an improvement in Ken Paxton’s favorability. It has, yes, maybe increased Talarico’s negatives a little bit, but he continues to be popular. People are actively voting because they like somebody this year in Texas. And then they actively dislike this other guy.

In fact, people are increasingly learning about him—which is crazy to think that not everybody knew who this was after all of the impeachments and all the money spent during the primary.

But as more people learn about him, the more they dislike Ken Paxton. So you see this opposite dynamic working, where we have a popular Democrat, we have a uniquely unpopular Republican, and all of this money has really not gotten them much in terms of making James unpopular.

Sargent: It’s wild. Trump exploded again on Truth Social, saying this: “James Talarico, who was running for U.S. Senate against the greatest attorney general in the history of Texas, recently stated, with a large mask covering his face as he spoke, that fossil fuels are destroying the planet. No more drilling for oil in Texas. That should be the end of his campaign.”

Nancy, I’m not sure what Trump’s referring to there, but it’s pretty sad that he’s trying to declare by decree that Talarico’s campaign is over.

Zdunkewicz: But it’s not particularly effective in a state where we see 54, 55 percent say that they dislike the president. In fact, please, come to Texas. Come campaign. Come campaign here. It’s not going to be helpful at all.

People are extremely disappointed in the president. They think that the economy is doing horribly. The more that he shows up, the more he reinforces this overall political environment that is demoralizing Republicans and fracturing independents and really motivating Democrats to come out in November and to vote to stop the Trump-aligned party.

Sargent: Let’s talk about why this race is tightening. Marist is a quality survey. It had Talarico up by two points. It had him 52 to 30 among independents, which seems like a healthy lead. And it has Talarico winning eight percent of Republicans. I’m wondering whether Talarico is still not winning enough Republicans to really put this thing away. Can you tell us what you’re seeing?

Zdunkewicz: Republicans are a majority of the electorate in Texas. I’m not talking registered Republicans. I’m saying people who say that they identify actively as a Republican or lean Republican: 52 percent. Fifty-four percent say that they always or usually vote for Republicans.

So if you look at the 52 percent who say that they identify as a Republican, the thinking here is you need 91 percent of those voters, plus those strong margins with independents, in order to win in Texas. And eight percent is where, you said, one of the polls, the Marist poll I believe, has him. That’s where I have him.

And I think that that is pretty darn close to what I’m hoping for, to get to a plurality plus one, or, you know, hopefully 50 percent. Just as a reminder, in a state like Texas, where you have a third party on the ballot, you don’t need 50 percent of the vote to win.

Sargent: Right. So I guess what you’re saying is that Talarico, if he’s getting around eight percent of Republicans right now, we’re getting very close to what he needs, especially with the double-digit lead he has among independents.

Let me ask it this way, then. Where do you want to see Talarico improve right now to feel a little bit better about where things are? Like, I think this is very close. It’s on a knife’s edge. Just in granular terms, where does he need to kind of bump himself up a little more in order to make us all breathe a little more easily?

Zdunkewicz: Right now we’re seeing some healthy two-to-one margins with Hispanic voters. I’m feeling very good about where South Texas is, and where these Hispanic-majority districts and the increasingly Hispanic and growing areas that are sort of the suburbs along I-35—doing quite well there.

I’m thinking a lot about the voters that are in places like, you know, Cypress, and, you know, suburbs within Harris County. These are going to be more college-educated voters. For the first time already, we are seeing a Democrat tied with college-educated voters in Texas, with white college-educated voters.

That has always been the distinction for people in the Midwest, is that you would see white college-educated voters were kind of increasingly the backbone of the Democratic coalition. And yet in the South, that was not the case. But we’re seeing this now. And I think if we can continue to do that, that would be pretty impressive.

Sargent: So basically what you want to see here is, you want to see Talarico just pad his numbers with white college-educated voters in some of the suburbs of Texas. Is that basically where we are?

Zdunkewicz: Yeah, the suburbs are so diverse in Texas that I’m just going to say college-educated voters in general.

Sargent: Listen to this exchange between Republican Congressman Pat Fallon of Texas and a Fox anchor. It starts with Representative Fallon insulting Talarico and goes on from there.

Pat Fallon (voiceover): So this little radically woke soy boy is completely out of touch with Texans, and he’s lying to them, trying to fool them, selling them snake oil. Say ‘no’ for me.

Fox anchor (voiceover): But Congressman, let me challenge you on that. You can say he’s out of touch, and I know where you’re coming from on that, but he seems to be in touch with perhaps a majority of the people who are going to vote in this election. I guess I’m trying to understand—if the polling is somewhat accurate here, and we can debate that—has the character of Texas, has all the migration from places like California, is it changing the character of your state enough that a guy with all of the, let’s call him, defects that you just mentioned there can still resonate with maybe a majority of people who are going to vote in that state?

Fallon (voiceover): No, I think he will lose. But to your point, it is a tight race.


Sargent: So I think this is really striking, Nancy. Note how baffled they seem about the fact that their smears of Talarico aren’t sticking. It kind of calls to mind something you said a little earlier about Talarico’s campaign. This is a guy who’s really, really successfully carved out a very unique and independent kind of image for himself in a state like this.

He talks a language that I think sounds new to a lot of people, maybe doesn’t sound like the language of a Democrat to the ears of many people in Texas. And there you can kind of get a sense of why Republicans are spending hundreds of millions of dollars calling him trans or whatever the hell they think they’re calling him, freako or whatever. And that stuff isn’t really sticking. What do you make of all that?

Zdunkewicz: Yeah, as I said before, it is still a Republican state. And so if we make this a contest between a Democrat and a Republican, it’s just not going to ever work out in someone’s favor.

And so instead, this race has been defined not as Republican and Democrat, but right and wrong. And by having a really strong moral core, a really reason for running that is based in his faith, in a state where this resonates with a lot of people, that has allowed him this opportunity.

And I think that people are really sick of a politics that is about scoring political points, and are ready to hear something that feels more authentic. When you can go back not to somebody’s political ideology, but to understand I think I know where they’re coming from and how they might make a decision, because I feel like I know who they are, like, where are they grounded? And when that resonates with, you know, how you were raised, that really means something to a lot of people.

As I said before, he is actively liked here. And so when they throw out all of these insults, and they’re, what, that he’s too nice? God forbid. I think we’re all hungry to turn the page and have a politics that is less nasty and less full of hate. And I don’t blame people like the congressman and Donald Trump for being blind to it, because that’s where their politics is grounded in.

They can’t possibly understand why so many people might just like somebody because they think maybe we should help people, and we should be good, and that we shouldn’t call people names, and that that might be a better way of doing politics.

Sargent: That is so beautifully said. And I’m going to throw this out there. Every time Trump unleashes some deranged, crazed rant like that, it just reminds everybody of what they don’t want. And it could in fact make Talarico look good in comparison.

Zdunkewicz: Yeah. Yeah, the things aren’t sticking to him. He built up a really good foundation that people felt like they understood. And so when people throw these things out, it just doesn’t stick.

And the other good thing is, you know, I want to give all that credit where it’s due, but I also want to acknowledge that the terms are different than they were two years ago, because now Democrats aren’t in charge anymore. Republicans are in charge.

And so they focus a lot on these anti-trans attacks and these sort of masculinity attacks, and they just really are lacking credibility. And it’s because the shoe’s on the other foot now. It’s really interesting to see in polling just how little credibility some of these negatives had that were so tarnishing only two years ago.

Sargent: It really is extraordinary. It’s going to get tight, though, and a lot of money’s going to flow. So folks, just buckle up and be ready for this. Don’t freak out. Nancy Zdunkewicz, thank you so much for coming on. That was fascinating stuff.

Zdunkewicz: It was so great to join you today, Greg.

items.title: The Trump Scandal That Everyone Overlooked
items.content_text:
With the U.S. midterm elections less than three weeks away, is it any surprise that corruption has emerged as voters’ top concern? “Corrupt” was the adjective most often chosen when registered voters were asked for a single word to describe President Donald Trump, according to a survey conducted in September by The Economist and the market research firm YouGov, with 53 percent of respondents calling Trump “corrupt” and only 23 percent saying he is “honest.” A Pew Research Center poll in early October found that nearly seven in 10 (69 percent) of Americans are “not confident” that Trump keeps his business interests separate from his presidential decisions.

Americans can thank diligent investigative reporting for alerting them to much of the self-dealing by Trump, his family, and aides. For example, The Washington Post has reported that Trump’s sons, Don Jr. and Eric, were investors in 15 companies that “collectively generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the sons invested and an additional $3.1 billion in future contract options.” On Tuesday, in a rare retreat, the White House asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as U.S. ambassador to Greece after a Wall Street Journal investigation revealed that Guilfoyle promised political favors to a Trump donor if he would quietly pay off her $100,000 American Express credit card bill.

Throughout the history of modern polling, voters have usually ranked the economy (or its proxies, such as “the cost of living”) as their top issue. Now, linking corruption with the cost of living, “Democrats Are Making Corruption Messaging a Pocketbook Issue,” a recent Politico headline declared. The Democrats’ claim, The New York Times reported, “is that rampant corruption in Congress and the administration is directly costing average citizens who are paying more for necessities like groceries, gas, and medicine.”

Both Democrats and the press, however, so far, are overlooking one of the most overt and consequential examples of Trump’s pay-to-play behavior. On May 24, 2024, Josh Dawsey and Maxine Joselow of The Washington Post published a blockbuster exposé, reporting that Trump privately told a group of oil company CEOs they should donate $1 billion to his 2024 presidential campaign. It would be a good “deal” for the industry, Trump reportedly said, because of the tax and regulation benefits they would receive if he returned to the Oval Office.

Specifically, Trump reportedly said he would reverse the Biden administration’s pause on new liquefied natural gas, or LNG, export permits, approve more drilling for oil in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska, and roll back environmental regulations the industry didn’t like, including electric vehicle purchasing mandates and vehicle emissions limits. Dawsey and Joselow then published a follow-up, reporting that Trump also promised to soften Federal Trade Commission scrutiny of industry mergers and acquisitions.

Two and a half years later, his administration has delivered on each of these promises and then some. The Brennan Center has published a well-documented summary of Trump’s assault on climate policy—including his administration’s repeal of the “endangerment finding,” which granted the federal government the authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions—that connects the dots between Trump’s actions and the many billions of dollars the oil industry has reaped as a result, including many millions of dollars benefiting oil executives as individuals.

What makes all this relevant to the midterm elections—beyond the fact that the leader of the Republican Party is directly implicated—is that many of Trump’s accomplishments were only possible because of rubber-stamp support from Republicans in Congress. Now those same Republicans must face the voters. How will they explain themselves?

To be clear, Democrats don’t get a pass here; corruption has been part of politics forever, and one of the press’s central obligations is to expose and hold its perpetrators to account, whoever they may be. That requires following the facts where they lead. But it also requires challenging the practice, still common among old-school newsrooms, of false equivalence—of portraying both sides as equally culpable for a given transgression for fear that an accurate portrayal would look like “taking sides.” If most of the facts point in one direction, our reporting should have the integrity and courage to say so.

Most voters don’t have access to directly question candidates seeking their votes. It’s our job as journalists to ask questions on their behalf so they can make informed decisions about their leaders.

Corruption is understandably a hot issue these days. Meanwhile, new scientific analysis from the nonprofit Climate Central shows that every congressional district in the country is hotter than it was in 1970, thanks to climate change. No surprise, then, that polling also shows that the vast majority of people want their government to take stronger climate action. Journalism that connects those dots—accurately and fairly, and without pulling any punches—is a true public service.

items.title: Youth Is a Devastating Comedy About an Overlooked Stage of Motherhood
items.content_text:
Youth is full of women running out of time. Alex (Sharon Horgan) is a divorced, 50-year-old literary agent with a college-age son. At this moment in her life, she’s either at the end of her rope or at the start of a new era—it’s often hard for her to tell which. Sometimes, the ticking clock manifests in ordinary ways. At a book fair in Germany, Alex has a distracted meeting with an editor who reminds her that she’s “a bit stretched for time.” Later, as Alex regales a potential client—a psychology advice columnist—with the trials and tribulations of her love life, the client warningly interjects, “I only have an hour.”

More often, Alex’s time crunch has an apocalyptic bent. When Patrick (Rupert Friend), an old flame who’s recently reappeared in her life, asks if it’s the right time for her to start a relationship, she replies indignantly, “It is the right time, it has to be the right time, because another time’s gonna be too late.” Later, when Alex briefly explores a relationship with Michael, a much older man, the problem of time becomes fatally strange. Describing his mother’s passing, he tells Alex with a look of profundity, “Her last words to me really stuck: ‘I’ll be dead tomorrow, and so will you.’” Alex recoils, but he explains, “Yeah, she meant live every day like it’s your last.” Alex, a mother herself, is skeptical about Michael’s extraction of such a neat moral from such a bizarre final utterance. “Did she?”

Youth, which airs on HBO, is one of several extraordinary series Horgan has created on the subject of motherhood. Time is each show’s most deranged and deranging element. In Catastrophe (2015–2019), time moves too fast. In each of its four seasons, Sharon (also played by Horgan) is either pregnant or the mother of a small child. The time jump from season one to two takes her from a newlywed in the process of delivering her first child to a soon-to-be mother of two. Motherland (2016–2022), which Horgan co-created but does not star in, focuses on the harried, endless grind that characterizes being the parent of school-age kids. From managing schedules to managing feelings, the time moves impossibly fast, but it also drags. When Julia (Anna Maxwell Martin) loses the childcare she has relied on up to now (her own mother, who flatly quits), an avalanche of new duties falls on her, impeding the orderly forward motion of her life.

At the center of Youth is the period of parental life that critic Nina Renata Aron recently named “middle motherhood.” The world of culture, Aron argues, is filled with compelling, dramatic narratives of new motherhood, which she describes as “a time to swoon, and also to rage and cry.” That world is not similarly filled with narratives of mothers whose children have, to some degree or another, grown up, whose motherhood is no longer new, raw, exciting, rupturing. These motherhood narratives, if and when they’re even recognized as motherhood narratives, are few and far between. And yet, their fast-approaching but glacially unfolding temporality makes them rich stories to tell. “I can actually feel myself occupying a new developmental phase,” Aron writes of her own middle motherhood, “taking a different place in the generational order.” Stories of new motherhood are about being caught up in the rush of a new biological current; middle motherhood stories are about finding a new place in history.

Youth is a story about this transitional state, and it’s told by a writer and performer very much aware of the way such stories remain often unseen, unheard, untold. With her characteristic fizzing wit, blinkered charm, and soulful realism, Horgan has opened up a new stage of her own career. When I think back to Michael’s recounting of his mother’s last words, what strikes me is not so much that Michael extracts a trite maxim from her enigmatic phrase; it’s that Alex understands immediately that that’s not really what she said. This woman, at the end—not the beginning or even the middle—of life, of motherhood, of womanhood, said something way weirder than carpe diem. You just have to listen.


It is something of a reductive synopsis to say that Youth is just a show about motherhood. Indeed, the first episode presents us with a woman who is ready and eager to send her son off to college and explore the world as someone who is no longer defined by being a parent, no longer constrained by the demands of raising her son. Her ex-husband, a middling actor, has lived his life heedlessly, leaving all the child-rearing to Alex as he remarries a younger woman and prepares to leave the country for a sci-fi pilot shoot. As her son, Ruarí (Aran Murphy), gets in the car to drive off to school, Alex runs desperately after it only to burst out laughing. She sets to transforming his old room into a yoga studio, alternately collapsing into sobs and rising up with giddy glee. Later that week, she brings a man home for a successful fling, only to find Ruarí—surly, upset, uncommunicative—has reclaimed his bed. Alex would love her story to have stopped being about motherhood any longer; Youth is about the uncanny disappointment of finding out that hasn’t happened.

So, Youth is not a narrative of the disappearance or recession of motherhood from Alex’s identity so much as it’s a narrative of its eccentric reassertion. Rather than a series about the liberation from motherhood or a wish fulfillment tale of Alex getting her groove back in her perimenopause era, the show thinks about the different, weird ways motherhood adapts itself to this new stage of life.

The most direct way is through the manosphere-curious Ruarí. When we meet him, he’s seemingly embarked upon a self-destructive spiral. He stages a cheeky, disruptive protest at his high school graduation ceremony; he squeezes burrata all over himself and his family at a celebration dinner; and then there are the circumstances of his sudden return from uni. While it takes a few episodes for us to learn the whole story, it’s immediately clear that ­Ruarí has conducted himself poorly, and that this has made him unwelcome on campus. Back at home, he retreats into old clips of Mitch Hedberg’s stand-up and videos about semen retention. Alex is both terrified by her son’s sudden sullen mania and ill-equipped to get him to divulge what’s wrong. For much of the season, Ruarí is a mute stranger, haunting her halls. For a show as regularly funny as this one, it’s an upsetting portrait of a seemingly common contemporary phenomenon: a son lost to the online void, now become a man you can’t seem to fully trust.

So, as Alex navigates the physical changes of her age—her ailments range from spontaneous lockjaw to surprise menstruation—she’s also dealing with the emotional ravages of being both thrust back into active motherly service and rejected for that job. The seeming stable solution to these problems is Patrick, her longtime, on-again-off-again, “institutionally single” ex-lover. Alex and Patrick have an easy chemistry—Horgan has always known how to write great, crackling, funny flirtation—but it’s underlaid with a barely unspoken tension. The problem of their relationship is both that Ruarí still takes up too much of Alex’s life and that Alex can’t, and won’t, ever be able to give Patrick children of his own. It’s a banal kind of star-crossed love. What would it mean to accept someone for who they are when they are both too much and not enough of a mother?


“I live with the dim awareness that a tragedy is unfolding,” writes Nina Renata Aron. “The tragedy of mortality, of time passing, of exiting the phase of life where it’s possible to make new life.” Aron acknowledges the sexism of this tragic framing, the idea that women’s aging itself is a kind of death. Youth is nonetheless preoccupied with the sticky feeling of loss that comes with Alex’s feelings of liberation. The challenge of assembling a new life mostly out of available, remaining parts. The judgment that comes with that assertion of continued existence.

Midway through the season, on a holiday in Spain, Alex becomes kind of obsessed with a woman her age or a bit older who seems to breeze through the world with confidence, wisdom, and panache. She dines alone with gusto, her voluminous hair proudly showing its gray. On one occasion, Alex catches her eye, only to start coughing on smoke from her own cigarette. Later, Alex spies her again and tries to express what an inspiration she is, how her small example of living out loud has given Alex strength and courage. “I wanted to tell you, you look great,” she says. “So cool and content and comfortable in your skin, just you by yourself.” But the woman doesn’t speak English. Instead of picking up on Alex’s gratitude, she reads only anxiety and discomfort. The woman calls for help. “I think there’s something wrong with her,” she says, in Spanish.

Youth is a sexy, dazzling, often devastating comedy of middle motherhood. It’s a show with no neat maxims and plenty of weird, wise things to say about being alive, and a woman, and 50 all at once.

items.title: Ilhan Omar Is the Right Kind of American. Trump Is the Wrong Kind.
items.content_text:
On October 15, 1969, Somali President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke was slain by an assassin’s bullet. Unrest had prevailed in the country ever since … well, in many ways, ever since independence was won in 1960, but particularly over the previous couple years. Then as now, Somalia didn’t register much in most Americans’ minds, but the editors of The New York Times judged the event newsworthy enough that it made the front page, with a report noting the imposition of a curfew in “Mogadiscio,” as the capital was then styled by the paper of record.

Six days later, a military junta took control of the country under the leadership of Mohamed Siad Barre. He was a socialist, and he imposed Marxist-Leninist government, aligning with the Soviet Union. But over time, his relationship with Moscow soured. The Soviets frowned upon Somalia’s 1977 invasion of Ethiopia and switched allegiances. According to a 1982 New York Times op-ed by the respected comparative political scientist David D. Laitin, Washington began to take an interest in Siad Barre. Jimmy Carter did so tentatively, but “President Reagan, abandoning caution, gave Mr. Siad Barre a warm welcome in Washington” that March, Laitin wrote. Little countries like Somalia at the time were just pieces on a Cold War chessboard on which the Reagan administration moved around its pawns with particular aggression.

By the late 1980s, discontent with Siad Barre was such that rebel groups began engaging government forces; a civil war erupted. By the early 1990s, Somalia was a failed state. Siad Barre went into exile. Governments couldn’t patch the nation together. And around that time, Somalis began to flee to Kenya—hundreds of thousands of them, into refugee camps. The largest, Dadaab, is still home to some 400,000 Somali refugees, 35 years later.

Why should all this matter to you right now? Because one of those refugees, Nur Omar Mohammed, took his children to Dadaab. By 1995, they were granted asylum by the United States of America and came here, eventually applying for citizenship. One of those children was 17 or 18 at the time of the citizenship application. That wouldn’t seem to matter much in the broad scheme of things, whether a youngster was this age or that some 30 years ago. But today, that youngster is Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar, and Donald Trump and his subordinates are moving heaven and earth to use that alleged discrepancy to get her expelled not only from Congress but from the United States that once welcomed her.

The Trump administration’s move against Omar is repulsive. And it’s sure not happening because her father might have recorded her age inaccurately half a lifetime ago (an allegation that, as yet, remains unproven publicly). It’s happening first and foremost because she’s a very vocal critic of Trump and MAGA-ism. True, alongside her criticisms of Trump, she’s also made some remarks that smacked of antisemitism, and which were deserving of denunciation. But in this country, it’s the voters who decide whether such comments disqualify someone from office. And Omar’s voters have returned her to Congress three times after her initial election in 2018, and they’re about to do so again. And since she hasn’t been stopped at the ballot box, Trump is now searching for other means to do so.

And by the way, those voters include citizens in the heavily Jewish enclave of St. Louis Park, the famous home of the Coen Brothers and Al Franken. If homegrown opposition to Omar was to arise, it would have been from there. She did win the 2022 Democratic primary narrowly, but in 2024, she won the primary handily, and in the general, she carried nearly 70 percent of the vote in St. Louis Park.

But let’s be real. This is also happening because Omar is Somali—because she’s a Black Muslim woman who wears a hijab. These things aren’t quantifiable, and of course Trump and his spokespeople, at least the ones who haven’t lied about their legal careers, would never admit to these aspects of this piece of political persecution. But we all know it’s there.

Actually, now that I think about it, Trump has admitted to his hatred of Somalis and has done so rather openly. Ever since details spilled out about large-scale welfare fraud in the Minneapolis Somali community, Trump has been talking and posting about it incessantly and trying to connect it to Omar. It’s undeniably true that the scale of the fraud is nightmarish. But there’s no evidence of any such connection. (The Biden Justice Department opened an unrelated investigation into Omar’s finances, but it “stalled for lack of evidence.”)

That hasn’t stopped Trump from calling Omar “garbage,” as he did in a Cabinet meeting last year, and from ranting about Somalis generally in a way that can plainly be called racist and can arguably be called fascist. Am I being melodramatic here? Consider these Trump sentences, from an October 8 Truth Social post: “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

The racism is apparent in the first two sentences, which seek to incite hatred based specifically on the nationality of the population in question. But those third and fourth sentences … how exactly is he proposing that Minnesotans “fight back”? And when he says the federal government will “come to your rescue,” what precisely does he mean? And who is the “you” he is addressing?

I think we have a pretty good idea—he means that if certain “real” Minnesotans were to take the matter of the “Somalians” into their own hands, he’d order in armed troops to back them up.
