So if you look at the 52 percent who say that they identify as a Republican, the thinking here is you need 91 percent of those voters, plus those strong margins with independents, in order to win in Texas. And eight percent is where, you said, one of the polls, the Marist poll I believe, has him. That’s where I have him.

And I think that that is pretty darn close to what I’m hoping for, to get to a plurality plus one, or, you know, hopefully 50 percent. Just as a reminder, in a state like Texas, where you have a third party on the ballot, you don’t need 50 percent of the vote to win.

Sargent: Right. So I guess what you’re saying is that Talarico, if he’s getting around eight percent of Republicans right now, we’re getting very close to what he needs, especially with the double-digit lead he has among independents.

Let me ask it this way, then. Where do you want to see Talarico improve right now to feel a little bit better about where things are? Like, I think this is very close. It’s on a knife’s edge. Just in granular terms, where does he need to kind of bump himself up a little more in order to make us all breathe a little more easily?

Zdunkewicz: Right now we’re seeing some healthy two-to-one margins with Hispanic voters. I’m feeling very good about where South Texas is, and where these Hispanic-majority districts and the increasingly Hispanic and growing areas that are sort of the suburbs along I-35—doing quite well there.

I’m thinking a lot about the voters that are in places like, you know, Cypress, and, you know, suburbs within Harris County. These are going to be more college-educated voters. For the first time already, we are seeing a Democrat tied with college-educated voters in Texas, with white college-educated voters.

That has always been the distinction for people in the Midwest, is that you would see white college-educated voters were kind of increasingly the backbone of the Democratic coalition. And yet in the South, that was not the case. But we’re seeing this now. And I think if we can continue to do that, that would be pretty impressive.

Sargent: So basically what you want to see here is, you want to see Talarico just pad his numbers with white college-educated voters in some of the suburbs of Texas. Is that basically where we are?

Zdunkewicz: Yeah, the suburbs are so diverse in Texas that I’m just going to say college-educated voters in general.

Sargent: Listen to this exchange between Republican Congressman Pat Fallon of Texas and a Fox anchor. It starts with Representative Fallon insulting Talarico and goes on from there.

Pat Fallon (voiceover): So this little radically woke soy boy is completely out of touch with Texans, and he’s lying to them, trying to fool them, selling them snake oil. Say ‘no’ for me.

Fox anchor (voiceover): But Congressman, let me challenge you on that. You can say he’s out of touch, and I know where you’re coming from on that, but he seems to be in touch with perhaps a majority of the people who are going to vote in this election. I guess I’m trying to understand—if the polling is somewhat accurate here, and we can debate that—has the character of Texas, has all the migration from places like California, is it changing the character of your state enough that a guy with all of the, let’s call him, defects that you just mentioned there can still resonate with maybe a majority of people who are going to vote in that state?

Fallon (voiceover): No, I think he will lose. But to your point, it is a tight race.


Sargent: So I think this is really striking, Nancy. Note how baffled they seem about the fact that their smears of Talarico aren’t sticking. It kind of calls to mind something you said a little earlier about Talarico’s campaign. This is a guy who’s really, really successfully carved out a very unique and independent kind of image for himself in a state like this.

He talks a language that I think sounds new to a lot of people, maybe doesn’t sound like the language of a Democrat to the ears of many people in Texas. And there you can kind of get a sense of why Republicans are spending hundreds of millions of dollars calling him trans or whatever the hell they think they’re calling him, freako or whatever. And that stuff isn’t really sticking. What do you make of all that?

Zdunkewicz: Yeah, as I said before, it is still a Republican state. And so if we make this a contest between a Democrat and a Republican, it’s just not going to ever work out in someone’s favor.

And so instead, this race has been defined not as Republican and Democrat, but right and wrong. And by having a really strong moral core, a really reason for running that is based in his faith, in a state where this resonates with a lot of people, that has allowed him this opportunity.

And I think that people are really sick of a politics that is about scoring political points, and are ready to hear something that feels more authentic. When you can go back not to somebody’s political ideology, but to understand I think I know where they’re coming from and how they might make a decision, because I feel like I know who they are, like, where are they grounded? And when that resonates with, you know, how you were raised, that really means something to a lot of people.

As I said before, he is actively liked here. And so when they throw out all of these insults, and they’re, what, that he’s too nice? God forbid. I think we’re all hungry to turn the page and have a politics that is less nasty and less full of hate. And I don’t blame people like the congressman and Donald Trump for being blind to it, because that’s where their politics is grounded in.

They can’t possibly understand why so many people might just like somebody because they think maybe we should help people, and we should be good, and that we shouldn’t call people names, and that that might be a better way of doing politics.

Sargent: That is so beautifully said. And I’m going to throw this out there. Every time Trump unleashes some deranged, crazed rant like that, it just reminds everybody of what they don’t want. And it could in fact make Talarico look good in comparison.

Zdunkewicz: Yeah. Yeah, the things aren’t sticking to him. He built up a really good foundation that people felt like they understood. And so when people throw these things out, it just doesn’t stick.

And the other good thing is, you know, I want to give all that credit where it’s due, but I also want to acknowledge that the terms are different than they were two years ago, because now Democrats aren’t in charge anymore. Republicans are in charge.

And so they focus a lot on these anti-trans attacks and these sort of masculinity attacks, and they just really are lacking credibility. And it’s because the shoe’s on the other foot now. It’s really interesting to see in polling just how little credibility some of these negatives had that were so tarnishing only two years ago.

Sargent: It really is extraordinary. It’s going to get tight, though, and a lot of money’s going to flow. So folks, just buckle up and be ready for this. Don’t freak out. Nancy Zdunkewicz, thank you so much for coming on. That was fascinating stuff.

Zdunkewicz: It was so great to join you today, Greg.

items.title: The Trump Scandal That Everyone Overlooked
items.content_text:
With the U.S. midterm elections less than three weeks away, is it any surprise that corruption has emerged as voters’ top concern? “Corrupt” was the adjective most often chosen when registered voters were asked for a single word to describe President Donald Trump, according to a survey conducted in September by The Economist and the market research firm YouGov, with 53 percent of respondents calling Trump “corrupt” and only 23 percent saying he is “honest.” A Pew Research Center poll in early October found that nearly seven in 10 (69 percent) of Americans are “not confident” that Trump keeps his business interests separate from his presidential decisions.

Americans can thank diligent investigative reporting for alerting them to much of the self-dealing by Trump, his family, and aides. For example, The Washington Post has reported that Trump’s sons, Don Jr. and Eric, were investors in 15 companies that “collectively generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the sons invested and an additional $3.1 billion in future contract options.” On Tuesday, in a rare retreat, the White House asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as U.S. ambassador to Greece after a Wall Street Journal investigation revealed that Guilfoyle promised political favors to a Trump donor if he would quietly pay off her $100,000 American Express credit card bill.

Throughout the history of modern polling, voters have usually ranked the economy (or its proxies, such as “the cost of living”) as their top issue. Now, linking corruption with the cost of living, “Democrats Are Making Corruption Messaging a Pocketbook Issue,” a recent Politico headline declared. The Democrats’ claim, The New York Times reported, “is that rampant corruption in Congress and the administration is directly costing average citizens who are paying more for necessities like groceries, gas, and medicine.”

Both Democrats and the press, however, so far, are overlooking one of the most overt and consequential examples of Trump’s pay-to-play behavior. On May 24, 2024, Josh Dawsey and Maxine Joselow of The Washington Post published a blockbuster exposé, reporting that Trump privately told a group of oil company CEOs they should donate $1 billion to his 2024 presidential campaign. It would be a good “deal” for the industry, Trump reportedly said, because of the tax and regulation benefits they would receive if he returned to the Oval Office.

Specifically, Trump reportedly said he would reverse the Biden administration’s pause on new liquefied natural gas, or LNG, export permits, approve more drilling for oil in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska, and roll back environmental regulations the industry didn’t like, including electric vehicle purchasing mandates and vehicle emissions limits. Dawsey and Joselow then published a follow-up, reporting that Trump also promised to soften Federal Trade Commission scrutiny of industry mergers and acquisitions.

Two and a half years later, his administration has delivered on each of these promises and then some. The Brennan Center has published a well-documented summary of Trump’s assault on climate policy—including his administration’s repeal of the “endangerment finding,” which granted the federal government the authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions—that connects the dots between Trump’s actions and the many billions of dollars the oil industry has reaped as a result, including many millions of dollars benefiting oil executives as individuals.

What makes all this relevant to the midterm elections—beyond the fact that the leader of the Republican Party is directly implicated—is that many of Trump’s accomplishments were only possible because of rubber-stamp support from Republicans in Congress. Now those same Republicans must face the voters. How will they explain themselves?

To be clear, Democrats don’t get a pass here; corruption has been part of politics forever, and one of the press’s central obligations is to expose and hold its perpetrators to account, whoever they may be. That requires following the facts where they lead. But it also requires challenging the practice, still common among old-school newsrooms, of false equivalence—of portraying both sides as equally culpable for a given transgression for fear that an accurate portrayal would look like “taking sides.” If most of the facts point in one direction, our reporting should have the integrity and courage to say so.

Most voters don’t have access to directly question candidates seeking their votes. It’s our job as journalists to ask questions on their behalf so they can make informed decisions about their leaders.

Corruption is understandably a hot issue these days. Meanwhile, new scientific analysis from the nonprofit Climate Central shows that every congressional district in the country is hotter than it was in 1970, thanks to climate change. No surprise, then, that polling also shows that the vast majority of people want their government to take stronger climate action. Journalism that connects those dots—accurately and fairly, and without pulling any punches—is a true public service.

items.title: Youth Is a Devastating Comedy About an Overlooked Stage of Motherhood
items.content_text:
Youth is full of women running out of time. Alex (Sharon Horgan) is a divorced, 50-year-old literary agent with a college-age son. At this moment in her life, she’s either at the end of her rope or at the start of a new era—it’s often hard for her to tell which. Sometimes, the ticking clock manifests in ordinary ways. At a book fair in Germany, Alex has a distracted meeting with an editor who reminds her that she’s “a bit stretched for time.” Later, as Alex regales a potential client—a psychology advice columnist—with the trials and tribulations of her love life, the client warningly interjects, “I only have an hour.”

More often, Alex’s time crunch has an apocalyptic bent. When Patrick (Rupert Friend), an old flame who’s recently reappeared in her life, asks if it’s the right time for her to start a relationship, she replies indignantly, “It is the right time, it has to be the right time, because another time’s gonna be too late.” Later, when Alex briefly explores a relationship with Michael, a much older man, the problem of time becomes fatally strange. Describing his mother’s passing, he tells Alex with a look of profundity, “Her last words to me really stuck: ‘I’ll be dead tomorrow, and so will you.’” Alex recoils, but he explains, “Yeah, she meant live every day like it’s your last.” Alex, a mother herself, is skeptical about Michael’s extraction of such a neat moral from such a bizarre final utterance. “Did she?”

Youth, which airs on HBO, is one of several extraordinary series Horgan has created on the subject of motherhood. Time is each show’s most deranged and deranging element. In Catastrophe (2015–2019), time moves too fast. In each of its four seasons, Sharon (also played by Horgan) is either pregnant or the mother of a small child. The time jump from season one to two takes her from a newlywed in the process of delivering her first child to a soon-to-be mother of two. Motherland (2016–2022), which Horgan co-created but does not star in, focuses on the harried, endless grind that characterizes being the parent of school-age kids. From managing schedules to managing feelings, the time moves impossibly fast, but it also drags. When Julia (Anna Maxwell Martin) loses the childcare she has relied on up to now (her own mother, who flatly quits), an avalanche of new duties falls on her, impeding the orderly forward motion of her life.

At the center of Youth is the period of parental life that critic Nina Renata Aron recently named “middle motherhood.” The world of culture, Aron argues, is filled with compelling, dramatic narratives of new motherhood, which she describes as “a time to swoon, and also to rage and cry.” That world is not similarly filled with narratives of mothers whose children have, to some degree or another, grown up, whose motherhood is no longer new, raw, exciting, rupturing. These motherhood narratives, if and when they’re even recognized as motherhood narratives, are few and far between. And yet, their fast-approaching but glacially unfolding temporality makes them rich stories to tell. “I can actually feel myself occupying a new developmental phase,” Aron writes of her own middle motherhood, “taking a different place in the generational order.” Stories of new motherhood are about being caught up in the rush of a new biological current; middle motherhood stories are about finding a new place in history.

Youth is a story about this transitional state, and it’s told by a writer and performer very much aware of the way such stories remain often unseen, unheard, untold. With her characteristic fizzing wit, blinkered charm, and soulful realism, Horgan has opened up a new stage of her own career. When I think back to Michael’s recounting of his mother’s last words, what strikes me is not so much that Michael extracts a trite maxim from her enigmatic phrase; it’s that Alex understands immediately that that’s not really what she said. This woman, at the end—not the beginning or even the middle—of life, of motherhood, of womanhood, said something way weirder than carpe diem. You just have to listen.


It is something of a reductive synopsis to say that Youth is just a show about motherhood. Indeed, the first episode presents us with a woman who is ready and eager to send her son off to college and explore the world as someone who is no longer defined by being a parent, no longer constrained by the demands of raising her son. Her ex-husband, a middling actor, has lived his life heedlessly, leaving all the child-rearing to Alex as he remarries a younger woman and prepares to leave the country for a sci-fi pilot shoot. As her son, Ruarí (Aran Murphy), gets in the car to drive off to school, Alex runs desperately after it only to burst out laughing. She sets to transforming his old room into a yoga studio, alternately collapsing into sobs and rising up with giddy glee. Later that week, she brings a man home for a successful fling, only to find Ruarí—surly, upset, uncommunicative—has reclaimed his bed. Alex would love her story to have stopped being about motherhood any longer; Youth is about the uncanny disappointment of finding out that hasn’t happened.

So, Youth is not a narrative of the disappearance or recession of motherhood from Alex’s identity so much as it’s a narrative of its eccentric reassertion. Rather than a series about the liberation from motherhood or a wish fulfillment tale of Alex getting her groove back in her perimenopause era, the show thinks about the different, weird ways motherhood adapts itself to this new stage of life.

The most direct way is through the manosphere-curious Ruarí. When we meet him, he’s seemingly embarked upon a self-destructive spiral. He stages a cheeky, disruptive protest at his high school graduation ceremony; he squeezes burrata all over himself and his family at a celebration dinner; and then there are the circumstances of his sudden return from uni. While it takes a few episodes for us to learn the whole story, it’s immediately clear that ­Ruarí has conducted himself poorly, and that this has made him unwelcome on campus. Back at home, he retreats into old clips of Mitch Hedberg’s stand-up and videos about semen retention. Alex is both terrified by her son’s sudden sullen mania and ill-equipped to get him to divulge what’s wrong. For much of the season, Ruarí is a mute stranger, haunting her halls. For a show as regularly funny as this one, it’s an upsetting portrait of a seemingly common contemporary phenomenon: a son lost to the online void, now become a man you can’t seem to fully trust.

So, as Alex navigates the physical changes of her age—her ailments range from spontaneous lockjaw to surprise menstruation—she’s also dealing with the emotional ravages of being both thrust back into active motherly service and rejected for that job. The seeming stable solution to these problems is Patrick, her longtime, on-again-off-again, “institutionally single” ex-lover. Alex and Patrick have an easy chemistry—Horgan has always known how to write great, crackling, funny flirtation—but it’s underlaid with a barely unspoken tension. The problem of their relationship is both that Ruarí still takes up too much of Alex’s life and that Alex can’t, and won’t, ever be able to give Patrick children of his own. It’s a banal kind of star-crossed love. What would it mean to accept someone for who they are when they are both too much and not enough of a mother?


“I live with the dim awareness that a tragedy is unfolding,” writes Nina Renata Aron. “The tragedy of mortality, of time passing, of exiting the phase of life where it’s possible to make new life.” Aron acknowledges the sexism of this tragic framing, the idea that women’s aging itself is a kind of death. Youth is nonetheless preoccupied with the sticky feeling of loss that comes with Alex’s feelings of liberation. The challenge of assembling a new life mostly out of available, remaining parts. The judgment that comes with that assertion of continued existence.

Midway through the season, on a holiday in Spain, Alex becomes kind of obsessed with a woman her age or a bit older who seems to breeze through the world with confidence, wisdom, and panache. She dines alone with gusto, her voluminous hair proudly showing its gray. On one occasion, Alex catches her eye, only to start coughing on smoke from her own cigarette. Later, Alex spies her again and tries to express what an inspiration she is, how her small example of living out loud has given Alex strength and courage. “I wanted to tell you, you look great,” she says. “So cool and content and comfortable in your skin, just you by yourself.” But the woman doesn’t speak English. Instead of picking up on Alex’s gratitude, she reads only anxiety and discomfort. The woman calls for help. “I think there’s something wrong with her,” she says, in Spanish.

Youth is a sexy, dazzling, often devastating comedy of middle motherhood. It’s a show with no neat maxims and plenty of weird, wise things to say about being alive, and a woman, and 50 all at once.

items.title: Ilhan Omar Is the Right Kind of American. Trump Is the Wrong Kind.
items.content_text:
On October 15, 1969, Somali President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke was slain by an assassin’s bullet. Unrest had prevailed in the country ever since … well, in many ways, ever since independence was won in 1960, but particularly over the previous couple years. Then as now, Somalia didn’t register much in most Americans’ minds, but the editors of The New York Times judged the event newsworthy enough that it made the front page, with a report noting the imposition of a curfew in “Mogadiscio,” as the capital was then styled by the paper of record.

Six days later, a military junta took control of the country under the leadership of Mohamed Siad Barre. He was a socialist, and he imposed Marxist-Leninist government, aligning with the Soviet Union. But over time, his relationship with Moscow soured. The Soviets frowned upon Somalia’s 1977 invasion of Ethiopia and switched allegiances. According to a 1982 New York Times op-ed by the respected comparative political scientist David D. Laitin, Washington began to take an interest in Siad Barre. Jimmy Carter did so tentatively, but “President Reagan, abandoning caution, gave Mr. Siad Barre a warm welcome in Washington” that March, Laitin wrote. Little countries like Somalia at the time were just pieces on a Cold War chessboard on which the Reagan administration moved around its pawns with particular aggression.

By the late 1980s, discontent with Siad Barre was such that rebel groups began engaging government forces; a civil war erupted. By the early 1990s, Somalia was a failed state. Siad Barre went into exile. Governments couldn’t patch the nation together. And around that time, Somalis began to flee to Kenya—hundreds of thousands of them, into refugee camps. The largest, Dadaab, is still home to some 400,000 Somali refugees, 35 years later.

Why should all this matter to you right now? Because one of those refugees, Nur Omar Mohammed, took his children to Dadaab. By 1995, they were granted asylum by the United States of America and came here, eventually applying for citizenship. One of those children was 17 or 18 at the time of the citizenship application. That wouldn’t seem to matter much in the broad scheme of things, whether a youngster was this age or that some 30 years ago. But today, that youngster is Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar, and Donald Trump and his subordinates are moving heaven and earth to use that alleged discrepancy to get her expelled not only from Congress but from the United States that once welcomed her.

The Trump administration’s move against Omar is repulsive. And it’s sure not happening because her father might have recorded her age inaccurately half a lifetime ago (an allegation that, as yet, remains unproven publicly). It’s happening first and foremost because she’s a very vocal critic of Trump and MAGA-ism. True, alongside her criticisms of Trump, she’s also made some remarks that smacked of antisemitism, and which were deserving of denunciation. But in this country, it’s the voters who decide whether such comments disqualify someone from office. And Omar’s voters have returned her to Congress three times after her initial election in 2018, and they’re about to do so again. And since she hasn’t been stopped at the ballot box, Trump is now searching for other means to do so.

And by the way, those voters include citizens in the heavily Jewish enclave of St. Louis Park, the famous home of the Coen Brothers and Al Franken. If homegrown opposition to Omar was to arise, it would have been from there. She did win the 2022 Democratic primary narrowly, but in 2024, she won the primary handily, and in the general, she carried nearly 70 percent of the vote in St. Louis Park.

But let’s be real. This is also happening because Omar is Somali—because she’s a Black Muslim woman who wears a hijab. These things aren’t quantifiable, and of course Trump and his spokespeople, at least the ones who haven’t lied about their legal careers, would never admit to these aspects of this piece of political persecution. But we all know it’s there.

Actually, now that I think about it, Trump has admitted to his hatred of Somalis and has done so rather openly. Ever since details spilled out about large-scale welfare fraud in the Minneapolis Somali community, Trump has been talking and posting about it incessantly and trying to connect it to Omar. It’s undeniably true that the scale of the fraud is nightmarish. But there’s no evidence of any such connection. (The Biden Justice Department opened an unrelated investigation into Omar’s finances, but it “stalled for lack of evidence.”)

That hasn’t stopped Trump from calling Omar “garbage,” as he did in a Cabinet meeting last year, and from ranting about Somalis generally in a way that can plainly be called racist and can arguably be called fascist. Am I being melodramatic here? Consider these Trump sentences, from an October 8 Truth Social post: “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

The racism is apparent in the first two sentences, which seek to incite hatred based specifically on the nationality of the population in question. But those third and fourth sentences … how exactly is he proposing that Minnesotans “fight back”? And when he says the federal government will “come to your rescue,” what precisely does he mean? And who is the “you” he is addressing?

I think we have a pretty good idea—he means that if certain “real” Minnesotans were to take the matter of the “Somalians” into their own hands, he’d order in armed troops to back them up. Whether this is fascist is in the eye of the beholder. But I’ll just note this: On April 1, 1933, the Nazis organized a boycott of Jewish shops and department stores. Brownshirts who stood outside the stores held signs: “Germans, defend yourselves against the Jewish atrocity propaganda, buy only at German shops!”

We’re not there just yet. But what if a few Minnesotans—good, pure, white, ancestral Minnesotans—barreled into Cedar-Riverside, Minneapolis’s “Little Mogadishu,” incensed in part by the incendiary rhetoric of the president of the United States, and had themselves a little shoot-up, or broke a few shop windows? Trump has already committed the federal government—a phrase that implicates all of us, by the way—to coming to their “rescue.”

And what of his pursuit of Omar? Trump has been firing blanks in courtrooms his entire second term in his jihad against his political enemies, so there’s reason to think that this one will crumble the way all the others have.

In the meantime, it’s the duty of every antifascist American, however one might feel about some of Omar’s past comments, to stand arm in arm with her here. She is in this country as a result of a tragic chain of events that the United States, playing Cold War roulette, helped set in train. But this country did make amends by welcoming her to its shores. And once here, far from asking for handouts—the right’s standard caricature of people like her—she got herself educated and elected to the Minnesota state house and, finally, to the U.S. House of Representatives.

If Omar were a Republican with a last name like Schultz, Trump sure wouldn’t be ordering people to raid her house and asking what year she was born—he would be effusing over her American success story. But to Trump, who has nothing but contempt for this country’s founding principles and its immigrant fabric, she is the wrong kind of American. He’s right that there are wrong kinds of Americans. He’s just wrong about who they are.

items.title: A Guide to Trump’s Body Parts
items.content_text:
The forthcoming midterm elections are a referendum on President Donald Trump’s policies, not his health. But when those policies include renaming the Atlantic “Trump Ocean,” or affecting indifference about whether Iran might “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego, or prohibiting nominees for executive branch positions from saying out loud, “Joe Biden won the 2020 election,” that changes the equation. With directives like these emanating from the White House, it’s everybody’s civic duty to consider whether its occupant is a well man.

Navy Captain Sean Barbabella, who is physician to President Trump, pronounced five months ago that Trump is “fully fit to carry out all duties of the Commander-in-Chief and Head of State.” Barbabella said much the same after Trump’s chest and belly underwent a CT scan the previous October. But no presidential physician has ever dared state otherwise. Rear Admiral Cary Grayson said Woodrow Wilson’s stroke in 1919 was merely a bout of “nervous exhaustion.” Dr. Janet Travell lied her head off to cover up John F. Kennedy’s Addison’s disease. Even the autopsy report sent to the Warren Commission omitted that Kennedy’s adrenal glands were only barely still present, presumably because these pathologists didn’t want to acknowledge the undisclosed cause.

Compared to Trump, though, Wilson and JFK were compulsive truth-tellers. So what are the odds we’re getting the straight story about the president’s physical and mental fitness now? Any serious inquiry into Trump’s health must weigh the official line against medical doctors’ analyses of what they see on television; observations from Trump’s staff; and various reports from books, newspapers, magazines, and so on. We scrounge for evidence where we can.

Diagnosing any patient from afar is a tricky business, especially when the diagnostician (me) never attended medical school. It is also perhaps unkind. But to any who would criticize the following inventory as cruel, let me remind you that, 22 months into his presidency, Trump still habitually blames “Sleepy Joe Biden” or “Slow Joe” for everything that goes wrong. Other countries, Trump said last October, “looked at him falling down stairs every day, every day the guy’s falling down stairs.” In January, Trump told The New York Times: “I think Joe Biden is the worst thing that ever happened to old people.” When Biden disclosed that he had Stage 4 prostate cancer, Trump said: “If you feel sorry for him, don’t feel so sorry, because he’s vicious.”

In saying such manifestly cruel things, Trump forfeits any right to deference about his own physical frailties. Plus, he’s the president! In that spirit, let’s plunge our tweezers into President Cavity Sam, and try not to set off too many buzzers.

Hair

It’s dyed. Natural hair doesn’t change color except to turn gray or white, and nobody would wear a toupee this bad. Trump’s hair is sometimes blonde, sometimes orange, and sometimes a little pink, though that may just be Trump’s angry-red scalp peeking through an ever less convincing comb-over. Male-pattern baldness has reportedly stalked Trump for decades. According to Harry Hurt III’s book Lost Tycoon, Trump had scalp reduction surgery in the 1980s and it didn’t go well. Jeffrey Epstein confirmed Trump had the procedure, but Trump has denied it.

Why such weird colors? Ivanka Trump has reportedly said her father uses a product called Just for Men that you’re supposed to apply slowly, but Trump lacks the patience to do that, so he ends up with weird coloration. Michael Wolff reported this in Fire and Fury (2018), so take it with a grain of salt; the book’s reliability is a matter of debate, and besides, nearly a decade has passed. Wolff said recently on his podcast that Trump has an emergency hair kit, carried by Natalie Harp or perhaps someone else, containing “small tufts of hair that match whatever color his hair might be at the time. And those are applied if needed and necessary.” Interesting, if true.

Face

Clearly Trump sprays or slathers something on it. The consensus is that it’s some self-tanning product like Man Tan. That would also explain the white circles frequently seen around his eyes. Wearing goggles under a tanning bed would do that too, but Trump’s former press secretary Stephanie Grisham wrote in her 2021 book, I’ll Take Your Questions Now, that, at least during Trump’s first term, the White House was tanning bed–free. Grisham writes, “The president’s look was created with makeup that he put on his face every morning,” and that before one public appearance, Trump borrowed her face powder. Grisham refers in the book to an “arsenal of products” that an aide traveling with Trump would carry, but she doesn’t enumerate what they were.

Brain

This is of course the principal area of concern. I reviewed serious reasons for worry in some detail last month (“Why Trump May Not Serve Out His Presidency”). To summarize: STAT News reported nine years ago that neurolinguistics and cognition experts comparing old videos of Trump with more recent ones observed deterioration in the complexity of Trump’s unscripted public utterances. Former Maryland Governor Martin O’Malley compared Trump’s 2016 rhetorical style to “a monkey with a machinegun.” (That’s not a medical opinion, but it’s very good.) Groups of mental health experts again declared in 2024 that Trump displayed signs of cognitive decline, and 18 months later that he’d “deteriorated even further.” Trump falls asleep a lot during White House meetings. He says crazy stuff all the time. The latest expert to note this is Trump himself. At a MAGA rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, earlier this month, Trump said, “I could say the stupidest things, and you’d clap me.”

Right ear

This is the most famous presidential body part; it’s Trump’s battle scar from the attempt on his life in Meridian, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. The bullet created a two-centimeter wound, according to the former White House presidential physician Ronny Jackson, who by then was a Republican House member from Texas. There’s apparently a scar on Trump’s ear now, but in September 2024 Trump showed it to New York magazine’s Olivia Nuzzi and she said she couldn’t see it. Nuzzi, however, has come to be regarded as a potentially problematic source.

Neck

Asked last March about some really alarming redness on the right side of Trump’s neck, Barbabella said, “President Trump is using a very common cream on the right side of his neck, which is a preventative skin treatment. The president is using the treatment for one week, and the redness is expected to last for a few weeks.”

Can you indulge me one pet peeve? The word is preventive. More substantively, Barbabella left unanswered the following questions: 1) What was it that the offending cream was intended to prevent? 2) If the cream was causing that angry rash, why was it still being applied?

The rash does seem to have gone away.

Heart

Yes, he has one. So far as we know it’s in decent shape; we don’t know why Trump’s doctors last year felt it necessary to do a CT scan of it. Trump takes two drugs, rosuvastatin and ezetimibe, to manage his cholesterol, which as a result is within normal range. Trump takes Bayer aspirin daily to reduce the risk of a heart attack. But for some bizarre reason his favored dose is 325 milligrams, which his doctors have repeatedly told him is about four times too much. A dose that high increases Trump’s risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Trump’s doctors want him to drop down to 81 milligrams, but he refuses to do that. Is our teetotaling commander in chief an aspirin junkie, like the murderer Perry Smith in In Cold Blood? We can’t rule it out. Aspirin-use disorder is, according to one 2019 study, “an underreported condition.”

Belly

Trump’s May physical measured his weight at 238 pounds. At a reported six feet, three inches, Trump’s body mass index was 29.7. That would put him a whisker shy of “obese.” But Trump isn’t six foot three; he’s six foot two. That’s what Trump’s driver’s license said in 2012, Politico’s Darren Samuelsohn reported in 2016, and it’s what his draft card said in 1968, The Washington Post’s Craig Whitlock reported in 2015. As people age, they don’t get taller, they get shorter, so probably Trump is now closer to six foot one. But let’s be generous and say he’s still six foot two. That would put his BMI at 30.6 and make him officially “obese.” Indeed, 30.6 is higher than the BMI of any previous president excepting William Howard Taft (reigning champ at 42.3), Grover Cleveland (34.6), and Trump’s hero, William McKinley (31.1). However, Trump has a lower BMI than our other two obese presidents, Zachary Taylor and Theodore Roosevelt (both 30.2). Trump’s doctors have told him to lose weight.

Since you were about to ask: Yes, as of February 2024, “Sleepy” Joe Biden’s BMI was 23.1, classifying him as “healthy.”

Backside

Not an important concern, but a delicate one: Does Trump wear an adult diaper? He would hardly be the first national politician to do so, nor even necessarily the first president. I’m guessing there are at least four or five diapers in our superannuated Congress. But put me down for a probable “no.”

Our main source on the Trump diaper rumor is Noel Casler, a stand-up comedian who says he worked six seasons for The Apprentice, the reality-TV show Trump starred in from 2004 to 2015. (Starting in 2008, it was called The Celebrity Apprentice.) Like everything else in Casler’s story, Casler’s work for The Apprentice is unverified. In 2020, Casler said Trump’s “incontinence stems from his decades of stimulant abuse and fast-food diet.” Casler went on to explain that the stimulant in question was Adderall: “He snorts Adderall as his maintenance high. When he gets too wired, this is tempered with benzodiazepines.” Around the time Casler added that Trump “sent his secretaries to the CVS on 57th Street to pick up his scripts for ... herpes treatment,” I concluded the man was a teller of tall tales who just doesn’t like Trump.

Why, then, only a “probable” no to a Trump diaper? Because former Republican Representative Adam Kinzinger, who made an enemy of Trump by voting for his impeachment after the January 6 insurrection, and as a consequence felt compelled to retire in 2022, said afterward that Trump constantly smells bad.* “I’m genuinely surprised how people close to Trump haven’t talked about the odor,” Kinzinger tweeted in December 2023. “It’s truly something to behold. Wear a mask if you can.”

The following year, Kinzinger said on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, “If you take, like, armpits, ketchup, makeup and a little butt, it’s probably like that, all mixed up.… A little bit of a pungent odor, I would say.” If Kinzinger was telling the truth, this might simply be an unusually bad case of flatulence. But if so, then, why is Trump’s posture sometimes peculiar, and what’s with the strange bulge sometimes seen in his pants? I can’t say.

Right hand

We’ve seen weird bruising on Trump’s right hand for well over a year now. Sometimes he covers it up with makeup, but you can still see it. The White House said it was from shaking hands, but then the condition spread to Trump’s left hand. This may indicate circulation problems. The White House said that the underlying cause was Trump’s overconsumption of aspirin, which is plausible. But if Trump refuses to cut back on his daily 325 Bayer milligrams even as it turns his hands purple, that strengthens the hypothesis that Trump is hooked on aspirin.

Legs, ankles

I mentioned already Trump’s awkward posture, and how that may (emphasize may) mean he’s a nappies guy. The official diagnosis is chronic venous insufficiency, which is not life-threatening. The unofficial speculation is that, like Woodrow Wilson, Trump may have suffered an unreported stroke. Professor Bruce Davidson of Washington State University’s medical school told Sidney Blumenthal and Sean Wilentz, on their podcast The Court of History, that he thinks Trump had a stroke perhaps six months ago and that it was “on the left side of the brain, which controls the right side of the body.” There’s also been speculation that Trump is wearing some sort of leg brace, based on footage that appears to show something under his left trouser leg.

I’ll skip Trump’s feet, which at one point had bone spurs that kept him out of the Vietnam War, because the spurs vanished the moment Richard Nixon ended the draft in January 1973. The point of this exercise has not been to engage in body-shaming, or even, really, draft-dodger-shaming. I wouldn’t do it if the Cavity Sam in question weren’t president of the United States. But he is the president, he’s entered his ninth decade, and he’s been acting and looking weirder than usual. That has implications for the health of the republic.

But let me close by conceding, once again, that I am not a doctor. I’m just a guy poking some tweezers into the body politic.

* This post originally misstated the reason Kinzinger left office.

items.title: The Atlantic Publishes List of “50 Unforgettable Love Stories”
items.content_text:
Today The Atlantic launches “50 Unforgettable Love Stories,” a new editorial project that highlights stories of romantic love. The list includes works published across more than four centuries—from its earliest selection, Astrophil and Stella by Philip Sidney, published in 1591, to its most recent, The Safekeep by Yael van der Wouden, published in 2024. The list below is an effort to name the love stories—novels, of course, but also poetry, plays, and short stories—that are the most enduring.

To arrive at 50 titles, The Atlantic’s Books team asked a jury of scholars, librarians, critics, and authors across genres, as well as many colleagues, to name their favorite titles that were originally written in English. As the introduction to the list says: “We thought of our own personal touchstones, deliberated over the choices, and emerged with a group of standouts: 50 titles you won’t soon forget.”

The editors write that across centuries, “the love story, with all of its attendant joys and sorrows, was an organizing principle of life—and of literature … Today, fictional love is associated with the romance genre and its proliferating subcategories, and you’ll find examples of those books here, but we aimed to think more expansively about its literary manifestations. The love story belongs as much to Arundhati Roy as to Jane Austen; its pulse beats as strongly in the knotty poetry of Anne Carson as it does in the steamy historicals of Beverly Jenkins. It is by turns ecstatic, tragic, cerebral, enthralling, and enlightening. For so many of us, it’s a reason to live and to read.”

“50 Unforgettable Love Stories” is part of The Atlantic’s robust Books section, devoted to essays, criticism, reporting, original fiction, poetry, and book recommendations, as well as The Atlantic’s weekly Books Briefing newsletter. This follows The Atlantic’s earlier books projects “65 Essential Children’s Books,” released in October 2025, “The Best American Poetry of the 21st Century (So Far),” published in March 2025, and “The Great American Novels,” released in 2024.

Press Contacts:
Paul Jackson and Sammi Sontag | The Atlantic
press@theatlantic.com

items.title: Donald Trump Cancels Second Mainstream Interview in Days

Donald Trump pulled out of another mainstream interview Thursday–this time nixing a sit-down with NBC News.

items.title: Mitch McConnell Called Donald Trump a ‘Stupid’ and ‘Despicable Human Being’

McConnell made the withering assessments in a series of private “personal oral histories” that he gave to Michael Tackett, the deputy Washington bureau chief of the Associated Press, who has a forthcoming biography about the Kentucky senator called The Price of Power. items.title: Menendez Family Members: We Had ‘Gut-Level’ Fears Erik and Lyle Were Sexually Abused

After a press conference in which they’d called for the imprisoned siblings’ freedom, the family members told Chris Cuomo on NewsNation about how their suspicions only deepened as time passed.

“Over the years we really did know that there was abuse at gut-level. But as time goes on and we all talked to each other more and more, it validates the fears and the gut-level reactions that we had,” the brothers’ cousin Karen VanderMolen-Copley told Cuomo. “That solidified the knowledge that the sexual abuse actually did occur, because that’s not something you want to believe, and then once you talk to each other it becomes more and more obvious.”

items.title: Liam Payne 911 Caller Said One Direction Star’s Life Could Be in Danger Minutes Before Death
items.content_text:
A hotel worker called 911 to request urgent assistance before musician Liam Payne fell to his death from the third floor of the building in Buenos Aires on Wednesday.

The 31-year-old British singer and former member of the boy band One Direction died after he “jumped from the balcony of his room,” Buenos Aires Security Ministry Communications Director Pablo Policicchio told the Associated Press. He added that police had been called to the Casa Sur Hotel in the Argentine capital after receiving an emergency call shortly after 5 p.m. local time about an “aggressive man who could be under the influence of drugs or alcohol.”

A transcript of a 911 call published by the BBC shows a worker at the hotel telling the operator that they have “a guest who is high on drugs and who is trashing the room” and the staff therefore “need someone to come.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Stormy Daniels Says Trump Is Trying to Silence Her Again
items.content_text:
It appears Donald Trump is once again attempting to silence Stormy Daniels, despite his recent convictions in that category.

MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow reports that Trump’s lawyers tried to “get another hush money deal” with the adult film star, to keep her from making any “public or private statements related to any alleged past interactions” with the former president. In exchange for her written agreement, Trump’s team reportedly offered to adjust the debt she owes Trump for the unsuccessful defamation case her lawyer brought against him in 2018.

Daniels still needs to pay “hundreds of thousands of dollars” in legal fees, Maddow explained, and in hammering out the exact amount, Trump’s lawyers allegedly offered to “pretend” she owed their client “less than they actually believed” she did. Whereas they first estimated Daniels’ debt at $650,000, Maddow reported, they said they would settle her tab for $620,000, if she promised not to make any “defamatory or disparaging statements about him, his business, and/or any affiliates, or his suitability as a candidate for president.” They then adjusted the fee, asking $635,000 if she refused to sign a non-disclosure agreement. Daniels reportedly turned them down, paying $627,500 and declining to sign the NDA.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Tegan and Sara: The Pop-Rock Twins Driven Mad by a Wild Catfishing Scheme
items.content_text:
Online interactions are based on trust, since there are few definitive ways to certify the identity of the person with whom one is communicating. Naturally, this situation can lead to deception and manipulation, as it has—to tormenting effect—for Tegan and Sara, the popular indie rock duo whose lives have been turned upside down by a mysterious bad faith actor who, for more than a decade, has impersonated Tegan with fans, friends, and business partners.

Fanatical: The Catfishing of Tegan and Sara is an investigation into the myriad means by which the internet can be wielded to nefarious ends. More than that, though, it’s an anatomy of a crime and the complicated wreckage wrought by it, not just for the famous artists but also for the innocent admirers who were tricked into believing that fiction was reality.

Premiering on Hulu on Oct. 18, following its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, Erin Lee Carr’s documentary is a chilling snapshot of the unholy marriage of corrosive fandom and online duplicity. At its center are Tegan and Sara, the identical twin songstresses who began making a name for themselves in the early 2000s both for their talent and for being openly gay. This earned them a loyal fanbase of queer women and men who saw themselves reflected in Tegan and Sara, and that bond was strengthened by the siblings’ active interest in interacting with fans in person—Tegan would chat with show attendees in line and at the merch table—and on LiveJournal and other budding message-board platforms that afforded a previously unavailable degree of contact.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: ‘Anora’: The Screwball Stripper Odyssey That Should Win All the Oscars
items.content_text:
Movies can’t, by definition, be all things to all people, and yet Anora—winner of the Cannes Film Festival’s highest honor, the Palme d’Or—manages to vacillate between assorted registers with stunning, and ultimately affecting, aplomb.

Another of The Florida Project and Red Rocket writer/director Sean Baker’s tales of marginalized individuals struggling to survive and find themselves in an often-unforgiving world, the film is a character study, romance, crime saga, screwball comedy, and vérité drama all wrapped into one unique and dexterous package. More impressive than its nimbleness, however, is its poise and empathy, the latter of which is chiefly bestowed upon its protagonist, whose life is thrown for a rollercoaster-grade loop-di-loop thanks to a chance introduction.

Ani (Mikey Madison, in a star-making turn) is a Brighton Beach 23-year-old who lives with her sister and earns a living stripping at a local club. Anora, which hits theaters Oct. 18, introduces her at the end of a long pan along a bench where men are receiving lap dances from erotic professionals. Fixating on Ani’s face as she flashes the fake smile that her customers crave and her superiors demand, Baker’s camera creates immediate, intimate engagement with the young woman, and that continues as it presents snapshots of her daily (or, rather, nightly) routine at her place of employment.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Jimmy Kimmel Mocks Fox News’ Post-Harris Interview ‘Orgy’

items.title: Anderson Cooper Literally Calls Bulls*** on Surrogate’s Trump Defense
items.content_text:
CNN anchor Anderson Cooper was flabbergasted Wednesday by a surrogate’s defense of Donald Trump, calling his explanation for the former president’s bombastic statements literal “bulls---.”

On AC360, former California Lieutenant Gov. Abel Maldonado, a Republican, said that Trump’s recent comments calling for the military to “handle” Democrats were simply his way of expressing his inner New Yorker. “He’s a fighter,” Maldonado added.

The conversation began when Cooper brought up Trump’s former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Mark Milley, who, alongside other military leaders, have begun to warn of the dangers of re-electing the former president. Milley has called Trump a “fascist to his core.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Liam Payne’s Snapchat Story Seemingly Sheds Light on Singer’s Final Hours
items.content_text:
Liam Payne was seemingly having a “lovely day in Argentina” just hours before his death on Wednesday, according to what appear to be a series of final posts made to his Snapchat account.

The former One Direction member was found dead in the courtyard of a Buenos Aires hotel, having apparently plunged 13 to 14 meters from his balcony, according to local police. A cause of death has not officially been determined, and it was unclear whether the fall was accidental or intentional.

On his Snapchat Story, however, it would have appeared to any fan that Payne was having a relaxing vacation. In since-deleted posts in the hours before his death, he posted a front-facing video in which he told followers, “It’s a lovely day here in Argentina. This is the breakfast table. Just enjoying coffee and breakfast even though it’s 1 p.m.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Chris Hayes Furious With Fox Over ‘Edited’ Soundbite in Harris Interview
items.content_text:
MSNBC’s Chris Hayes called out Fox News for not showing the full context of Donald Trump’s “enemy within” comments during Vice President Kamala Harris’ interview on the network earlier Wednesday.

The anchor of All In opened his broadcast by calling attention to something that Harris herself did in the sit-down with Fox’s Bret Baier. The clip that the right-wing network showed to Harris as part of Baier’s question was of Trump during his all-female town hall event in Georgia—the one where Trump bizarrely argued he was the “father of IVF.”

In the clip that Fox aired directly to Harris during her interview, Trump wasn’t heard talking about how former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi or Rep. Adam Schiff are the “enemy within.” Instead, Fox made it so Harris had to react to him talking more mildly about “phony investigations.” The network omitted Trump’s line about “the enemy within.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: ‘Real Housewives of Salt Lake City’: Is Heather Gay a Hypocrite for Taking Ozempic?
items.content_text:
The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City is TV’s best soap opera, week after week offering twists more shocking than secret twins and characters returning from the dead. That’s because it’s all real, happening in the most haunted suburb in the continental United States.

Where else do two women connect over knowing the long-lost birth father of one’s child? Is there another city where women squabble over body positivity in a parking lot off the side of a snowy mountain? Surely, there’s no other place on Earth where Lisa Barlow could come across anywhere near a voice of reason.

But that all happens here in Salt Lake City. Five episodes in, Season 5 has continued to evolve into the most captivating season in modern Real Housewives history, carried by the ever-changing bonds between our OGs and a team of wonderfully bizarre newbies.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Review: Will Adam Driver Explode in ‘Hold on to Me Darling’?
items.content_text:
It doesn’t matter how long a play is: sometimes 75 minutes can feel like 3 hours if the play is bad, while a three-hour play may first elicit an inner groan, then flow pleasurably by if the writing and performances are in well-oiled tandem.

Kenneth Lonergan’s Hold on to Me Darling (Lucille Lortel Theatre, to Dec. 22) belongs, mostly, to the latter category: it is long, and it feels long, but that’s OK; not gold-standard wow, but far more than pleasant. This is down to Lonergan’s engaging writing and a collection of differently distinctive, carefully drawn performances, led by Adam Driver as a famous country star called Strings (real name Clarence), wondering if he could/should give up all the trappings of fame for a simpler life after his mother’s death.

It is an off-Broadway treat to see Driver, most recently seen on the big screen as the star of Francis Ford Coppola’s polarizing epic Megalopolis, here bestriding—he is so tall, he is really bestriding—the compact Lucille Lortel stage. Theater fans last saw him on Broadway in Burn This, for which he was nominated for the Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play. He is renowned for playing powder-keg personas. With characters like Adam in Girls, Charlie in Marriage Story, and Pale in Burn This, the question, the bubbling menace, was when will Adam Driver go off? Those characters memorably combusted—thrashing, shouting, snarling and occupying spaces that could barely contain them—and Driver made it so that you recoiled from their crackling fury.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Fox News’ Bret Baier Whines About Harris After Bad-Tempered Interview
items.content_text:
Fox News host Bret Baier recapped his Wednesday night interview with Vice President Kamala Harris, telling his colleagues that he got a sense early on that Harris “was going to be tough to redirect without me trying to interrupt.”

The interview, Harris’ first on the right-wing network since becoming the Democratic nominee, was broadcast on Special Report after being filmed in the previous hour. According to Baier, the interview had been scheduled for 5 p.m., but Harris showed up 15 minutes late. This, he complained, was like “icing the kicker” in football.

“We were supposed to start at 5 p.m. This was the time they gave us. Originally, we were going to do 25 or 30 minutes. They came in and said, ‘Well, maybe 20.’ So, it’s already getting whittled down. And then the vice president showed up at about 5:15 p.m. We were pushing the envelope to be able to turn it around for the top of the 6 p.m.. So that’s how it started,” Baier said.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Defiant JD Vance Says ‘No,’ Trump Did Not Lose 2020 Election
items.content_text:
Republican vice presidential candidate JD Vance boldly said “no,” Donald Trump did not lose the 2020 election, when pressed on the issue at a campaign event Wednesday in Williamsport, Pennsylvania.

The Ohio senator has avoided directly denying the results over the past few weeks.

When quizzed by The New York Times about the results over the weekend, for example, he refused multiple times to answer the question, on one occasion claiming he was “focused on the future”—echoing an answer he gave to Democratic opponent Tim Walz at the vice presidential debate.

items.title: Liam Payne Was Embroiled in Bitter Legal Fight With Ex When He Died
items.content_text:
Prior to his untimely death in Argentina on Wednesday, One Direction’s Liam Payne, 31, was in the middle of a legal spat with his ex-fiancée Maya Henry.

On Monday, The Sun reported that Henry, 23, had lawyered up in an attempt to stop Payne from constantly messaging her family and friends.

“Maya Henry issued a cease and desist last week to Liam Payne following the emergence of new and concerning information…She has retained attorneys Marco Crawford and Daniel Cerna to represent her. At this time, that is her only comment on the matter,” a spokesperson for Henry told the tabloid.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Harris Shuts Down Bret Baier as He Plays the MAGA Hits
items.content_text:
In a contentious interview with Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris, Fox News host Bret Baier spent no time going after the vice president with a laundry list of the subjects often highlighted by former President Donald Trump on the campaign trail.

Immediately after the interview kicked off, Baier opened by asking: “How many illegal immigrants would you estimate your administration has released into the country over the last three and a half years?”

Harris began a carefully worded answer, but Baier consistently interrupted her before she could finish a sentence.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Watch Liam Payne’s Phenomenal ‘X-Factor’ Audition That Made Him a Star
items.content_text:
A collective gasp echoed like a thunderclap in a valley in our Daily Beast newsroom late Wednesday afternoon at the news that singer Liam Payne, who became famous as a member of the group One Direction, died at age 31.

TMZ reports that Payne fell from a hotel balcony in Argentina, where he had reunited with bandmates at 1D-er Niall Horan’s concert. He had, according to the site, been behaving “erratically,” earlier in the day, and was spotted smashing a laptop in the hotel lobby and having to be carried back to his room. He had been in headlines on gossip blogs over tension with his ex-fiancée Maya Henry, who, TMZ says, alleged “he'd left her after asking her to get an abortion.”

In the shock of his death, fans couldn’t ignore the eerie nature that Payne had just connected with his One Direction bandmates. Dark questions emerge when a celebrity dies so young: What role did the often horrific toll of fame have on a person like Payne, who has been open about addiction and suicidal ideation? But there’s also an impulse to go back to the roots of a person’s talent, to revisit what it was that we all fell in love with—and was their passion—in the first place.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Billionaire Bill Ackman Admits Debate Conspiracy He Pushed Is Fake
items.content_text:
Billionaire Bill Ackman spent days after the ABC presidential debate promoting false claims that a network “whistleblower” had allegedly uncovered collusion between ABC and Kamala Harris’ campaign. Now, a month and multiple denials later, he sees the claims differently.

“It seems pretty clear that the alleged @abc whistleblower debate story claiming that @KamalaHarris was given questions in advance and other advantages was a fake,” Ackman posted on X alongside a blog post by Megyn Kelly discussing the dubious claims.

What Ackman, CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management, did not acknowledge, however, is that he was one of falsehood’s early boosters. After an X account named “Black Insurrectionist” claimed it had been in touch with a whistleblower who alleged the Harris campaign had been given debate topics ahead of the showdown with Donald Trump and had demanded Trump—and Trump alone—be fact-checked.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: CNN’s Stars Get Massive Salaries Frozen as Bosses Sharpen Ax
items.content_text:

That’s according to The Ankler, which reported Wednesday that 77-year-old Chris Wallace—whose already been relegated to a weekend program—is among the network’s most well-known names whose future is in limbo.

Wallace’s $8.5 million contract, signed by the ex-CNN boss Jeff Zucker to recruit him away from Fox News three years ago, is reportedly up and he was spotted in CEO Mark Thompson’s office on Tuesday.

items.title: One Direction Star Liam Payne Dead After Fall in Argentina
items.content_text:
Liam Payne, a former member of the boy band One Direction, was found dead in a hotel courtyard in Buenos Aires, Argentina on Wednesday evening, according to CNN and La Nacion, both of which cited local police.

The singer died after an apparent fall from the balcony of his third-floor hotel room. Argentinian authorities told Good Morning America that Payne had been staying at the hotel CasaSur in the upscale neighborhood of Palermo.

He was 31.

items.title: Kamala’s GOP Posse Predicts ‘Hidden Harris’ Victory
items.content_text:
WASHINGTON CROSSING, Pennsylvania—At a campaign rally in the most important swing state in the country, anti-Trump activist George Conway told the Daily Beast why he thinks Kamala Harris can win over Republicans.

“She’s kind of done it already,” he said. “Look at all those people who voted for [Nikki] Haley when she was already done. I actually think there’s kind of a hidden Harris vote for Republicans who are just exhausted by Donald Trump.”

Turnout is another factor that plays to Democrat’s advantage, Conway predicted. “I also think that even the people who are still for Trump and won’t vote for Harris, I don’t think the turnout’s going to be great for him.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

A 社的 Agent 工时是人类的六倍，为啥开的会却越来越多了？

上午看了 Anthropic 刚发布的内部人员工作变化的研究报告，挺有意思。

它结合了人员、招聘、Agent 日志和日历等数据，包括 17 位员工的访谈，试图研究 AI 是怎样改变工作的。

截至 8 月，A 社员工使用的交互式 Agent 运行时长，达到人类工时的约六倍。与此同时，员工开会时间的中位数，也比一年前增加了约 20%。技术岗的会议时间同样增加了 16%。
